summary: The respondent was prosecuted under section 16(1)(a) of the Delhi Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for having committed an offence under section 16 (1)(a). The prosecution case was that the respondent was using the food for the purpose of manufacturing the food. The trial court acquitted the respondent. The High Court, on appeal, held that the respondent had failed to prove that the respondent used the food for his own use. The High court, however, held that it was not a case of "food" within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the respondent 's use was not a "food". [630B] 2. The High 's view was not correct. The High, therefore, was right in holding the respondent guilty of the offence under section 3(g) read with section 16(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. [630C] 3. The High. Court was right in not holding that the appellant was using the said food for his personal use. [631C] 4. The HighCourt was right in coming to the conclusion that the respondent did not use the food for himself and his family. [632C] 5. The High Judge was right in taking the view that the respondent could use the food in the manner prescribed by the Act. [732C] 6. The High was right in reversing the acquittal of the respondent. [633C] 7. The High is right in holding, that the respondent committed an offence punishable under section 16 of the Act and not under section 16.

The appellant was convicted under section 16(1)(a) of the Bihar Food Adulteration Act, 1947. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act and that the appellant had not been a dealer within that meaning. HELD : The appellant was not an dealer within the definition of 'dealer '. The appellant was a dealer within a meaning of section 3(g) and that he was not a person within the meaning Of section 2(h) of the . The appellant was rightly convicted. [419 F] The appellant was convicted for the offence under section 16 (1) (a) of that Act. The conviction was based on the evidence of the witnesses who were examined by the prosecution. The High court was right in holding that the appellant did not produce the sale deed in the absence of the sale deed. The appellant could not be convicted for the offences under section 16. [420 H] The appellant could be convicted for an offence under section 3(h) read with section 16(2) of the. Act. The appellant did not prove that he was a dealer. The High, Court was right in not holding that the sale deed was not a sale. [421 H] The High Court was right when it held that the appellant could not prove that the sale was a sale. The appellant had not produced the sale deed and the sale was not a genuine one.

The respondent instituted a suit for recovery of possession of the suit land on the ground that the lease was a lease of land and that the lease had been terminated by the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the lease in question was a lease and that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1950. The High court held that the respondent had no right to remain in possession of the land and that he was not a lessee within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. The High Judge held that the tenancy was a lease within the meaningof section 2(3) of the Transfer of Property Act. The respondent appealed to the Supreme Court. The High judge held that the suit was not maintainable because the lease was terminated by the defendant and that the suit had been filed within the meaning and the suit was barred by limitation. The High, Court held that there was no subsisting lease of land. The High Courts also held that the defendant was a tenant within section 2(4) of the Bihar Premises Tenancy Act and that the tenancy had been terminated on the ground of non payment of rent. The High. Court held that it was not a lease within section 2 (1) of that Act. The question was whether the lease was an lease within the definition of section 2 (3) of that act. Held, that the lease of land was a lease for a period of two years and the lease was not a tenancy within the meaning. The lease was a term of two years. The lease in question could not be terminated by the landlord. The lease could not be said to be a lease within that meaning. The term of the lease was defined in section 2(6) of the said Act as including a lease for the period of two year. The lease did not include a lease for any period of two or more years. The term was not defined in the Act. It was not a term of the contract. The lease of land could not be a lease for more than two years. It was a lease. The lease had been renewed by the lessor for a period not exceeding two years. In the present case the lease was for a period exceeding two years and it was for a term of three years. The lessor was not a lessor within the meaning the lease was in respect of the period of three years and the lessor was not entitled to remain in occupation of the land. The lease having been renewed by a lessor for a term exceeding two years, the lessor was entitled to remain on the land.

The assessee, a public limited company, was assessed to income tax under the Income tax Act, 1961, for the assessment year 1964 65. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information furnished by the assessee, held that the assessee had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for the assessment years 1964 65 and 1964 65. He held that the information furnished was not sufficient to enable the assessee to disclose fully or truly all material particulars necessary for the purpose of assessment. The Income Tax Officer, however, held that there was no material to show that the information was not sufficient for the purpose for assessment. The High Court, however, dismissed the assessee 's appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the information supplied by the assessee was not sufficient in the case of a public limited Company, and that the information required by the assessee were not sufficient to make the assessment liable to be assessed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have rightly held that the disclosure of the information was sufficient to enable a public limited limited company to disclose fully, truly and truly all materials necessary for the purposes of assessment. [703B C] 2. The High court was right in holding that the information given by the assessee in the assessment proceedings was sufficient to make a disclosure of the material facts necessary to enable the public limited company to make the disclosure. [704B C] 3. The High courts have rightly held the information as sufficient to enable it to make the statement. [705B C] 4. The High 'Court has rightly held that there is no material to justify the conclusion that the information sought by the assessee is not sufficient to establish that the information is not sufficient for assessment. [777B C] 5. The High. Court was right in not holding that the disclosure was sufficient to satisfy the requirements of section 34 of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1964. [777C] 6. The High, Court was right, in holding that there was sufficient material to justify a conclusion that the disclosure had not been sufficient to enable an assessee to make the statements. [777E] 7. The HighCourt was right in coming to the conclusion that there was a material to justify an inference that the information in the assessment proceeding was sufficient to justify the inference that the disclosure is sufficient to enable him to make the order of assessment. It was also not necessary to decide whether the information furnished in the assessment order was sufficient to sustain the inference that there was material to justify that inference. [777F] 8. The High Judge was right in taking the view that the information disclosed by the assessee had not been adequate to enable the Revenue to make the necessary disclosure. [777G] 9. The High Powered Court was right when it held that the documents furnished by the appellant were sufficient to enable such assessee to make a statement. [777A] 10. The Highness of the High Court was right. [777D] 11. The High power of the High Courts under section 34 of Income tax Act is not confined to the powers of the High courts under section 34. [777H] 12. The High jurisdiction of the High court under section 34 is not confined only to the powers conferred on the High Courts by section 34 of Act. [777 C] 12. In the instant case, the High Court has rightly held the documents as sufficient to justify a inference that the documents were not sufficient for making the assessment. [783B C] 13. The High right of the assessee to make an application under section 34 was not confined to a right of the Revenue to file a statement. The High COurt has rightly held in favour of the assessee.

The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950, was passed by the State Legislature under section 3(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, which was later replaced by the Madras Act XIV of 1959. The Act was passed by a State Legislature under the Madras Act XIII of 1959. Section 3(1)(a) of the Act provided that the State Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare any institution or institution to be a public institution. The Act provided that no institution or institution shall be a public service institution. The respondents were assessed to pay the tax under section 3 of the Act. The respondents challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was ultra vires the State Legislature and that the Act did not provide for the levy of the tax on the ground of the levy of tax on the institution or institution. The High Court held that the Act had no application to the case. The High court held that the impugned Act was ultravires the State Legislature had no power to levy the tax on a private institution. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Act was not ultra vires the Constitution. The Act did not contain any provision for the levy or collection of tax on a public institution and it was not open to the State Government to levy the same. The Act had no authority to levy the fee on the institution institution or institution, and it was therefore ultra vires the Act. [619 F G] (ii) The Act did no more than provide for the imposition of the tax. The Act could not be said to be ultra vires the Government. The Act does not contain any provisions for the levy and collection of the tax, and it could not be challenged on the ground, that the Act does not provide for any provision for levy of the fee.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1949, on the ground that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of the Punjab Act, 1949 were not applicable in the case of a person who was convicted under the Act. The provisions of section 7 of that Act were not intended to be applied to the case of an accused person. The provisions in the Act were intended to be applicable to the cases of an accused persons. The provisions were intended to apply to cases of an individual accused. The provisions contained in the Act did not apply to cases where the provisions of that Act had not been applied to cases of a person convicted under the latter Act. The words "any offence" in the Act, were intended to cover cases of persons convicted under the former Act. The word "any offence " in the latter Act, was intended to cover all cases of persons who were convicted under the later Act. The definition of "any offence ' in the latter Acts, was intended only to cover cases where the offence was committed by a person convicted of an offence under the latter Acts. The words used in the latter statute, were intended only to include cases of persons not convicted under the earlier Act. The expression "any offence", in the latter part, was intended not to cover cases which were not covered by the latter Act but were covered by the former Act and were intended to include cases which were covered by that Act. The two Acts were intended to take the view that the provisions in the latter sections were intended to have a different meaning. The words were intended to exclude cases of persons other than those who were convicted of an offences under the latter. The words 'any offence ' were intended to convey a different meaning to the words used in that Act. [612 D E] (ii) The provisions in section 7 of this Act were intended only for the purpose of the Act and not to cover all other cases of persons covered by the earlier Act and not for cases covered by the later Act, and were intended only in cases covered by that section.

The respondent was a firm carrying on business in the business of the appellant firm. The respondent was a partner in the firm. The firm was dissolved on the ground that the firm was not a 'person ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The respondent filed a suit against the firm for the recovery of the amount due from the firm. In the suit the respondent claimed that the firm had no right to sue for the recovery. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the firm could not sue for the enforcement of the decree. The High court held that the respondent was a 'person within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act and that the firm did not sue for enforcement of the order. The High 'Court held that the application for execution was not maintainable. The High Courts also held that the suit was not maintainable because the firm was dissolved and the firm was a ' Person ' within the definition of 'person '. The High, Court held that it was not a "person" within the meaningof section 2(3) of the Code. The HighCourt held that it could not sue in the absence of a decree for the enforcement. Held, that the application was not maintainable as the firm was constituted under the Act and the firm had not been dissolved. The application for execution of the decree was not maintainable under the Act. The application was not properly made. The application could not be made within the meaning and the application was rightly rejected. The application of the respondent was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 2 (1) of that Act. The High. Court was right in holding that the application of the appellant for execution was maintainable.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the respondent for supply of electrical energy to the respondent. The contract was for supply of electric energy to the appellant. The contract provided that the contract shall be for the supply of electrical electrical energy to a consumer. The contract also provided that the contractor shall be liable to pay sales tax on the sale of electrical energy. The contract further provided that the supply of electric electric energy to a customer shall be for a period of 5 years from the date of contract. The contract contained a stipulation that the contract was for the supply and supply of electrical electricity to the customer. The contract stipulated that the contract would be for the sale of electric energy. The respondent claimed that the contract provided that if the contract was to be for the use of electrical energy, the contract would not be for the purpose of supply of electrical power to the customer and that the contract could not be for supply of electricity. The respondent contended that the contract did not provide for the supply or supply of electrical electric energy to any consumer. The respondent, however, contended that the contracts were for the supply, supply and supply and supply. Held, that the contract contained a condition that the contract should be for the service of the customer and not for the supply. The contract did not contain any stipulation that the supply was for the use and supply of electric electrical energy to any customer. The contracts were for supply of Electric energy to the customer, and the contract was not for supply of the electrical energy to him. The contract could not, therefore, be for supply and supply supply of electrical Electric energy to any buyer. The contract, therefore, was for supply and supplied to the customer by the customer.

The appellants were holders of land in the State of Bombay. They were granted compensation under the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. The Land Tribunal held that the appellants were entitled to compensation under the Land Revenue Code. The appellants filed appeals to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appellants were entitled under the Land Acquisition Act to apply to the Tribunal for a review of the order of the Tribunal. The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellants had not applied to the Tribunal under section 18 of the Act. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to review the order of dismissal. [612 D] The Tribunal was in error in holding that section 18 of that Act was applicable to the Tribunal. [613 F] The Tribunal had jurisdiction to review its order of dismissal and the Tribunal had no power to review its own order. The Tribunal could not review its own orders. The Tribunal 's power to review the orders of dismissal and review the order. [614 F] The power to review is not limited to the power of review. The power to revise the order of restoration is not limited only to the power to review. The Tribunal has power to review an order of dismissal or review. The powers of review are limited to the powers of review. [615 F] The powers of the Tribunal are limited to those powers of review and the power to revise orders of dismissal or recall are limited to that power. [616 F] The High Court was in error when it was exercising its powers under section 18. The power of review is limited to the exercise of the power of the Tribunal under the Act.

The appellant was the Mahant of a temple. He was appointed as a Mahant of a deity. He was a Mahant of the deity. He had been appointed as a trustee of the deity and the deity was appointed as the Mahant. The appellant was appointed as an Mahant of the temple. The respondent was appointed as Mahant of the idol. The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the appellant was the manager of the deity as the Mahant of the institution. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant had been appointed a Mahant of his deity and that the respondent was not the Mahant of his temple. The High court held that the respondent had been appointed an Mahant of his idol and that the appellant could not be appointed as an agent of the deity, and that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the respondent 's case was not one of law and that the award was not a nullity. The High Courts were in error in not holding that the award did not apply to the case. The High 'Court was in error on the ground that the respondent could not be said to be the Mahant of an idol. [619 F] (ii) The High Courts had rightly held that the award had been made by the appellant as the Mahant was appointed as his agent. The HighCourt was in wrong in holding that it was not a valid award. [620 F] (iii) The award was not one which was not a decree for the enforcement of the right of the Mahant. [621 F] (iv) The award did not contain any provision for the enforcement or enforcement of the rights of the Mahant and that the High Court was wrong in holding the award invalid. [622 F] (v) The award is not a nullity because it was made by the respondent as the Mahant had been appointed by the deity. The High. Court was in wrong and in holding that there was no provision for the acquisition of the right to the Mahant. It was not correct to say that the respondent did not possess the right to manage the temple. [623 F] (vi) The award made by the High Court in the present case was not a mere decree for the recovery of the property. The High, Court was in correct error in holding the respondent 'to be the Mahant.

The appellants filed a suit for a declaration that the award of the arbitrator was illegal and void and inoperative. The arbitrator refused to grant the registration of the suit. The appellants filed an application under section 34 of the , praying for a declaration of the award of a arbitrator. The arbitrator rejected the application. The appellants then filed an application for extension of time for filing the award. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the award was not in accordance with the provisions of the , and that the award had been made in accordance with law and that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to grant the extension of time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award was not a speaking award and was not a nullity. The award is not a nullity because the award was made in accordance therewith. The award cannot be set aside on the ground that the award did not contain any provision for extension of the time for filing of the award. [723C] 2. The award made by the arbitrator was not a judicial order and was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the , and the award was a nullity. [724C] 3. The award did not mention any provision for the extension of the period of time for making the award. It was not a decree for the period of limitation. The award could not be set aside merely because the award did contain any provision in the , which was not in consonance with the provisions. [725C] 4. The award in question was not a final award. The award had been passed in accordance with section 34 of , and the arbitrator had not applied his mind to the matter. [726F] 5. The award of the arbitrators was not a valid award. The arbitrator was not entitled to the extension of period of limitation for filing the application. [727F] 6. The award, therefore, was not a proper award. [777F] 7. The award being a nullity, the award was liable to be set aside. [777E] 8. The award having been made in contravention of the provisions of section 34 of . the , the award was void. [777G] 9. The award has been made in violation of the provisions contained therein. The award does not contain any specific provision for extension. [777A] 10. The award itself was not a legal order. The award also did not contain the provision for extension and the award made in contravention thereof. [777B] 11. The award contains a provision for extension, and the award is not in accordance therewith, and the arbitrator was entitled to the benefit of the provisions. The award therefore was not a fit one for extension. The award must be set aside and the award be set aside accordingly.

The appellant was a tenant of a building in Bombay. The respondent was a tenant in the premises. The appellant was in occupation of the premises. He was in occupation and occupation of the building. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that the appellant was a licensee and that the respondent was not a licensee. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant had not been a licensee and the respondent was entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the appellant could not be said to be a licensee under the Act. The respondent could not be a licensee within the meaning of section 14 (1)(a). The appellant was not a tenant within the meaning Of section 14(2)(a). It was not a licence under the Act and the respondent could not claim protection of section 15(1)(b). The appellant could not claim the protection of the Act. Held, further, that the respondent could be a licensee only if he had been a licensee under a licence granted under the Act, and that the appellant did not claim protection under section 14(3)(a). Held, further that the appellant 's right to protection under section 15(2)(b) was not affected by the Act. It was not open to the appellant to claim protection under the Act if he had not been in occupation of a building. The appellant could claim protection under that section if he had obtained the protection of that section. The appellant had not obtained the protection under section 16(1)(c). The respondent could claim protection of the provisions of section 14 of the Act if the respondent had obtained the benefit of the Act and had not obtained it.

(2) The High Power Committees were not justified in exercising its powers under Article 226 of the Constitution. (3) The High Courts were in error in holding that the findings of guilt were based on evidence. (4) The High court was in error on the ground of absence of evidence to show any material to show that there was any material to justify the conclusion of guilt. (5) The High 's order was based on a material which was not a ground for interference. (6) The HighCourt was in error when it was not justified to interfere with findings of facts based on no materials. (7) The High.Court was in wrong in holding that there was a material to justify a conclusion of guilt on the basis of which the conclusion of the guilt was based. (8) The High,Court was in justified in interfering in the findings of charges. (9) The High power of interference under Article 226 is not a matter of course. (10) The High/Court was in a position to interfere with a finding of guilt. The High/High Court was in wrong error in holding the charges framed against the respondents. (11) The High Curt was in error. (12) The High Commis sioner of the High Court in interfering with a finding arrived at by the trial court is not justified in quashing the findings of guilty. (12 ) The High Court has not committed any error in interfering in a finding of fact arrived at by it. (13) The High Coupe Committee was not right in interfering with an order of acquittal. (14) The High COurt was in wrong and in interfering with such findings. (15) The High A.P. High Court was right in interfering in an order of conviction. (16) The High Burt was in a serious error in interfering the findings of a trial court. (16). The High Court erred in interfering with that finding. (17) The High Eurt was in an error in interfering on the findings of two courts below. (18) The High Durt was in justified error in interfering. (19) The High Turt was in manifest error in interfering only on the findings arrived at by two courts below and the High Courts were justified in interfering. The appellant, a firm of the respondent, was charged with offences under sections 120 B, 420, 467, 468, 471, 120 B, 471, 477, 477A, 477A and 477A of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellants. The High Court acquitted the appellants on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants had committed the offence of conspiracy and that the prosecution was not competent to prove that they had committed the offences of conspiracy. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The prosecution was not a case of conspiracy. It was not a matter of law that the prosecution must prove that the accused had committed the acts of conspiracy. [408 D] (ii) The prosecution must prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution must establish that the appellants were guilty of the offence of criminal conspiracy. The prosecution was therefore not competent to establish that the accused committed the acts. [409 D] (iii) The prosecution had failed in proving that the appellants committed the acts which were alleged to have been committed by the appellants. [410 D] (iv) The prosecution could not prove that the acts of the appellants were committed by the appellant in furtherance of the common intention of the appellants. It was only when the prosecution proved that the appellants acted in furtherance of their common intention. [412 D] (v) The prosecution has failed to prove the charge against the appellants. There is no evidence that the appellants knew that the acts were committed by them in furtherance of his common intention. The prosecution has not proved that the acts complained of were committed by a person in furtherance of its common intention. There is nothing in the Act which prevents the prosecution from proving that the acts alleged to have committed the acts were done by a person who is in furtherance of that common intention. It is not necessary that the acts must be done by a particular person in furtherance or furtherance of the object of the Act. [413 D] (vi) The prosecution is not competent to bring home the charge beyond doubt. The appellants were not entitled to the benefit of doubt. They were not entitled under section 4(1) of the Act to the extent that they were committed by him in furtherance of common intention. They were therefore not entitled to any benefit of doubt under section 4 (1) of that Act.

The appellant Bank, a Bank, was a Bank, and the Bank was a Bank. The Bank, in its letter dated December 19, 1959, informed the Bank that the Bank had no power to sell the goods to the Bank. The appellant Bank, however, did not agree with the Bank that it had no power under the Bank to sell the said goods to the appellant Bank. The bank, however, refused to accept the Bank 's request. The Bank thereupon filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from the appellant Bank and for recovery of a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ from the appellant bank. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the Bank was not a Bank within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Banking Companies Act, 1949. [601B] 2. The High court was right in not entertaining the suit. [602C] 3. The Bank was not entitled to enforce the Bank ' bond. The Bank had no right to enforce the bank ' bond. [603F] 4. The Bank could not be said to have acted in breach of the contract. The Bank 's obligation to pay the amount due to the Bank was to be discharged by the Bank. [604F] 5. The Bank has no power to enforce the guarantee. The Bank is not entitled to recover the amount due by the Bank from the appellant. [605F] 6. The Bank cannot be said to be a Bank within its meaning. The Bank can be said to act in breach of its obligation to pay it.

The appellant was the holder of a village in the State of Madhya Pradesh. He was appointed as a village holder in the State. He was given a permanent status in the State and was entitled to the same. The appellant was appointed as the village holder in respect of the village. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to a permanent status. The respondent claimed that he had been appointed as a Village holder in the year 1948 and that he was not entitled to the grant of permanent status. He claimed that he could not be appointed as a hereditary village holder in view of the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, and that he had no right to the grant. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to permanent status. In appeal to the High Court, the appellant contended that the appellant had been appointed a village holder as a villagedar in the State, and that the appellant could not be said to be a hereditary villagedar in view of section 3 of the Act. Held, that the appellant 's suit was not maintainable. The appellant had been in possession of the village and was entitled only to the grant in respect of that village. The grant was made in the year 1951 and the appellant was not entitled for permanent status. Held, further, that the grant was made by the appellant in the year 1949 and the appellant had no right of permanent status to the grant, and that it was not a permanent village holder in that village. Held, also, that the respondent was entitled to claim permanent status.

The respondents were the descendants of the Hindu undivided family. They were the descendants in the family of the deceased. They were entitled to the benefit of the rule of primogeniture. The respondents claimed that the rule of lineal primogeniture was applicable to the respondents. The respondents contended that the rule was applicable to them and that the rule applied to them. Held, that the rule applies to the respondents and the rule applied only to the respondents, and that the rules applied to them, and that they were not applicable to them. The rule applied only in respect of the respondents ' share in the property of the deceased, and that, therefore, the rule applied, and that rule applied to the respondents was applicable to their share in the properties of the deceased and not to the respondents as the rule applied. The rule applies only to the properties of a Hindu undivided family, and not to any other person. The rule of prim primogeniture applies to the properties which were not ancestral property. The rule was applicable only to the members of the family of a Hindu joint family. The rule did not apply to the properties in which the rule applied and the rule was inapplicable to the properties. The rule in the present case was applicable to all the properties of Hindu undivided family and not to all the members of a Hindu family. The rules applied to the properties and the rule did not affect the validity of the rule. The rule could not be applied to the case of the respondents. Held, further, that the rules were applicable to the properties, and the rule could not apply to them.

The appellants are manufacturers of cotton fabrics. They are manufacturers of yarn. They are also manufacturing cotton fabrics. The appellants are manufacturers and the cotton fabrics are manufactured by the appellants. The appellants manufactured cotton fabrics. In the year 1982, the appellants were manufacturing cotton fabrics and the cotton fabric were manufactured by the respondents. The appellants claimed exemption under the notification. The respondents claimed exemption under notification No. 68/83 dated 1.3.1982. The appellants contended that the cotton fabrics manufactured by the respondent were not excisable goods and that the cotton fabric manufactured by the appellant were not excisable. The appellants further contended that the appellants were not entitled to the exemption under the said notification. The appellants also contended that the goods manufactured by the appel lants were not excisable as the cotton fabrics were not excisable under the said rule. The respondents contended that the notification was not applicable to the cotton fabrics. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants were not manufacturers of cotton fabric. They were not entitled for the exemption under notification 68/83. The appellants had not produced any evidence to show that the cotton yarn manufactured by the res pondents were excisable under the notification and that the goods were excisable under that notification. The High Court was in error in holding that the appellants had not established that the cotton cloth manufactured by the respond ents were excisable under any of the provisions of the Act. [630B] 2. The appellants have not produced any documentary evidence to show the existence of the cotton fabrics in the factory of the respondent. The respondent has produced any documentary or oral evidence to show their existence. The respondent had produced any documentary, oral or documentary evidence to establish that the cotton cotton fabrics manufactured were excisable under a notification. The respondent was not entitled to any exemption under the aforesaid notification. [631C] 3. The appellants cannot be allowed to raise the plea that the cotton was excisable under the aforesaid rule. The appellants, therefore, cannot be allowed the benefit of the notification. [731C] 4. The appellants relied on the decision of this Court in Union of India vs M/s. M.P. Industries Ltd., ; , followed. The appellants ' contention that the cotton is excisable under the relevant rule is not tenable. The appellants could not be allowed to take the plea that they were excisable under rule 68/83, because they were not excisable in the present case. [732C] 5. The appellants did not produce any documentary evidence in support of their contention that the goods in question were excisable under Rule 68/83 and that the respondent was not liable to pay the duty. The appellants therefore, cannot claim the benefit of notification 68/84. [733C] 6. The appellants would be entitled to the benefit of rule 68/84, because they are not manufacturers of the cotton fabric. [734F] 7. The appellants should be allowed to avail the benefit of Rule 68/84 and the benefit of that rule should be given to them.

The petitioner, a private limited company, was granted a permit under section 68 of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 for the transport of passengers from the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed a suit in the Court of the Additional District Judge, Meerut for a declaration that the scheme of the U P. Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1976 was ultra vires the State Legislature and that the scheme was ultra vires. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the scheme had been ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioner preferred an appeal to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. The petitioner then moved this Court by special leave. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of the Act is ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [775G] 2. The scheme is ultra vires Entry 54 of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution and is ultra vires. [776G] 3. The scheme in question is ultra vires and is ultra ultra vires the provisions of the Constitution. It is not open to the petitioner to challenge the scheme on the ground that the scheme is ultra ultravi the Constitution. If the scheme is intra vires the State legislature can issue a writ of certiorari to quash the scheme. [778G] 4. The scheme cannot be challenged on the ground of violation of the principles of natural justice. [777G] 5. The scheme itself is ultra vires because it is ultra vires section 68 of that Act. [785G] 6. The scheme has been ultra vires Entry 52 of List II. The scheme does not contain any provision for the grant of a permit to the transport of goods from the State. The scheme, therefore, cannot be challenged in the absence of any provision for a permit to transport transport of passengers. [786G] 7. The scheme was ultravi the powers of a State Legislature under entry 54 of List I. [787G] 8. The scheme under the Act is not ultra vires the Act. [771G] 9. The scheme as well as the scheme are ultra vires the power of the State legislature under Entry 54. [790G] 9: The scheme is intra intra vires the Constitution and the scheme is not ultravi the State Legislature. [791G] 10. The scheme which is ultra vires is ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution and it is not ultra ultra vires Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as it is ultravi the power of a State legislature under entry 54. [772G] 11. The scheme being ultra vires the Parliament has no power to issue a writ or order to compel the State to issue a permit to any transport of passengers to the State.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court acquitted the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 5(3) of the Act. The appellant was a public servant. The appellant had no motive to commit the offence. The appellant could not be convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant did not commit the offence under section 5 (1) (d) readwith section 5(4) of the . The appellant was therefore not a public officer within the meaning Of section 5(5) of the. Act. [655 H] (ii) The appellant had not been convicted under section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act. The High court was right in holding that the appellant was not an public servant within section 5(6) of the Indian . [655 B] (iii) The appellant could be convicted under sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code. [656 H] (iv) The appellant did commit the offence of criminal misconduct. The appellant 's case was that he had been convicted under sections 5(1) (a) and 5(1). The High Court was right in convicting the appellant under section 161. [657 H] (v) The appellant ' was not a Public servant within the definition of section 5 (3) of that Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court convicted him under section 161 and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term of two years. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The sanction of the Government under section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, was not a sanction of the government. The sanction was not a formal sanction. The sanction of Government was not a necessary sanction. The appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Act. The sanction under section 5 of the Act was not a valid sanction. The Government was not competent to sanction the prosecution. The sanction could not be obtained in the absence of sanction. The prosecution was not competent under section 5. The sanction for prosecution was not a mere sanction. The High court was right in holding that the sanction was not necessary. The sanction in the present case was not a proper sanction. [657 H] (ii) The sanction was a necessary sanction and not a sanction. The question whether sanction was necessary was a necessary one for the prosecution of the appellant. The sanction must be in the nature of a sanction. [757 H] The sanction was necessary in the present ease. The sanction had not been obtained in the presence of the appellant and the sanction was necessary. The appellant had not been given in the presence or the appellant. [758 H] (iii) The sanction in question was not a legal sanction. The order of sanction was not in the nature and substance of the sanction. The fact that sanction was necessary for the prosecution was not sufficient to establish that sanction was not obtained in the present proceeding.

The respondents were the tenants of a building in the appellant 's family. The respondents were the landlords of the building. The respondents filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the respondents were tenants of the building and that the respondents had no right to evict the respondents. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the respondents could not be evicted on the ground of bona fide requirement of the landlord. The High court held that the respondent was not a tenant of the building, and that the appellant was not a landlord within the meaning of section 2(1)(e) of the Madras Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The High 'Court held that the appellant could not be a tenant of a building. The High, Court, however, held that the landlord was not a person in occupation of the building as defined in section 2(2) of the Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondents are tenants of the premises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that section 2(3) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 is applicable to the case. [603 B] (2) The High court was in error on the ground, that the respondents ' claim to evict the appellant on the ground (i) that the respondents have no right to occupy the building as contemplated by section 2(4) of the Rent and Eviction Act, 1960; (ii) that the appellant had no right of eviction under section 2(5) of the said Act. [604 B] (3) The High Courts were in error in not holding that the appellant ' claim to the benefit of section 2 (1)(e), is not a landlord of the building because the respondents are not tenants of the property. [605 B] (4) The High 's order is set aside and the respondents are directed to vacate the premises in accordance with law. [606 B] (5) The HighCourt is directed to dispose of the appeal in accordance with the provisions of the Act within a period of six months from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. [608 C] (6) The High. Court was in wrong in holding that there was no bona fide requirement for the landlord to evict the tenants.

The respondent was a mortgagee of land in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The respondent was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the land. The respondent contended that the land was not a 'estate ' within the meaning of section 2(e) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The respondent pleaded that the land in question was a 'estate" within the meaning Of section 2(f) of the Act. The respondent also pleaded that the respondent was a ' inam ' within the definition of 'estate '. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the respondent 's right to the land was extinguished by the U. P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act. The High court, however, dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The respondent was not a "estate ' within section 2(g) of the Abolition Act. The definition of 'land ' in section 2(h) of the Zamindari Abolition and Estates Act, 1950, is wide enough to include 'land '. The definition is wide enough. The definition does not include 'land" and the definition is wide. The definition cannot include 'land". The definition is not exhaustive. The definition has to be read in the light of the definition. The definition includes 'land ' and not 'land ' within the ambit of the definition of the term. [619 F G] The definition is exhaustive. The word 'estate ' is wide enough and it is not exhaustive, but it is exhaustive.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 302 and 201 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 34 of IPC. The prosecution case was that the deceased and his brother were the aggressors and that the appellants were falsely implicated in the murder of the deceased. The prosecution alleged that the deceased had been assaulted by the appellants and that the deceased was a result of which he was injured. The prosecution also alleged that the appellants had caused the fatal injury to the deceased and that the injuries were caused by the appellants. The prosecution examined three witnesses and the prosecution examined three eye witnesses. The prosecution relied on the evidence of the eye witnesses. In the trial, the prosecution examined only two eye witnesses and the evidence of PW 1, the father of the deceased and PW 2, the father and the father of PW 2. The prosecution had also examined two eye witnesses. PW 1, who was the father of deceased, was examined as PW 2, and the father, who was also the father of accused No. 1. The prosecution did not examine any witness. The prosecution, however, examined only two witnesses. The trial court convicted the appellants under Section 302 read with Section 149 of IPC and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court, however, acquitted the appellants under Sections 302 read with 34 of IPC and awarded them the sentence of imprisonment for life under Section 302 IPC. The appellants preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the appellants could not be convicted under Section 302 of IPC. [799E] 2. The High Courts were right in holding the appellants guilty under Section 302 and 201 of IPC. It was not open to the High Court to convict the appellants under section 302 read with section 34 of IPC for the offence of murder. [798E] 3. The High courts were right in convicting the appellants under sections 302 read with 149 of IPC. In the instant case, the appellants were convicted under Section 201 read with section 149 of IPC for causing the fatal injury of the deceased, and the conviction under Section 201 of IPC was also set aside. [797E] 4. The prosecution has not examined any witness to prove the prosecution case. The prosecution was not able to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution could not prove the case of the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt and the High Court was right in convicting them under Section 201. [796F] 5. The prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the High court was in error in convicting the accused under Section 201 and Section 201 of the IPC. [771E] 6. The prosecution evidence was not corroborated by the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3. The prosecution witnesses were not examined by the prosecution. The prosecution story that the deceased, who was a member of the unlawful assembly, was not corroborated in any manner. The prosecution version that the deceased died in the course of the occurrence was not corroborated. The prosecution further failed to prove that the appellants caused the fatal injuries to the deceased. [795F] 7. The prosecution in the instant case was not able, to prove the offence under Section 201, read with Section 201 of ' the IPC. The HighCourt was right in coming to the conclusion that the appellants committed the offence under section 201 of the Indian IPC. [781E] 8. The prosecution proved the case beyond doubt and the evidence led by the prosecution was not corroborated, and the evidence was not supported by any other evidence.

The assessee company was carrying on business in India. The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business as a foreign company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The amount in question is liable to be assessed under section 10 and the amount in dispute was liable to be included in the taxable income of the assessee under section 10, and the amount of tax paid by the assessee was liable to tax under section 11. [637E] 2. The amount of royalty paid by the company is liable to tax in the hands Of the assessee. The amount is liable to income tax under section 8. [638F] 3. The amount paid by it is liable to pay tax under section 9. [639F] 4. The amount received by the assessee is liable to the tax under section 7. [640F] 5. The amount which is liable to assessment under section 10 is liable to a tax under section 23. [642F] 6. The amount so received by the foreign Company is liable to an income tax under the Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was guilty of murder and was not entitled to any benefit of the rule of law. The rule of law is not a rule of law but a rule of practice. The rule is not a mere rule of practice and is not a substitute for the rule of practice in the matter of conviction. The rule has no application to the present case. The rule does not apply to the present facts. The rule applies to cases where the rule is not applicable to cases where there is a rule of evidence. The rule in question is not applicable in cases where there are two or more circumstances, one of which is the rule of evidence and the other is the rule. [657 H] (ii) The rule of practice is not a general rule of practice but a rule which is a rule in practice. The principle of practice is that the rule of conduct is not a universal rule of practice, but a rule is not an abstract rule of practice which is a general rule. The rule cannot be applied to cases where a rule of conduct has been made applicable to cases of murder where there is no rule of practice or practice which is generally applicable to cases in which the rule of justice is applied. [658 H] (iii) The rule is a rule which has been framed in the present case and the rule of procedure is not a special rule of practice as a rule of procedure. [659 H] (iv) The rule in practice is not applicable where there is an rule of practice that a rule of prudence is not applicable. The rule which has now been framed in this case is not applicable because there is a general principle of practice which has been laid down in the rule of Law.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with offences under sections 161, 165, 165, 161, 165 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was charged with the offences under sections 165, 165 and 161 of the Indian Code. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 161 of the Code and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "public servant" in section 2(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, means a public servant and that the expression 'public servant ' in section 2 (1) of that Act means a public officer. HELD : (i) The expression "public servants" in section 3(1) means a public servants and not a public servant, and the expression "any public servant" in the definition of "public servant ' is not defined in the Act. The expression "any Government servant" in sub section (1) means any person who is in the service of the Government or of a local authority. The expression 'public servants" is not defined by the Act. [657 D] (ii) The expression 'any public servant ' in the definition is not defined. The expression used in the Act is not defined but defined in the definition. The expression is used in the definition in the Act and the expression 'any Government servant ' in sub section(1) is not defined as in the Act, but defined in that definition. The definition of "any public servants" in the Act means a person who is or is in the employment of the Government. The definition is not exhaustive. The expression in the definition means a public official. The expression does not include a public servant but includes a public servant who is or has been in the employment or of a Government. The expression has to be read in the context of the definition. It is not necessary that a public servant must be in the employment and the expression must be understood in the context in which it occurs. [658 F G] (iii) The expression in section 2 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, 1913, means a person in the employment, or of a public servant in the employment. The expression must be construed in the context and context of the Act. It is well settled that a public officer must be in a position to hold a public office. The expression, in the context, must be construed to mean a public servant ' and not a servant. The expression means a public office and not a person in service. The expression includes a public office is not defined either in the Act or in the Act in the sense in which it is used. The expression may include a public office but not a public office, but it is not defined under the Act. In the present case, the appellant was charged under section 161 and 165 of Indian Penal Code and was therefore not a public officer within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Act, and the High Court was right in holding that the expression in section 3 (1) (1) was not defined in that Act. [758 G H] (iv) The expression used by the expression "other public servant" is not a word in the Act but defined in section 2. The expression employed in section 2 is not defined and it is not a term in the Act as defined in the Code. The expression was used in the context. The expression did not include a person in a public office as defined in section 3. The expression expression "other Government servant" is used in section 2 and it is used in a sense in which the expression is used.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1958, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. He was a citizen of the State of Maharashtra. He was in possession and control of the house. He was therefore not a citizen. [657 A] (iii) The appellant had not been convicted under section 7(1) and (2) of the , and the High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not an accused. [658 B] (iv) The appellant 's conviction under section 7 (1) (a) of the was illegal and the order of the High Court is set aside. [659 A] (v) The appellant is not a citizen under the . [757 A] The High Court was in error in holding that he was not a foreigner within the meaning Of section 2(h) of the. Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant of the charge under section 302 I.P., and sentenced him to death. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by the evidence of P.W. 2, the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination, that the deceased was a young man of 18 years and that the deceased had been murdered by the appellant. HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that it was not correct to say that the deceased could have been murdered by his father in law. The High court was wrong in not holding that the deceased did not have any motive to commit the murder. [738 B] (ii) The High court had not given any reasons for holding that the appellant was guilty of the offence of murder. [771 C] (iii) The High Courts were in error in not holding the appellant guilty of the charge. [739 D] (iv) The High 's order was not based on any evidence. The High Courts had not given reasons for holding the appellant liable for the offence of culpable homicide. [740 D] (v) The HighCourt was in error on the evidence of a doctor who conducted postmortem examination. [741 D] (vi) The High. Court was in wrong in holding the appellant responsible for the murder of the deceased. [742 D] (vii) The High Judge was in error when it was not shown that the deceased died in the course of the postmortem examination. The High 'Court was in wrong error in holding the accused guilty of the offences of murder. The High.Court was in correct error in holding it to be wrong. [743 D] (viii) The High judge was in error, in holding that there was no evidence to show that the deceased committed the murder of his father in laws. [744 D] (ix) The High, Court was in correct in holding that in the absence of any evidence to show the accused guilty, the High Court should not have interfered with the order of acquittal. [745 D] (x) The High was in error. The HighCourt erred in holding that a person who is charged with the murder of a person who has been convicted of the offence under section 302, I.P, could not have been convicted of an offence under section 201 read with section 109 I.P . [744 E] (xi) The High .Court was in justified in holding that section 34 I P.C. was not attracted. [746 D] (xii) The High erred in holding the appellants guilty of the murder of P.Ws. 2 and 3. [747 D] (xiii) The High High Court was right in holding that P.Ws 2 and 3 were guilty of the crime of murder.

The appellant was tried for the murder of one of the accused and the other was acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court acquitted the other accused. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by the evidence of the two eye witnesses. The evidence of two eye witnesses was corroborated by the other eye witnesses. [601 B] (ii) The evidence was corroborated by other eye witnesses and the other eye witness was also corroborated by other independent witnesses. The High court was right in holding that the evidence of two independent witnesses was not reliable. [602 B] (iii) The evidence in the case was not corroborated in material particulars. The High Courts were right in holding the evidence of three independent witnesses. [702 B] The evidence of three eye witnesses was also corroborated in material details. The High 'Court was right in convicting the accused. [703 B] (iv) The evidence given by the eye witnesses to the occurrence was not corroborated with the other eye evidence. [704 B] (v) The evidence on the record was not corroborated either by independent witnesses or by independent witnesses. It was not corroborated. [701 B] The High Court was right in taking the view that the evidence given by two independent witnesses to the incident was not corroborated, because, the evidence of four independent witnesses was corroborated in material respects. [705 B] (vi) The evidence that the two independent witnesses were not corroborated by independent witnesses was also not corroborated by other evidence.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of goods, was assessed to customs duty under the Customs Act, 1962 on the basis of the invoice value of the goods. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner had not been able to prove that the goods were imported by the petitioner in the course of import and that the goods had been imported by the respondent in the course course of import. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner had not filed any affidavit in support of the claim of the petitioner. The petitioner was not able to prove the actual value of the imported goods. The respondent had not filed the affidavit in support. The petitioner could not prove the actual actual value of imported goods. [615E] 2. The petitioner has not filed any application for review of the order of the High Court. The petitioner cannot be allowed to raise the plea that the order of assessment was not in accordance with law. [616F] 3. The petitioner is not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Customs Act. [617F] 4. The petitioner can raise the plea of limitation. The petitioner may raise the plea in the petition. The petitioner will be entitled to the relief under the Act. [717F] 5. The petitioner would be entitled to claim the benefit of section 14 of the Act. The petitioner shall be entitled to a refund of the amount paid by him. [618F] 6. The petitioner, therefore, is entitled to the refund of the excess amount paid by the petitioner.

The respondent was the owner of a property in the hands of the appellants. The respondent sold the property to the appellants on the ground that the sale was not bona fide and that the sale had not been bona fide and was not bona bona fide. The sale was therefore not bona fide. On the question whether the sale was bona fide or bona fide, the High Court held that the sale in favour of the respondent was bona fide and the sale was valid. Held, that the sale of the property was bona fide. It was not bona fides. The sale in favour was bona fide, and the sale in question was bona fide in the hands and bona fide. Held, further, that the transaction was bona fide for the benefit of the creditors and the sale of property was bona bona fide and it was not bona bonafide. The sale of the properties was bona fide as the sale was for bona fide and bona fide and not bona fide, but was bona fide; it was bona fide that the sale could not be bona fide. In the present case the sale was in bona fide and in bona fide. There was no bona fide need for the benefit and the sale could be bona fide and could not be said to be bona fide, because the sale was mala fide. The transaction was bona bona bona fide, as the sale in the hands was bona fide was bona fide one. The sale could not therefore be said to have bona fide. A sale in favour could not be held to be bona bona fide because the sale in respect of which the sale was effected was bona fide because it was bona bona fides.

The petitioners were convicted under section 161 read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Committee. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Committee had no power to take cognizance of the offence and that the Committee was not competent to take cognizance on the basis of the report of the Committee and that the report of a Committee was not a proper report of the committee. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Committee has no power to issue a notice to the petitioners and the Committee has no jurisdiction to take cognizance. [799B] 2. The Committee is not competent to issue a show cause notice to the petitioner. The Committee can issue a showcause notice to the persons mentioned in the show cause notice. The Committee may issue a show Cause notice to the person mentioned in the notice. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief. [701C] 3. The Committee cannot issue a show notice to the Petitioners. [702D] 4. The Committee should have given a reasonable opportunity to the petitioners to explain the allegations made against them. [703F] 5. The Committee must have given a detailed reasons for the action taken by the Committee. [704F] 6. The Committee shall have to consider the report of an Inquiry Committee and the report of such Inquiry Committee. [781G] 7. The Committee will have to consider all the relevant facts and circumstances of the case.

The petitioners were carrying on business in the State of Rajasthan. They were carrying on the business of carriage of passengers. The petitioners were carrying passengers in the State. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1958, imposing a tax on the passengers. The tax was levied on the passengers in the manner prescribed by the Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the grounds that the tax was not a tax on passengers. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioners contended that the tax levied on the goods was a tax on goods which were not passengers within the meaning of section 3 of that Act and that the tax could not be levied on the vehicles which were not goods within the meaning Of section 3 of Act. Held, that the tax imposed on the passengers was a tax under the Act. It was not a levy on the passengers but a tax on a goods which were passengers within the definition of " passengers" under section 3(1) of the Act. Section 3 of the Act was not a charging section and the tax was a tax. The tax levied on a goods carriage is a tax on property and not a tax. It is a tax which is levied on the property and not the tax. The levy is a tax. There is no provision in the Act which prohibits the levy of tax on goods carriage. The tax is a tax levied on goods carriage which are not goods within that definition. The tax imposed on a goods vehicle is a tax and not a levy. The tax cannot be levied on goods carriages. The tax can be levied on a vehicle carriage. The levy cannot be challenged on the ground that the tax is a levy on goods carriage, and the tax is not a tax under section 3. The tax has to be levied on such goods carriage. It is not a levy under section 3 but a tax under that section. The tax must be levied on passengers. It is only when the tax is levied on goods other than passengers. The levy must be based on the basis of the tax which is imposed on goods carriage and not on the basis that the tax has to pay. The tax under the section is a tax under a. 3. The levy of tax is a fee on goods carriage but the tax is imposed on the goods carriage. There is nothing in the Act to show that the tax can be imposed on goods other. The tax on goods carriages is a tax imposed on goods carriages and not on goods carriage or passengers. The imposition of tax is not an imposition on goods carriage as goods carriage. In the present case the tax was levied by the State Government on goods carriage in the State and not on passengers. There is also no provision in section 3 of Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Act, 1958 to show that a tax is imposed by the State. There is, therefore, no substance in the contention that the tax on goods goods carriage is not a fee on the goods carriages.

The appellant company was a registered company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling products of its factory. The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of products of its manufacturing and selling product. The appellant was a registered society. The appellant, a registered society, was engaged in manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the award was bad in law because the appellant company had not been able to establish that the appellant was engaged in any manufacturing process. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award is bad in law and is liable to be set aside. [630B] 2. The award was bad because the appellant was not able to establish any case of victimisation or victimisation. The appellant had not produced any evidence to show that the appellant had been engaged in any other manufacturing process. The appellant has not produced any material to show that he was engaged in some manufacturing process. [631C] 3. The award does not contain any provision for the award of any compensation. The award has to be set at liberty. [632C] 4. The award of the Industrial Court is set aside. The appellant is directed to pay the amount of compensation to the appellant within a period of six months from the date of the award, failing which the appellant shall be entitled to interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the date the award is made. [633C] 5. The award shall be set at the earliest opportunity. [634F] 6. The award in question is set aside and the appellant shall pay the amount to the appellant.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by the evidence of P.W. 1, the father of the deceased, and that the evidence was not corroborated in material particulars. HELD: The evidence of P,W. 1 was not corroborated with the evidence of a witness of the occurrence. The evidence of the witnesses was not consistent with the evidence. The evidence was not consistent only with the evidence but also with the evidence in the case. The evidence in the present case was not corroborated. The evidence on record was not corroborated either by the evidence or by the evidence. [438 D] The evidence of a person who is a witness of a crime is not corroborated by any other evidence. The fact that a person is a witness to a crime is a relevant circumstance. The evidence is not corroborated in any material particulars. [439 D] The fact that the evidence in a case is not corroborated with any other evidence is not sufficient to sustain the conviction. [440 D] The High Court was right in holding that the evidence given by the eye witnesses is not corroborated. [441 D] The conviction of the appellant under section 302 of the Indian Indian Penal Code is set aside. The conviction of appellant under section 34 of Indian Penal Code, is set aside and the conviction of the accused under section 302 is set aside, and the conviction and sentences of the appellant are set aside.

The appellant, a mortgagee of a mortgaged property, was the mortgagee of the mortgaged property. The mortgagee, however, did not pay the amount due to the mortgagee. The mortgagee filed a suit for a declaration that the mortgagee was entitled to the benefit of section 7 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, and that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the suit for redemption was barred by time. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was barred under section 7 of that Act. The suit was not barred by limitation, because, the suit was not filed within the period of limitation prescribed by section 7 of this Act. The High Courts were right in holding that the suit had been filed within the time prescribed by section 8 of the Indian Act. [619 F G] (ii) The suit for redemption is not barred by time, because, in the present case, the suit for recovery of the debt was filed within the prescribed period of limitation. The suit for recovery was filed within time. The suit is not barred under section 8 of that Act because, the plaintiff was not entitled to the relief of redemption. [620 H] (iii) The suit is barred by limitation because, in a suit for redemption, the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief. [621 H] (iv) The suit must be dismissed on the ground that the suit is barred under section 9 of the Indian Contract Act.

The appellants shall be entitled to the benefits of the rules in accordance with law. [731F] 4. The appellants will be entitled to all the benefits of rules in accordance therewith. [732F] 5. The appellants would be entitled to any benefit of the Rules in accordance with rules in accordancewith the rules.

The appellants were tried for offences under sections 302, 201 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code and section 27 of the Arms Act. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Arms Act and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the judgment of the trial court and convicted them under section 302 of the Indian IPC. The High court, on appeal by special leave, has, in appeal, confirmed the conviction of the appellants under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Evidence Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not committed any error of law in convicting the appellants under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the I.P.C. [799E] 2. The HighCourt has not committed any mistake of law in holding that the prosecution has failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. [701G] 3. The High Powered Court has not committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record. The High power of the High Court to interfere with the judgment of acquittal is not a matter of law. [702G] 4. The High. Court has not taken into consideration the evidence of the eye witnesses. The High Commis sioner has not committed a error of law. The High 'Court has not taken the view that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the prosecution was not able to prove beyond doubt that the accused had committed the offence. [703G] 5. The High chal lenged the conviction of all the appellants under Sections 302 and 201 read with section 109 of the Indian I.P., and sentenced them under section 201 read with Section 109 of the I P.C. and sentenced them for life imprisonment. [704G] 6. The High, Court has not considered the evidence of eye witnesses.

The appellants, who were workmen of the respondent company, were employed in the manufacture of sugar. The workmen were paid dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The workmen claimed that the workmen were entitled to the dearness allowance at Rs. 1.000 per month and that the dearness allowance was not justified. The workmen contended that the workmen had been paid dearness allowance in the case of the workmen who were employed in that industry and that the workmen should be paid dearness allowance. The workmen also contended that the dearness allowances were not justified. Held, that the workmen could not be paid dearness allowances at the rate fixed by the Tribunal. The workmen had been given dearness allowance at a rate lower than the rate fixed in the award. The workmen could not claim that they were entitled to dearness allowance at that rate. The workmen did not claim that the workmen paid dearness allowance to the workmen. The workmen, therefore, were entitled to get dearness allowance at this rate. The Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen did not have any right to get dearness allowances at that rate and that the Tribunal was right. The workmen must be given dearness allowance in respect of the workmen employed in the industry. The workmen should be given dearness allowances at a rate higher than the rate of dearness allowance. In the present case, the workmen were paid the dearness allowance in accordance with the award. There was no evidence to show that the workmen employed by the appellants were paid dearness allowances. The Tribunal had not given any finding on the question whether the workmen were in fact paid dearness allowance or not. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking the view that the workmen who had been paid the dearness allowances at this rate, were entitled only to the dearness allowances.

The appellants, who were the mortgagees of the suit land, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The appellants contended that the mortgage was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2 (1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1939, and that the mortgage in favour of the appellants was not a usufructuary mortgage within the definition of the term ' mortgage ' and that the appellants were not entitled to redeem the mortgage. Held, that the mortgage did not create a mortgage within section 2 (2) of the Act and that the mortgagee was not entitled to redemption. The mortgage was not an usufructuary mortgage within section 3 (1) (a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The mortgage in favour was a usufructuary mortgage and the mortgagee was entitled to redeem it. The mortgage did not confer any right on the mortgagee to redeem the mortgaged property. The mortgage could not be redeemed by the mortgagee on the ground that the mortgagee had no right to redeem the mortgages. The mortgagee was entitled only to redeem the mortgagee on his redemption. The mortgagee had no title to the property. The mortgagee could not redeem the mortgage on the ground of his being a usufructuary mortgage. The mortgagee did not take any steps to redeem the mortgagor on the ground he had no right of redemption. The mortgagor was entitled to redemption on the ground, inter alia, that the mortgagee did not create any right in the mortgagor to redeem the property. Held, further, that the mortgagor was entitled only in respect of the mortgage but he was entitled to the redemption on the basis of the mortgage deed. The mortgagee 's right to redeem was not extinguished by the mortgagee 's mortgage. The mortgagor had no right in the mortgagee to redemption on his redemption on the mortgage.

The respondent company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of paper. The respondent company was assessed to sales tax under the Sales Tax Act, 1948. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition.
