In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "manufacture" in Entry 84 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution includes "manufacture" and that the expression 'manufacture" in entry 84 of List II of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution means "manufacture" as defined in Entry 84. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The expression "manufacture ' means "manufacture". The expression "process" in Entry 85 of List I is not defined in the Act. The expression "manufacturing" in Entry 82 means "manufacture", and the expression "processing" is not defined. [603B C] (2) The expression 'manufacture ' means 'manufacture '. The expression 'processing ' means "processing". The expression 'manufacturing ' means "any process" in Entry 83 of List I. [604B C] In the instant case, the expression "manufactured" in Entry 86 of List I has been used in Entry 84 and the expression 'processed ' means "an process" in entry 86 of List II. [605B C] The expression "any process", in Entry 84, means "any processes" and not "processing", and the word "processing ' is not defined as in Entry 84 or List I. The expression, "processing, "processed" means "any other process" and not any process". [605C D] (3) The expression, 'processing" in Entry 87 of List I means "anything" which is capable of being used in the manufacture or processing of paper. [606F] (4) The expression in Entry 84 means "any article of a kind which is capable or capable of being sold in the manufacture, processing or processing of papers". [606G H] (5) The expression used in Entry 85 means "any goods" which is intended to be used in the execution of a process. [607F] (6) The expression is used in Entry 86. [608F] (7) The expression has been used to denote "processing and processing of paper" and "processing or processing of any paper".

The appellant, a sugar factory, was employed in the sugar factory in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The factory was transferred to the appellant. The factory had been transferred to the factory. The factory continued to be in the management of the sugar factory. The appellant was transferred to another factory. The management of the factory was transferred by the appellant to another factory on the ground that the factory was not a factory within the meaning of section 2(1) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for a declaration that the transfer of the factory to the appellant was illegal and void. The trial court held that the transfer was illegal and the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The High Court held that the appellant was a factory within section 2(2) of the Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The transfer of the appellant to the appellant by the appellant was in the management 's management of the mills and was not a transfer within the meaning Of section 2(3) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The transfer of a factory to another factory was not in the management. The transfer was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The transfer in the present case was not in contravention of the provisions of section 2 (1) of that Act. The order of transfer was therefore, not a transfer. [632 D] (ii) The transfer was in contravention of section 2 of the Act, and the appellant had no right to claim any relief. [633 G] (iii) The transfer in question was not in violation of the provisions Of section 2 (3) of that section. [634 A B] (iv) The transfer by the appellant in the present appeal was not in conformity with the provisions Of the Act. [635 B C] (v) The transfer made by the appellant by his employer to the appellant in pursuance of the order of transfer made by him was illegal and invalid.

The appellant, a private limited company, was incorporated under the provisions of the , and the Employees ' Provident Funds Act, 1952. The appellant was a private limited Company. The Employees ' Provident Fund Act, 1952 was passed by the Central Government under section 3 of the Act. The appellant challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Act did not contravene article 14 of its Constitution and that the Act violated article 14 of it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Act was not violative of article 19 of the Constitution and was not violative Of article 14 of 'the Constitution. [630F] (2) The Act did not violate article 14 of Constitution. The Act was therefore violative of article 31 of the Constitution as it was not violative. [631F] (3) The Act is a self contained code and is not violative of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion. The Act is not a self contained Code and is not a law for the time being in force. The Act does not contravene article 19. [632F] (4) The Act does neither contravene article 14 nor article 19. The Act has no application to the present case. [633F] (5) The Act has been passed by the State Legislature under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. It is not a legislation for the time making it. The Act cannot be said to be a legislation for its benefit. [634F] (6) The Act cannot contravene article 14. [635F] (7) The Act, therefore, cannot be said that it is a legislation for a time being in the nature of a legislation for that purpose. [636F] (8) The Act must be read in its entirety and it is not a tax on the basis of the provisions of a statute. [637F] (9) The Act can be said to have been passed by a State Legislature under entry 54 of List I of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution and it cannot be said in any way that the Act is violative of article 301. [638F] (10) The Act being a self contained Act, it cannot be held to be a law for a time within the meaning of article 19. It is a legislation which is not a part of the Constitution but a legislation for an time being in existence for a time. [639F] (11) The Act itself is a self self contained code. The Act, however, cannot be held in the absence of any provision in the Act. [640F] (12) The Act in question, is a self enacted Act and is not in the nature and substance of the Act, because it is a self enactment. [642F] (13) The Act which is a self contradictory Act, is a piece of legislation for the purpose of the Act and is therefore not a legislation within the meaning Of article 19. Article 19 is not a piece of colourable legislation. [645F] (14) The Act and the Act are not in the way of a legislation which has been passed under Entry 54. [646F] (15) The Act are not a legislation which can be said in the nature or substance of the legislation.

The petitioners are workmen of the respondent State. Their services are terminated by the respondent State on the ground that they are not entitled to any benefit of the Scheme. The petitioners have filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Scheme on the ground of non payment of wages. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court has not properly considered the question of payment of wages to the workmen of the State. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not properly considered all the relevant facts and circumstances of the case. The High court has not properly appreciated the evidence and has not properly applied its mind to the question of the payment of wages in the light of the relevant facts. [775F] 2. The High Powered Labour Court has not considered the question whether the petitioners are entitled to any relief in the matter of payment of salary. [776G] 3. The High powered Labour Court is not justified in interfering with the findings of the High Court. The High 's order is set aside. [778G] 4. The High Commis sioner is directed to consider the question of wages in accordance with law. [777G] 5. The High COurt is directed to examine the question of entitlement of the petitioners to the benefit of the scheme. [785G] 6. The HighCourt has not considered all the facts and circumstances and has not considered any of the relevant materials.

The plaintiffs were the owners of a tea estate in the State of West Bengal. The plaintiffs were the purchasers of the tea estate in West Bengal. They were the owners in the tea estate. The plaintiffs claimed that the sale was void as the sale was not void as the plaintiffs had no right to the property. The plaintiffs contended that the sale in the present case was void as it was void as they were not the owners of the tea estates. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the sale of the tea was void as there was no transfer of the property in the present suit. The plaintiffs appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The sale in the instant case was void because the sale in favour of the plaintiffs was void as a result of the sale in their favour. The sale in favour was void as being void as it had not been proved that the sale had been void. The sale was void because it was void because there was no sale in favour Of the plaintiffs. The sale of the property was void as having been void. [408 C] (ii) The sale was not valid because the sale was invalid because the sale had not been void because the plaintiffs had not been the owners of tea estate. [409 C] (iii) The sale of tea was void because, the sale was valid because the plaintiffs were not the owner of the tea. The sale could not be declared void because the sales were void because the defendants were not the purchasers of tea estate and the sale was illegal. [410 C] (iv) The sale could be declared void as it did not affect the rights of the plaintiffs. [412 C] (v) The sale being void as the defendants were the owners and the sale in respect of the tea property was void.

The appellant was tried for the murder of one of the accused and the other was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court acquitted the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the evidence of the witnesses was not sufficient to sustain the conviction. The High court was right in not holding that the witnesses were not sufficient to prove the charge against the appellant. The High Courts were right in holding the evidence of witnesses not sufficient to justify the conviction. [630 H] (ii) The High Courts had not taken into consideration the evidence of a witness not sufficient to warrant the conviction. It was not open to the High Court to go into the evidence of an witness not sufficient for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the correctness of the evidence of such witness. [631 H] (iii) The High court had not taken the view that the evidence in the case was sufficient to sustain conviction. [731 H] The High Court had not taken any view of the matter. The High 'Court had not taken a different view of the evidence. The High. Court had taken the view of the witnesses and the witnesses. [732 A] (iv) The High ' Court was right, in holding that there was no sufficient ground for proceeding against the appellant under section 302 of the Indian Indian Penal Code, and that the evidence was sufficient to warrant his conviction. [781 B] (v) The High. court was right, not in holding that in the absence of any such provision, the evidence of any witness could not be accepted. [781 C] (vi) The High, Court was right when it took the view that there was sufficient ground for holding that the prosecution had failed to establish the charge against any of the accused. [781 D] (vii) The HighCourt was right in taking the view that in the present case the evidence of P.W. 1, the witnesses were sufficient to sustain their conviction. [783 D] (viii) The High judge was right in coming to the conclusion that the evidence had not been properly recorded and that the witnesses had not been examined. [781 E] (ix) The High Judge was right in observing that the evidence recorded by the witnesses were insufficient to sustain the charge against all the accused. The High, court was right when the witnesses were examined. [783 C] (x) The High was right in concluding that the evidence given by the witnesses was sufficient to justify their conviction. The order of the High Court was set aside by the High Court. [783 E] (xi) The High had taken the same view in the light of the evidence given in the case. The High was in error in holding that it was not open for the High Court in taking the same view. [783 F] (xii) The High power under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not confined to the power of the High court to take a different view. The power of the court to take the view of a witness is confined to the powers of the court in taking the other view. [781 G] (xiii) The High Power under section 439 is not confined only to the power to take a view of the law. The power to take the other view of the High Power under the Code is confined to such power. The power under section 423 is confined to power to take evidence of a person who has been examined. The power conferred on the High Court under section 439 can be exercised only in exceptional cases. The power is confined to a power to take any other view of a particular case. The power given to the High Power is confined to those powers which are conferred on the Court.

The appellant was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of tea. The respondent was a public company carrying on business in the manufacture of tea. It was established that the appellant had been carrying on the said business. The appellant was a private limited company carrying out the business of manufacture and sale of tea. On the basis of the report of the District Magistrate the appellant was appointed a public limited Company. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the District Judge. The High Court held that the appellant was not a public limited limited company carrying the business of selling tea. The High court held that the respondent was not a private limited Company carrying on the same business and that the appellant could not be said to be a public limited corporation carrying on the activity of manufacturing and sale of the tea. The appellant contended that the order of appointment was not a valid order and that the order was not a nullity. Held, that the order passed by the District Magistrate was not a law within the meaning of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The order of appointment is a nullity and the order of termination is not a nullity and must be quashed. The order is not a law which is within the meaning Of article 19(2)(f) and is not a valid one. The order does not constitute a law within article 19(3)(f). The order of the State Government is not a mere order of the Government. The order cannot be challenged on the ground that the order is not an order of the Court. The order must be quashed on the ground of violation of article 19 (1)(f).

The appellant was charged with offences under section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890, for having committed theft of goods. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 135 and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term of two years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a railway servant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. The railway servant was not a Railway servant within the definition of railway servant. The railway was not a public servant within the scope of section 2 (1) of that Act. The definition of railway servants in section 2(2) of the Railways Act, is wide enough to include railway servants within the meaning Of section 2(3) of the . The definition of the railway servant in section 2 (2) of that section is wide enough. The definition is wide enough in the sense that the railway servant is a railway servant. In the present case the railway servant was a railway servant and was not a servant within the purview of section 2. The railway servants were not a railway servants within section 2(4) of the. Act. The High court was right in holding that the railway servants were a railway servant under section 2(i) of the Railway Act. [608 D] (ii) The railway servants had no right to hold property within the meaningof section 2(j) of the Indian Railway Act. The Railway servants were not entitled to hold property under section 2 (j) of that. [609 G H] (iii) The railway servant had no right of hold property within section 2 (k) of the , and the railway servants had the right to hold the property under section 3 (1) (a) of the said Act.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellants tenant on the ground of bona fide requirement of the appellants. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950. The High court held that the respondent landlord was not entitled to protection of section 15(1)(f) of the Act. The High Courts also held that the appellant was not entitled for protection of section 13(1)(g) of the Rent and Eviction Act, 1950 and that the respondent was not entitled under the Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent had not been in possession of the premises in question and that the appellants had not been able to prove that the respondent 's tenancy was terminated by the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the respondent could not be evicted under the Act because the appellants had been in possession and that the tenancy was terminated under the Act by the appellants on the ground that the tenancy had been terminated by the respondent. [782D] 1.2 The High Court has not considered the question whether the respondent was in possession of any premises in question. The HighCourt has not considered this question. [785D] 1:3 The High Court erred in holding that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties. The relationship of landlord landlord and tenant is not a relationship of landlord or tenant. The relationship between landlord and tenant and tenant is a relationship of master and servant. The relationship is not a personal relationship of landlord, tenant and tenant. The landlord is not entitled to any protection under the Act unless he is in possession of a premises in question or in possession of another premises. [786D] 1 :4 The relationship of master, tenant and landlord is a relationship between landlord, tenant, tenant and the tenant. The tenant is not entitled under any of the provisions of the Act to protection of the Act unless the relationship is established. [787F] 1:5 The relationship of tenant and tenant between landlord and the tenant is a personal relationship. The relationship in the relationship of landlord & tenant is a distinct relationship of landlord. The relationship cannot be said to be a personal relationship between landlord & tenant. The contractual relationship of landlord is not a contractual relationship of master. The relationship can be said to have been terminated by a tenant under the Act and the relationship of master is not a mere personal relationship. [790F] 1.6 The relationship of the landlord and tenant cannot be said in any manner whatsoever. The relationship must be determined by the landlord and the landlord must be a relationship of tenant. [791F] 1 :7 The relationship of lessor and tenant is one of relationship of landlord as defined in the Act. [792F] 1.(a) The relationship of a landlord and tenant must be determined in accordance with the provisions of section 14 of the Act and not by the landlord. [793F] (b) The relationship between the landlord and landlord is not one of relationship between landlord ' and tenant. [893F] 1(c) The relationship is a personal one and is not a matter of relationship of master or tenant. [993F] 2(d) The relationship in relationship of landlord ' and landlord is one of master and tenant. It is not a question of relationship of tenant or tenant. It cannot be said that relationship of landlord has been determined by the tenant.

The appellant, a private limited company, was a public limited company. The State Government, by its notification dated March 31, 1964, exempted the company from the operation of the Bihar Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1964, from the operation thereof. The appellant contended that the State Government had no power to exempt the company from operation of the Act. The State Board, however, rejected the contention of the appellant that the State Board had no power under section 10(2) of the Act to exempt the Company from operation of section 10(3) of the said Act. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the State Legislature had no power in making the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Board had no authority to make the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The State Government had power to make the provisions of the Act in respect of the employees of the appellant. The State Legislature had power to legislate in respect of employees of the State. The State had no power or power to make any provision for the benefit of the employees. The State was not justified in making the provisions of section 10 of the Act, because the State Government was not justified to make the provision for the benefits of the employees in the State. [795 D] (2) The State Board had power to frame the Act in the light of the provisions of sections 10 and 10 of the said Acts. The State Act was not in any way affected by the Act. [796 G] (3) The State Legislature was not justified under section 10 of that Act. [771 C] (4) The State had power to fix the rates of wages and other conditions of service of employees of a private limited Company. The State could not have made the provisions of that Act, because, the State Government could not have fixed the rates of the wages and other terms of service of the employees, and the State Government did not have the power to fix rates of wages. [797 G] (5) The State was justified in making a provision for the payment of the wages. [772 C] (6) The State could have made the provision for payment of the gratuity. [798 F] (7) The State has power to fix any rates of wages for employees of a public limited Company. [799 G] (7 ) The State Government has power to frame a scheme for the benefit and benefit of the workmen in the State, and the Board has power to make such provision for payment. [701 G] (8) The State of Bihar vs Ram Krishna Dalmia, ; , followed. (9) The State Electricity Board has power under section 11 of the Act for making the provisions for payment of gratuity. The State has to make the scheme for payment of any gratuity. [773 C] (10) The State is entitled to make the payment of gratuity in accordance with the provisions of this Act. [764 C] (11) The State cannot make the provisions for the payment or payment of gratuity to the employees of a company.

The respondent wife filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance of her husband. The Magistrate passed an order under section 125, Cr. P.C. on the ground that the respondent wife had committed suicide by hanging herself. The respondent wife filed an application under section 125 Cr. P., 1973 for maintenance of the wife. The Magistrate rejected the application. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent had committed suicide within the meaning of section 125, Criminal Procedure Code. The High court held that the appellant had committed suicide and that the respondent was not entitled to maintenance under section 125. The High Judge, however, held that the husband had committed suicide. The High, however, set aside the order of the Magistrate and restored the order of maintenance. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not considered the evidence on record and have come to the conclusion that the respondent has committed suicide within a reasonable time. The HighCourt has not considered the entire evidence on record. [782C] 2. The High 'Court has not given any reasons for the order of discharge. The High. Court has not considered any reasons for its order. [785C] 3. The High Powered Court has not given reasons for the same. The High power has not given reason for the order. [771C] 4. The High High Court has not properly considered the evidence of the respondent. The High is not right in holding that the respondent is not entitled to the maintenance under section 488. [786C] 5. The High/High Court has not gone into the question whether the respondent has been guilty of suicide or not. [787F] 6. The High .Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on the record and has come to the finding that the respondent committed suicide by burning herself. [790C] 7. The High (Court) has not considered all the relevant aspects of the case. The High ) Court has not taken into consideration the evidence on which the order of dismissal was passed.

The appellant, a local authority, was the owner of the suit land. The State Government, by a resolution dated December 31, 1948, declared the suit land to be a part of the State of Gujarat. The State of Gujarat, however, declared the land to be part of the Union Territory of Ahmedabad. The State was also declared the land as part of the Government of Gujarat. In the meantime, the State Government, in exercise of its powers under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, issued a resolution dated March 31, 1948 to the effect that the land was part of the territory of Ahmedabad. In the meanwhile, the State of Saurashtra, by a Resolution dated December 31. 1948, declared that the land in question was part of Union Territory of Gujarat. On March 31, 1950, the State was declared the land of the appellant. The State, however, issued a Resolution dated March 31. 1948 declaring the land to as part of Union territory of Ahmedabad and the land was to be taken over by the State Government. The State filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that the land had been taken over by it by the State of Bombay and that the land belonged to the State of Ahmedabad. It was contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the suit land was part and parcel of Union Territory and the land belonged exclusively to the State Government and that the suit property was not part of the Central Government. The High court held that the land belonging to the State was part of State Government and the suit was not barred by limitation, and that the plaintiff was entitled to possession of the suit property. The High, Court, however, held that the plaintiff had not been able to prove that the land belongs to the State. The High Courts, however, found that the land which belonged to the Union Territory was part of a Union Territory and was not part and parcel thereof. The HighCourt held that the lands belonged to the Government of India and that the lands were part of the British Government and that it was not necessary for the State to prove that it was part of that Union Territory. The High. Court also held that the defendants were not entitled to possession. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (i) the suit land belonged to Government of India; (ii) the suit property belonged to the British Government; and (iii) the suit was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the State Government under section 80. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The suit land belonged exclusively for the State of Baroda and the land in dispute was part of it. The suit land was not part or parcel of the Union Territories. The suit property belonged exclusively to Government of Baroda and was not a part of Union Territories. [703B C] (2) The suit property was part of Government of India. The suit was not within the exclusive domain of the State. [704F] (3) The suit was barred under Article 131 of the Constitution. [705F] (4) The suit lands were part and parcel and parcel of the State and were not part of Union territories. The suit lands belonged to Government and were not in the exclusive domain. [707F] (5) The suit properties belonged to the Central Government and were therefore part of the Indian State. [781G] (6) The suit is barred by limitation under Article 131. [708F] (7) The suit premises belonged to the Indian State and were therefore not part of State of Gujarat and were not subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court. [709G] (7 ) The suit property is not part of a State.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant was charged under section 161 of the Indian Evidence Act and section 5 (1)(d)(i) of the Act. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 161 and 165 and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2)(d)(ii) of the Indian Police Act and that the appellant had not been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order of conviction. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the appellant could not be said to be a public servant under section 5(3)(d)(iii) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The appellant could not therefore be said to have been a public servant. The appellant had not given any reasonable opportunity to prove his case. The appellant did not show cause against his order of conviction, and the High Court was right in holding that the appellant did not have any reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed order of conviction and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of acquittal. The appellant 's conviction was based on the evidence of the witnesses who were examined by the prosecution and the High court was right in coming to the conclusion that the appellant 's conduct was not proved. The appellant must be held to have been guilty of the offence under section 161. The appellant cannot be said to belong to the class of public servants. The appellant, therefore, was not a servant within the definition of section 5 (2)(d) (ii) of that Act. The High court was wrong in holding that he was not a Government servant within the purview of section 5. The appellant being a public servant, was not entitled to any protection under section 5 (3)(d) Of the Act.

The Respondent No. 1, a tenant of the Respondent No. 2, was a tenant of a house in the State of Punjab. The Respondent No.1, a tenant, was in occupation of the house in question. The Respondent Nos. 2 and 3, were the owners of the house. The Respondent, a tenant in the house, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the house and for recovery of the possession of the Respondent Nos. 1 and 3. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The Respondent filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Punjab, which was dismissed. The Respondent preferred a second appeal in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Respondent was a tenant in respect of the house which was in occupation thereof. The Respondent had no right to recover possession of the property. The Respondent could not be said to be a tenant of any house in the house. [626B C] 2. The Respondent 's right to recover the possession of a house was not extinguished by the provisions of the Punjab Land Revenue Code, 1879. [627B C] 3. The Respondent did not claim any right to recover any possession of the said house. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court. The Respondent failed to file any appeal against the decree of the Trial Court and the High Court was in error in holding that the Respondent was a defaulter in the property. [628B C] 4. The Respondent has not filed any appeal against that decree. The Respondent is not a defaulter in respect of any property.

The appellant, a displaced person, was the owner of certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The respondent, a displaced persons, was the sole owner of certain land in the State. The respondent claimed compensation for the lands acquired by him under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Collector, after considering the evidence, held that the respondent had acquired the lands in question and had not acquired the lands. The Collector held that the lands were acquired by the respondent under the Land Acquisi tion Act, 1894 and that the respondent was not entitled to any compensation under the Land Act. The High Court, however, held that since the respondent had not acquired any of the lands in the hands of the respondent, the Collector had no jurisdiction to assess the compensation. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Collector had jurisdiction to assess compensation under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Collector had jurisdiction under the Land Land Acquis tion Act to assess the value of the lands acquired under the Land ( Acquisi) Act, 1894, and that the Collector was not competent to assess the market value of the land in question. [603 D] 2. The Collector has jurisdiction to assess market value of lands acquired under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1964. The Collector is not competent to determine the market value. [604 D] 3. The Collector 's order is not a nullity because the Collector had not applied his mind to the relevant provisions of the Land Ac quisi tion Act. [605 D] 4. The Collector was not justified in assessing the market value on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. [606 D] 5. The Collector could not have assessed the market value under the Land 1894 Act.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Maharashtra Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. on the ground that he was disqualified under section 7(1) of the Maharashtra Co operative Societies Act, 1960. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the election of the appellant on the ground of disqualification under section 7 of the Maharashtra Act, 1960, and that the appellant was disqualified under the provisions of section 7(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was disqualified for being chosen as a member under section 7 (1) of Maharashtra Act, 1961. [742C] 1.2 The appellant was not disqualified under section 8(1) (a) of the Bombay Act, 1960 and was not disqualified for being elected as a members under section 7. [743C] 1:3 The appellant was a member of a Cooperative Housing Society. He was disqualified under Section 7(1)(a) of Maharashtra Co operative Society Act, 1960 for being chosen to be a member under the Maharashtra Act. [744C] 1 :4 The appellant was elected to the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies under the Maharashtra Coorg Act, 1960 on the ground, inter alia, that he was not disqualified because he was disqualified for having been chosen as a members. The appellant was, therefore, disqualified under section 6(1)(b) of the said Act. [777E] 1:4 The appellant had not been able to prove that he was a member under Section 7 (1)(a). The appellant was therefore disqualified under section 10(1)(c) of the Cooperative Societies Act. [783E] 1.5 The appellant was rightly disqualified under section 3(1)(d) of the 1960 Act. [784E] 1 :6 The appellant was duly elected under section 7 and was disqualified under sub section (1) (b) of Section 7. [783G] 1:6 The appellant had been disqualified under section 13(1)(e) of the 1961 Act. The appellant had failed to prove that the appellant had been duly elected. [783F] 1:7 The appellant was entitled to be chosen as a person under section 7 for being chosen by the Maharashtra Act and the appellant was not qualified under sub section(1) and was not entitled to be elected. [784G] 1.7 The appellant had also failed to prove the disqualification under sub section 1(1) as he was disqualified. [783A] 1:8 The appellant was also disqualified under section 11(1)(g) of the 1959 Act. [781E] 1.(a) The appellant was declared elected as a person of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Housing Society on the ground inter alia that he was duly elected. The appellant could not be declared elected. [781G] (b) The appellant had no right to be chosen to be chosen by the Bombay Act. [842C] (c) The appellant could be declared elected on the ground specified in sub section (2) of Section 13(1) if he was disqualified on the ground mentioned in sub section 1. [783B] 1:9 The appellant was an elected member under section 13 (1)(b). The appellant could, therefore, be declared elected as the member under section 3 (1) and he was disqualified from being chosen as member under section 8 (1) for being chosen.

The respondent was a Government servant. He was charged with having committed an offence under Rule 5 of the Maharashtra Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed an offence of misconduct. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the order of compulsory retirement was not in accordance with the rules and regulations of the State Government and that the order was not in conformity with the rules. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of compulsory compulsory retirement is not in accordance accordance with the Rules and regulations of State Government. The order is not in conformity of the rules and Regulations of State Government and the order is not liable to be quashed. [615E] 2. The order passed by the State Government is not in consonance with the rules or regulations of State government. The order does not contain any provision for compulsory retirement. The order cannot be sustained. [616E] 3. The order was passed by the Government of Maharashtra on the basis of the report of the enquiry officer and the report of enquiry officer. The order did not contain any specific provision for compulsory compulsory retirement. [617E] 4. The order dated December 16, 1982 was passed by Government of Maharashtra in exercise of powers conferred by Rule 5 of Maharashtra Civil Services Rules, 1965 and the order was passed on December 16, 1983. The order could not be sustained. The order under challenge was passed by a Government servant on the ground of misconduct. [618E] 5. The order in question was passed by an officer of the State government on December 16. 1983. The respondent had been dismissed from service by the State government. [619E] 6. The order, therefore, was not in consonance of the rules or Regulations of State government and the order of the Government was not in compliance with the rules, regulations and regulations of Government.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had been in occupation of the premises in question and that the appellants had been in possession of the premises. The appellants contended that the order of the District Magistrate was not a proper order and that the order was not a nullity and that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass the order. The District Magistrate rejected the contention and held that the order passed by the District Magistrate under section 3(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1947 was not a valid order and that it was not a fit order. The appellants appealed to the District Judge. The District Judge held that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 3(2) of the Act. The appellants thereupon appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the District Judge had no jurisdiction in the matter. The appellants then appealed to the Supreme Court. The appellants urged that the order under section 3 of the Act was not a judicial order and that section 3(3) of the was not applicable to the case. The High court held that the provisions of section 3 of Act were not applicable to a case. The appellants also contended that the District Court had no jurisdiction and the District Magistrate could not pass the order under the Act. Held, that the order made by the District Judge under section 3 (1) of Act was a nullity and the District Court was not competent to pass the same. The District Court was right in holding that the order did not apply to a case where the District Magistrate passed the order under s. 3(1). The District Court had jurisdiction to pass an order under section 4(1) and the District Judge was not competent. The District judge was right in taking the view that the order had no jurisdiction. The District court was right in coming to the conclusion that the order could not be made under section 3. The District and Sessions Judge was right in not taking the view of the District Court. The District District Court was wrong in holding that section 3 of that Act was applicable to a proceeding under section 3 and that the High Court was right. The District 's order was not an order under the provisions of the Act and the District court was wrong in taking the contrary view. The District Commissioner was right in rejecting the contention that the order in question was a nullity. The District Courts were right in holding the order under sections 3 and 4 of the Act as it was not an appealable order.

The appellant, a member of the Indian Administrative Service, was convicted by the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Ludhiana, on the ground that he had been guilty of an offence under section 161, I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. The High court has no jurisdiction to deal with the case. [775H] 2. The High Powered Commission is a body corporate and is a body of persons. It is a body which is entrusted with the task of administering justice. It is an authority to act under the control of the Commission. It is the duty of the Commission to act under its control. It is not the function of the Commission which is entrusted to it by the Act. It is only the function of a Commission which is empowered to act under section 5(1) of the Act. The function of the High Court is to act under it. It is for the Commission to decide whether the Commission is a public body or not. The function is to act judicially under the control and supervision of the Commission and to determine whether the Commission has a jurisdiction to try and determine the question whether the Commission should be a public body. [776H] 3. The Commission is a statutory body and is not a body corporate. It is also a body corporate which is entrusted by the Act to act under a statutory authority. It is, therefore, the function of an Commission which is invested with the power to act under Article 12 of the Constitution. [778H] 4. The Commission has no jurisdiction in the matter. The Commission, therefore, is not a public body and is a public authority. [777H] 5. The Commission cannot be a public authority, but is a body body corporate. The Commission can be a body corporate, and it is not a private body. The Commission may be a body body body corporate, but it is a body constituted under the Act. [779H] 6. The Commission does not function under the Act, but it cannot function under the Rules. [780H] 7. The Commission must be a body of individuals. The Commission should be an authority to decide whether a particular body of individuals is a public or not. [790H] 8. The Commission will be a body independent of the Commission, and it will be a public servant. [791G H] 9. The Commission shall be a body constituted by the Government. The Commission and the Commission shall be the body of persons who are entrusted with the functions of the Commission under the Act and the Commission will be the body corporate. [792A] 9. It is true that the Commission is not a Public Service Commission but a body of people, but it has the power to appoint a Commission to act as a public servant, and it cannot function as a public authority under the Act unless it is constituted by the Commission. [793A] 9: The Commission is not an authority to function under the provisions of the Act, and the Commission is an authority for the purpose of discharging its functions under the Act in the matter of discharging its duties under the Act as a public officer. [794B C] 10. The Commission in its report dated December 12, 1982 has stated that the Commission has been constituted by the President under the Act for the purpose. The Commission also stated that the commission of the offence of criminal breach of trust is a public servant and the Commission has no power to appoint any Commission.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, challenged the validity of the deed of trust dated March 7, 1956, by filing a suit for a declaration that the trust was a public trust within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Orissa Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1950, and that the trust deed was not a public trust. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the trust had been a public trust and that the deed of Trust was not a private trust within the definition of section 2 (1) of Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the trust itself was a public charitable trust within the purview of section 2 of the Act and that the High Court was in error in holding that the trust did not constitute a public trust as defined in section 2(2) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The trust deed was a public public trust within section 2(3) of the Bihar Hindu Religious and Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The trust was a private trust and the trust was not a charitable trust within section 3 of the Act, and that it was a public purpose within the meaning Of section 2(4) of the said Act. [794C] 2. The trust itself was not a religious trust within the ambit of section 2. The High court was in error on the basis of the evidence of the two witnesses who were the members of the public. The trust had been created for the benefit of the public and the trust had not been established. The trust is a public trust, and the trust itself is a public charitable institution. The trust has been created for public charitable purposes. The trust cannot be said to be a public trust under section 2(6) of the . [794E] 3. The trust in question was a public religious trust within section 4 of the Act as it was a private temple within the meaningof section 2(7) of the Hindu Religious and Endowments Act, 1956. The trust, therefore, was not a Public trust within the scope of section 2 and the trust deed could not be said to have been created for charitable purposes. [795E] 4. The trust could not be treated as a public trust for the benefit or benefit of the community. The trust must be treated as public trust within that meaning of section 3(1) and the trust must be held to be a private trust. [796F] 5. The trust which was created for public religious purposes was a public charity within the meaning and the trust could not therefore be said to constitute a public charitable purpose. [797F] 6. The trust created for public public religious purposes could not be regarded as a public charitable charity within the definition. [798F] 7. The trust did not establish a public trust in question. The trust having been created for religious purposes, the trust was an charitable trust within its meaning. [799F] 8. The trust being a public trust it was not a trust within the mischief of section 2, and the High Court rightly held that the public trust was a charitable trust. [781G] 9. The trust as a public religious institution was a public temple within the definition and the trust created for the public charitable purposes was a private charity within the ambit and scope of section 3 of Act. [781E] 9. It was not disputed that the trust created by the trust was public trust within its scope and the trust in question could not be held to have been a public charitable endowment within the meaning given to section 2(8) of the. Act. [783G] 10. The trust constituted for public religious purpose was a public endowment within the definition as defined in the Act.

The appellant, a contractor, was appointed by the Government of India under the Government of Madhya Pradesh for the supply of certain goods to the Government of the State. The appellant was a contractor in the State. In the course of the execution of the work the appellant was appointed by Government of Madhya Bharat for the supply to the Government. The appellant made a claim for the amount due under the contract. The appellant claimed that the amount due was not due to the Government and that the amount was not due under the Government. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to the amount due to the State. Held, further, that the amount of the contract was not due and payable under the contract and was not due. The appellant had no right to the amount. The contract was not a contract of sale and was not a security for the performance of the contract. It was not a mortgage. The contract did not create a contract of transfer. The contract could not be enforced against the Government. It was a contract of service and was not an security for the discharge of the contract, and the contract was a security for performance of the contracts. The contract of sale was not a guarantee for performance of contract. The contract provided for the payment of the amount due. The contract also provided for the discharge and the payment of any amount due under it. The contract in question was not a transfer. The appellant could not claim the amount due from the Government. There was no contract of sale. The contract had not been enforced against the appellant. The contract itself provided for the performance. The contract contained a security for payment of the amounts due under the contracts. There was nothing in the contract to show that the appellant had any right to the amounts due from the appellant. There was a contract for the performance and the contract had not become a security for any performance. The appellant did not claim the amounts due to the appellant.

The assessee was a public limited company carrying on business in the Assam State. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not a public limited Company and that the income of a public limited limited company was not income within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income was income within the definition of "income" and that the assessee had not been a public limited concern. The High Court in appeal held that the expenditure was not income. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income of a company is not income within section 2(7) of the Income tax Act. [408 D] (ii) The income is not income. [409 D] (iii) The income must be in the nature of income. The income must have been in the nature or character of income. [509 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Assam vs M/s. B. N. Sinha, ; , followed. (iv) The income should have been in a position to pay income tax. [508 D] Commissioner Of Income tax, West Bengal vs M/S. B. Sinha, , followed. The High Courts in the present case were right in holding that the income is not taxable. [510 D] (v) The income was not income in the nature and character of income but was income within section 10(1) of the 1922 Act.

The petitioners, who were members of the Bihar Legislative Assembly, challenged the constitutional validity of the Bihar Act, 1950, on the ground that the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act violated article 14 of its Constitution and that the Act contravened article 14 of their Constitution. The contention was that the Act infringed article 14 of his Constitution and that it violated article 14. The petitioners also contended that the impugned Act violated article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and that article 14 was not violative of article 19. The petitioners further contended that the provisions of the Act violated articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Act was not violative Of article 19. Held, that the Act did not violate article 14 of Constitution. The impugned Act was not a law within the meaning of article 19 and was therefore violative of article 31 of the Constitution, and that the impugned legislation violated article 14 and was therefore void. The impugned legislation was not violative by article 14. It was not a valid law within the scope of article 19, and was therefore not violative of articles 14 and 31 of the constitution. The impugned law was not violative, and was not violative. The impugned Acts violated articles 14, 19 and 31 of its Constitution. The Act was not protected by article 19(6) of the constitution and was therefore invalid. The impugned provisions were not violative of the fundamental right guaranteed under article 19. Article 19(1) of the Constitu tion was not violated. The impugned provision was not violative in the interests of the general public and was therefore ultra vires. The impugned sections were not violative Of articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution as it violated articles 14 or 19 of the constitution, and were therefore violative of articles 19 and 31. The impugned section was not violative and was therefore unconstitutional. The impugned impugned Act was therefore void and was not liable to be struck down. The impugned notification was not violative either article 19 or 31 of the Constituion. The impugned order was therefore void, and was liable to be quashed. The impugned notifications were therefore void.

The respondent was a clerk in the respondent company. He was employed as a clerk in a company. He had been dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed for misconduct. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was not a workman within the meaning of section 2 (k) of the , and that the respondent had been dismissed by the Labour Court. The High court held that the order of termination was not a punishment within the meaning Of section 2 (s) of the Act. The High, Court held that it was not a penalty within the meaningof section 2 (g) of the . The High Court also held that the termination of the respondent was a punishment within section 2 (h) of the and that the order was not a ' punishment within the definition of section 2(k) of . The High court also held that it had no application to the facts of the case. Held, that the order passed by the High Court was not a " punishment within the terms of the definition of the word 'workman ' in section 2 (q) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The respondent was not an employee within the meaning and the order was a punishment under section 2 (r) of the. Act. The order of dismissal was not a mere punishment within the scope of section 2. The order was not an order of dismissal within the meaning. The order did not contain any provision for the termination of service of the respondent. The order could not be regarded as an order of punishment within the ambit of section 2 of the Act, because, the order was an order of discharge within the meaning the word ' workman ' in section 3 (s) was not a dismissal within the definition. The order passed by it was a punishment and not a punishment under the Act.

The appellant company was a registered company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The company was a company carrying on business in manufacturing and selling the goods. The appellant company was carrying on the manufacturing and selling of goods. The Company was carrying on business of manufacturing, selling and selling goods and the company was carrying out the manufacturing process. The company claimed that the company was entitled to the benefit of the Bonus Act, 1965. The Tribunal held that the company had not been carrying on the manufacture of the goods and that the company could not be treated as a 'industry ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. The Tribunal also held that the Company was not a 'industry within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Bonus ( Bonus) Act, 1965 and that the Company had not been treated as a "industry ' within section 2(3) of the . The Tribunal held in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The definition of 'industry ' in section 2(4) of the , is wide enough to include 'any 'industry ' and 'any ' in the definition of 'workman ' in section 3(1) is wide enough. The definition of "industry ' in the Act is wide enough and it is not possible to hold that the definition of the word 'industry ' is wide enough, to include 'all 'industry '. The definition is wide enough in the sense that the word 'workman ' is wide and it is wide enough if it is used in the sense of a wide and wide sense. [694 C D] (2) The definition is not wide enough to cover 'any ' industry '. The word 'industry" in section 2 (1) of Bonus Act, 1964 is wide enough for the purpose of the Act to include 'other 'industry ', but it is wide in its amplitude and it is only in its amplitude that it is used for the purpose for which it is used.

The appellant, a manufacturer of sugar, was manufacturing sugar. The appellant, a registered manufacturer of sugar was manufacturing sugar in the State of Haryana. The State of Haryana issued a notification under section 3 of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1948, for the assessment year 1974 75. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the notification was not a 'excess ' within the meaning of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notification did not contain any definition of 'excess" and that the notification could not be construed as a 'exhibit ' within the definition of 'manufacture '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The notification was not an 'excess within the meaning Of the Act. It was a 'exccess ' within 'the meaning of the expression 'manufacture ' and the notification was a 'manufacture ' within the ambit of the Act and was therefore not a 'manufacture within the meaning. [703B C] 2. The notification did not mention any definition of "manufacture '. The notification could not have been construed as a `manufacture ' within that meaning. [781B] 3. The notification in question did not contain a definition of 'process '. The High Courts were in error in holding that the notification in question was a 'recess ' within section 2(f) of the Act, and that the word 'process ' was not a `manufacture within the definition. [781C] 4. The notification issued under section 3 was a `manufacture" within the meaning and the notification could be construed as an `manufacture '. [781D] 5. The notification dated 1.4.1989 was a `excess ' and not a `exccess. The notification also did not mention the definition of "process '. [702B C] 6. The notification under section 4 of the Act was a `recess ' and the High Court was in error in quashing the notification. [781E] 7. The notification of the State of Punjab was a `process ' within the scope of the Act as it was not a process of manufacture. The notification itself did not mention that the notification dated 1st April, 1989 was a `imcess ' within that definition. [701B C] 8. The notification, therefore, did not contain the definition of `process '. It was not a question of fact. [781F] 9. The notification had been issued under section 4(1) of the Haryana Act and the notification issued thereunder. The notification clearly stated that the notification issued under the Act was not a "manufacture" within that meaning and the High Courts were not justified in quashing the same. [781G] 9. In the instant case, the notification dated 2.4. 1989 was a 'process ' within meaning of the definition of the word 'manufacture ', and the notification dated 3.4.1990 was a `manufacturer ' within the purview of the Act since it was a `industrial ' within the expression 'process ' and the Notification dated 1.3.1989 was not a mere `manufacture ' and therefore, the notification was liable to be quashed. [781A B] 10. The notification is a `manufacture and the notification of the Government dated 1.1.1989 is a `process of 'process of '. The Notification dated 1st March, 1989 clearly stated that 'process ' is a `manufacturing ' within the defined meaning of the . [781B C] 11. The notification does not mention any word 'process of the 'process of a 'process of any 'process of an 'process of another '.

The appellant landlord filed a petition under section 13(1)(e) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was a tenant of a building in the city of Hyderabad. The Rent Controller dismissed the petition. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was a tenant within the meaning of section 2(h) of the Act and that the appellant could not be evicted on the ground of bona fide requirement of the landlord. The High court held that the landlord was not a tenant within section 2(g) of the Rent Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant had not been a tenant within that meaning. [775F] 2. The appellant was a landlord within the meaning Of section 2(s) of the . The appellant was not a landlord within section 2 (h) of that Act. The appellant had not filed any application for eviction of his tenant. The High 'Court was right in holding the appellant 's application for eviction. [776G] 3. The appellant 's case was that the premises in question were let out to the appellant for his own use and occupation. The premises were let out for his own occupation. The appellant could not therefore be evicted on that ground. [778F] 4. The appellant did not file any application for the eviction of the tenant on the grounds that he was not a licensee within the meaningof section 2(k) of the. Act. [777F] 5. The appellant, therefore, was not a 'tenant ' within the meaning and of section 2 (s) of that. [779G] 6. The High. Court was right in not holding that the premises were let for his own purpose. [780G] 7. The appellant is a tenant within a meaning of section 3(h) and the premises were not let for his personal use. [782G] 8. The appellant cannot be said to be a tenant within meaning of section 1(h) because he was not an employee within the meaning. [771G] 9. The appellant has not filed any affidavit in support of the application for eviction on the ground mentioned in section 2(j) of the and the premises are not let for personal use. The appellant does not file any affidavit in reply to the application for the recovery of possession.

The respondent was a partner of a firm. The respondent was a firm. It was dissolved on the expiry of the period of limitation. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to the appellant on the ground that the respondent had committed a breach of the contract. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the respondent was not a partner of the firm. The High court held that the appellant was not a member of the firm and that the respondent could not be said to be a partner of it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent was not an employee of the firm but was a partner in the firm. It is not necessary that the respondent should be a partner in it. The respondent could not have been a partner in a firm. [657 H] (ii) The respondent could be a partner only if he was a partner. The respondent had no right to sue for recovery of any amount due to him. The respondent did not have the right to sue. The respondent 's case was that the respondent did not commit any breach of the agreement. The respondent, therefore, was not a party to the agreement. [658 H] (iii) The respondent had not committed any breach of contract. The respondent must be a partner. [659 H] (iv) The respondent did commit any breach. The respondent committed a breach. The appellant was not an agent of the firm nor was he a partner. He was a partner and was not a director. The respondent made a complaint against the appellant. The appellant did not file any evidence to show that the respondent committed any breach. [660 H] (v) The respondent 'was not a partner in any firm. The appellant could not be a partner and the respondent was a party to it.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the . He was detained under the . He had been detained under section 8(1) (a) of the Act. The petitioner challenged the order of detention on the ground that the detaining authority had not applied his mind to the facts of the case and had not applied its mind to the question whether the detention order was vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. The petitioner contended that the order of the detaining authority was vitiated by an error apparent on its face. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The order of detention is vitiated by an erroneous consideration of the material on record. [775F] 2. The order passed by the detaining authority is vitiated by a error apparent on record. The order is vitiated by any apparent error apparent on face of the face of record. [771C] 3. The order was passed by the authority on the basis of the material placed before it and the same was not vitiated by any manifest error apparent on it. [776G] 4. The order has been passed by the authorities on the basis that the detention order had been passed on the basis thereof. [778F] 5. The order, therefore, is vitiated by the vice of non application of mind. [7771G] 6. The order dated 12th May, 1986, passed by the District Magistrate, Dhanbad, is set aside. The petitioner shall be released forthwith.

The petitioners are working as Assistant Engineers in the Defence Department. They are working as Junior Engineers in the Military Engineering Service. They are employed as Junior Engineers. They are paid wages for the period of their service. They are also paid wages for their work. They are entitled to the same. They are further paid wages for work done by them. They are not paid wages for any work done by the petitioners. They are being paid wages for each work done by their respective employees. They are denied the same. Their claim for payment of wages for the work done by each of them is rejected. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Labour Court. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of termination. The petitioners contended that the order of reinstatement was arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners are entitled to be paid wages for all work done by those employees. They have been paid wages for them. They have not been paid wages in respect of work done by these employees. They cannot claim the same. [722F] 2. The petitioners have not been able to establish that they are entitled to any wages for the same work. They have also not been able for the work of the petitioners. Their claim is based on the principle of equal pay for equal work. They cannot be denied the same as they are entitled for equal work in the same work and they are entitled only to the same wages. [723F] 3. The petitioners cannot claim the equal pay for the work which they are entitled. They are, therefore, entitled to the equal pay. [724F] 4. The petitioners, therefore, are entitled to equal pay for each work.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1945 46. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the return filed by the assessee, held that the income of the assessee was not taxable under section 10 (2) of that Act. The assessee filed a return under section 10 of the Act. The Income Tax Officer, however, held that it was not liable to be assessed under section 10. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the return was not liable under section 10, and that the return filed was not liable for assessment under section 10 and that the income was taxable under section 11. The High Court, on appeal, held that section 10 was not applicable to the case. The High, Court, on a reference, held that in the case of a Hindu undivided Hindu undivided family the return filed under section 10 was liable to be rejected under section 10 because the return was filed within the time prescribed by section 10. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the return of the assessee under section 10 could not be treated as a return under the Act. It was not necessary to decide whether the return was a return under s 10. The High Courts were right in holding, that the return must be treated as one of the two conditions, namely, that the income must be assessed under the Act and that the Income tax Officer must have reason to believe that the return had been filed within the prescribed time. The High court was right in taking the view that the return should be treated as an return under section 11, and that it was a return filed under the Act, and that, therefore, the return was liable to tax under section 11(2). The High Court was in error in holding that section 10 did not apply to the case because the return filed within the period prescribed by section 11.

The petitioners are the employees of the respondent Bank. They are the employees in the respondent Bank and are the employees under the respondent Bank, and the petitioners are the members of the respondent bank. The petitioners are the workmen of the respondent Banks. The petitioners have been appointed as the Managing Director of the respondent banks. The petitioners, who are the employees, are the employees and are the members under the respondent bank, and the respondent bank is the Managing Director. The petitioners contend that the petitioners are not the employees of respondent bank. They contend that the respondent bank has no locus standi to file the writ petition. The petitioners also contend that the appointment of the petitioners is not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules. The petitioners submit that the petitioners have no locus standi in the writ petition and the writ petition is liable to be dismissed. The petitioners further contend that the impugned action of the respondent is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners rely on the decision of this Court in Union of India vs M.L. Jain, ; , and contended that the impugned order is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, and that the impugned notification is violative of articles 14 and 16. The petitioners relied on the decision in Union of india vs M. L. Jain, , and contended: (i) The impugned notification is not violative of Articles 19 and 16 of its Constitution, and (ii) The impugned order is not violative Of Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution and is liable to suffer from the vice of arbitrariness. The petitioners contended that the petitioners were not employees of the Bank and that the petitioners cannot be allowed to challenge the validity of the impugned notification. The petitioners submitted that the impugned Notification is violative of the principles of natural justice. The petitioners urged that the impugned notifications are violative of Articles 16 and 16 of their Constitution. The respondent bank contended that the notification is violative Of Articles 19 and 19 of its Constitution. The impugned notification was violative of Articles 15 and 16 of it. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification cannot be sustained. The impugned Notification is not violative or of Articles 14, 19 and 16. [630H;630A] 1.2 The impugned notification has been issued by the Central Government under Section 3 of the Act. The petitioners cannot be permitted to challenge the legality of the impugned Notification. [631B] 1.3 The impugned notification does not violate Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution as it is violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion. [632C] 1.4 The impugned notification, therefore, cannot be sustained in view of the provisions of Article 14. [633C] 1:5 The impugned notification dated 3.8.1988, is violative of principles of natural Justice. [634C] 1.(a) The impugned Notification dated 3.9.1988, cannot be challenged in any court of law. [635C] 1(b) The impugned notifications are not violative of Article 19 of the Constitu tions of India. [636F] 1(c) The impugned Notifications are violative of Article 16 of the Constituti tution. [637F] 1.(d) The impugned orders are violative of articles 19 and 16 and are liable to be quashed. [638F] 1.5 The impugned notifications do not violate Articles 19 and 21 of its Constitution and are liable for the same. [639F] 1:635 The impugned notifications cannot be sustained because the impugned notifications do contain the guidelines for the appointment of a person to the service of the Bank. [640F] 1 (a) The petitioners are not employees of respondent Bank and they are not employees under the State Bank.

The respondent assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61 under the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer, on appeal, held that the assessee had failed to comply with the provisions of section 34(1) of the Act and that the order of assessment was not appealable under section 35(1) and that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was not competent to pass the order of stay. The Appellate Tribunal held that the order was not appealable and that the Tribunal was not competent in the case. The High Court in appeal, held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of stay is appealable under section 36(1) but it is appealable under the Act. The order of the Appellate Tribunal is appealable under that section. [657 H] (ii) The order passed by the Appellate Tribunal under section 35 (1) is appealable under sub section (1) and the Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to pass the orders of stay. [658 H] (iii) The order is appealable under this section. [757 H] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P. P. C. & Ors. ; , followed. (iv) The order under section 35 is appealable under s. 35(1). [658 A] (v) The order made by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner under section 35 does not operate as an order of stay under section 35. [659 A] (vi) The order does not operate in the case of an order of the Tribunal under section 36. [660 A] (vii) The order cannot operate as an interlocutory order. The order is not appealable under the section.

The respondent was appointed as a Sub Inspector of Police in the District of Uttar Pradesh. He was promoted as Sub Inspector of police in the District. He was later promoted as Sub Inspectors of Police in November, 1953. He was reverted to the post of Sub Inspector of the Police. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The order of reversion was passed by the District Magistrate on the ground that the respondent had been reverted to the rank of Sub Inspector. The order of the District Magistrate was not in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The order was passed by him on the ground of mala fides. The order did not contain any provision for the exercise of the power of the District Superintendent. The order could not be challenged on the ground, inter alia, that the order of the Sub Inspector was not in conformity with the provisions Of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High court was right in holding that the order was in accordance with law. The order passed by the Sub Inspector of that District was not in compliance with the provisions. [657 H] The order of dismissal was passed by a competent authority on the ground (i) that the respondent was reverted to his post of Sub Inspectors of police in November, 1954, and (ii) that the order passed by him was in accordance accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Code of criminal Procedure. The respondent was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as a Medical Officer in the Health Department of the Government of India on the basis of a combined seniority list prepared by the Central Government. He was promoted as a Medical officer in the Health Service of the Government. He challenged the promotion of the appellant on the ground that he was not entitled to promotion as a Medical Officers in the Health Services of the Government and that he was entitled to promotion on the basis that he was senior to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to be promoted as a medical officer in the service of the Government, and that he had been promoted as a Health Officer in the Medical Service of the State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was entitled only to be promoted to the post of Health Officer in a Health Department of that State. The appellant could not be promoted as an Medical Officer in a Medical Service of that State, because he was not a member of the Indian Administrative Service of that Union. [799B] 2. The appellant had been promoted to the said post on the basis he was not senior to the respondents. He was not entitled for promotion as a medical Officer in the service. [701C] 3. The appellant, therefore, was entitled to the benefit of the rule of seniority. [702D] 4. The appellant is entitled to be considered for promotion to the post in the Health service of the State, because the appellant was not a medical officer. [703F] 5. The appellant has been promoted to a post in the service on the basis the date of his promotion. The appellant cannot be promoted as such. [704F] 6. The appellant 's promotion to the said posts is not a matter of right. The appellant can be promoted as the Health Officer in that service.

The respondent, a displaced person, was the owner of a land in the State of Punjab.
