The respondent, a tenant of a land, was allotted to him by the State Government under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The respondent was a displaced person. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Act violated article 14 of his Constitution. The State appealed to this Court. The question was whether the Act violated articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution and the High Court was right in holding that the Act contravened article 14 of its Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Act violated articles 19 and 19 of its Constitution and was not violative of article 19 of the Constitu tion. [730F] (2) The Act was not violative Of article 14 of Constitution. The Act was enacted to provide for the acquisition of land for the purpose of the Act. The Act did not provide for the transfer of land to displaced persons. The Act had no application to the land in question. The Act, therefore, was not violative. [731G] (3) The Act did provide for the abolition of land for a purpose other than the purpose for which it was acquired. The Act does not provide for abolition of land. The Act is a piece of legislation and is not a piece of colourable legislation. The Act has no application to a case where the land is acquired for a purpose connected with the acquisition of the land for a public purpose. [732G] (4) The Act is not a colourable legislation. It is a colourable legislation and is therefore not violative of articles 14 and19 of the Constitution, and is not violative of the Constitution.[732G H] (5) The Act does no more than provide for the extinguishment of land for any purpose connected with acquisition of land.

The appellants were the descendants of the Maharaja of Gwalior. The Maharaja of Gwalior was the holder of the estate of the Maharaja. The Maharaja was the holder in the estate of Gwalior. He was the holder. The Maharaja, therefore, was entitled to the estate of his Maharaja. The appellants filed a suit for the recovery of possession of the estate. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Maharaja was the owner of the estate and the Maharaja was not the holder of that estate. The High court held that the appellants were the holder of a estate and that the Maharaja had no right to the estate. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Maharaja was not a holder of the property. The Maharaja had no authority to make a declaration under section 6 of the Act. The Maharaja could not make a declaration in respect of the estate which was the holder and was not the owner of that estate, and the Maharaja could not claim any right to the property. [619 F G] (ii) The Maharaja could make a declaration as to the estate which had been the holder of an estate. The Maharaja did not make a statement in respect of that estate and the appellants were not the holder. [620 F G] The Maharaja was entitled to a declaration as regards the estate which he was entitled to. the estate. [621 F G] In the present case the Maharaja was a holder of an interest in the estate. He was not the proprietor of the estate but was the holder thereof. The Maharaja. was not the manager of the estate, and was not a person who was the holder, and was therefore entitled to the benefit of the estate under the Act.

The appellants were the tenants of the respondent firm. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the notice of demand was not served on them within the time prescribed by section 13(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the notice was not served within the time specified by section 13 (1) of that Act and that the notice served on the appellants was not served in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that the notice did not serve the purpose of the Act and that it was not served by the respondent within the time fixed by section 13 of the Act, and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notice in question was not served at the time of the notice and that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of section 13(2) of the Act as the notice was served on the appellant within the time stipulated by section 13. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice served on a tenant under section 13(3) of the Maharashtra Rents, Hotel & Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947 is a notice served on him within the time allowed by section 13 and that the period of limitation prescribed by section 12(2) is not applicable to the case. [794C] 2. The notice in question is a notice of demand served on the tenant under section 12(1) and not a notice of the demand. The notice is a notice under section 13. The notice of demand is a notice in the nature of a notice served by the tenant under the Act. [795C] 3. The notice under section 12 is a notice and the notice is a condition precedent to the filing of the suit. The notice must be in the nature and substance of the suit and the notice must be served within the period of one month from the date of service of the notice. [796C] 4. The notice issued under section 13 is a notice for the purpose of section 13. [797F] 5. The notice contemplated by section 13 is not a notice within the meaning of section 13 and is not a period of one year. [798F] 6. The notice was not a notice under the Act and the notice was a notice within one month of the service of the notices. [799F] 7. The notice to the appellants was a notice under s 13(1). The notice was a mere notice within the time provided by section 13, and the notice served by them was a notice in accordance with section 13(4). [797G] 8. The notice did not contain any provision for the filing of a suit within one month from its service. The notice could not be served within one month.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the Indian State. The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent was a company incorporated in the United Kingdom. The respondent, a company, was incorporated in India in the United States of America. The respondent had a share in the profits of the company. The respondent filed a return of the profits of its company. The Income tax Officer held that the respondent was a shareholder of the company and that the respondent had a right to vote for the company. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the company was a shareholder and that the company had a right of vote for the Company. The High Court, on appeal, held that the directors of the company were not a shareholder of a company and that they were not a shareholders of the company, and that the directors were not a director of the company as the directors were only a shareholder of that company. The High, on appeal by special leave, held that there was no question of the respondent being a shareholder of any company. Held, that the respondent company was not a shareholder and the respondent was not a director. The respondent could not be a shareholder of an company. The company was not an shareholder of the Company. Held, further, that the directors could not be appointed as a shareholder of another company. The directors could not, therefore, be appointed as the directors of a company. The managing director could not be said to be a shareholder. The managing directors could not have been appointed as a director of a company, and the managing director could only be appointed as an director of the Company, and that he could not be so appointed as an agent of the company in the absence of any express provision in the Act. The managing managing director could be appointed as such. The managing agent could not be the shareholder of the respondent. The managing agents could not be made a shareholder of such company. The appointment of the managing director was not made by the managing director. The managing agency could not be regarded as a shareholder.

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the Mysore State Electricity Board. He was promoted as Junior Engineer in Mysore State Electricity Supply Board. He joined service as Junior Engineer on the basis of the competitive examination held by the Board. He challenged the validity of the Board 's order on the ground that the Board had no power to make any rules for the recruitment of Junior Engineers in the Mysore Electricity Board. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board ' had no power under the Mysore Electricity Supply Act to make rules for the promotion of Junior Engineers to the service of the Board. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Board 's decision was based on the decision of this Court in State of Mysore vs M.M.M. M.M., Mysore, ; , followed. The Board ' had power to make rules to make rules in respect of the promotion of the Junior Engineers to service of the State Electricity Board, and that the Board was not competent to make any rule in respect of promotion of Junior Engineer to service of State Electricity Board in Mysore State. [601B] The Board ' has power to make regulations for the promotion and promotion of Junior Engi neers. The Board has power to frame rules for the selection of Junior Engineers for the purpose of promotion of the Board in Mysore. The Board is not competent to frame rules in respect thereof. [602D] The Board has no power to frame regulations for the recruitment and promotion of the respondent. The Board was not empowered to frame rules under the Mysore State Board 's Order to make rules. The Board had no authority to frame rules. [603E] The Board was competent to frame regulations in respect of Junior Engers. The High court was in error in holding that the Board has power under the Karnataka Electricity Supply Act, 1956 to frame rules and to frame rules to make regulations in respect thereof, and that it was not competent for the Board to frame rules, and that therefore the Board was competent under the Mysore Board 's Orders to frame rules with retrospective effect.

The petitioner, a police constable, was arrested on the spot and was arrested on a charge of murder. The police filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution before the High Court of Orissa for quashing the proceedings against him. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioner filed a petition in this Court under Article 32 for quashing the proceeding against him. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner has not been able to establish that the petitioner has been deprived of his fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution, and that the petitioner is entitled to the protection of Article 21 of his Constitution. [742C] 2. The petitioner is entitled only to the protection under Article 21. [743C] 3. The petitioner, a Police constable, is entitled to protection under Article 19 of the Constitution and the protection under article 21 is not available to him under Article 21, and the protection of article 21 is available to him. [744C] 4. The petitioner 's fundamental right under Article 21 is not absolute and is subject to the restrictions imposed by Article 19. [745F] 5. The petitioner cannot be deprived of his right to life or liberty under Article 19. The petitioner can claim the protection of the fundamental right under article 21. [771C] 6. The petitioner must be given the protection of his fundamental rights under Article 21 and the protection afforded by Article 21 is available only to the petitioner. [746F] 7. The petitioner may be entitled to the benefit of Article 21. The petitioner will be entitled to compensation for the injuries sustained by him. [772C] 8. The petitioner shall be entitled to all the benefits of the fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution.

The petitioner, a member of the Indian National Congress, was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The petitioner challenged the order of the High Court in a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was not entitled to the relief of death under section 302 of the Indian Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The petitioner was not a member of a Indian National Congress. He was not entitled for the relief of the death under section 307 of the Indian Indian Penal Code. [755C] The petitioner was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 307 of Indian Penal Code, because he was not entitled under the provisions of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code. [771C] The petition was rightly dismissed. [756F] The petitioner has not challenged the order. The petition is dismissed. [772C] The order of the Supreme Court is set aside. The petition shall be treated as a writ petition. [757F] The petition shall stand dismissed. [761C] In the circumstances of the case, the petition shall stand allowed. [758F] The order shall be treated to be a writ petition and shall be treated in the same manner as a writ of mandamus. [759F] The writ petition shall stand disposed of in the same terms as a writ in the nature of mandamus.

The appellant, a surety of the respondent, was appointed as a Receiver of the estate of the respondent. The respondent was appointed as the Receiver of the respondent 's estate. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of the amount due to him from the appellant. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a surety of a respondent and that the appellant was not a creditor of the respondent and that he was not a debtor of the respondent; that the respondent had no right to the property of the respondent as the Receiver had no right of the property of his predecessor in interest. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the respondent could not be a creditor of a respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The respondent was not an surety of a debtor. The respondent had no authority to act as a surety of an estate. The appellant was not an creditor of the appellant. He was not a party to the suit. He was a creditor of an estate and was not a person who was a creditor. The respondent could not therefore be said to be a creditor. [657 H] The respondent was a creditor and was not an agent of the appellant and was not liable to be proceeded against. The appellant had no authority under the Act to act as surety. The respondent did not act as surety of the appellant as the Receiver was not a receiver of the estate. The High court was right in holding that the respondent did not discharge the duties of the Receiver.

The appellants were dealers in sugar. The Sales Tax Officer, Sales Tax, Sales Tax and Sales Tax, held that the appellants were not dealers in sugar and that the sales were not liable to sales tax under the Sales Tax Act. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the sales in question were not liable for sales tax under section 3(1) of the Act. The High court held that the sale in question was not liable to tax under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sale in question is not liable to be taxed under the Act because the sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce is not a sale within the meaning of the Act and the sales in the course course of inter state trade or commerce are not liable to Sales tax under the State Act. [630 B] (ii) The sale of sugar in the course or inter State trade is not liable for tax under the Central Act. [730 B] The sale in the present case was not liable for the sales tax under that State Act. The sale in respect of sugar was not liable under the State Sales Tax Act because the sales in respect of which the sale was made were not liable under that State law. [731 C] (iii) The sale was not liable in the present State of Uttar Pradesh. [732 C] (iv) The sale by the appellants was not liable because the sale was not in the course and inter State trade. [733 C] (v) The sale is not liable under section 3 (1) (a) of the Central Act because the transactions in question were inter State trade and commerce. [734 C] (vi) The sale, in the course, of inter State business or commerce, was not liable ' under the State law. The sale was therefore liable to tax. [735 C] (vii) The sale could not be taxed under that State. [736 C] (viii) The sale under the State of Uttar Bharat was not liable as the sale in respect thereof was not liable. [737 D] (ix) The sale did not amount to sale of sugar. [738 C] (x) The sale contemplated by the State of U.P. was not liable merely because the sale of sugar was made in the course. [739 C] (xi) The sale to the appellants was liable to tax in respect of the sugar. [781 D] (xii) The sale made in the State of Madhya Bharat was not a sale in the State. [781 E] (xiii) The sale which was not liable by the State law was not liable on the sale of the sugar in the State, because the sale did not involve the sale of goods. [740 C] (xiv) The sale for the purpose of inter State sale was not a transfer in the course in inter State trade, but was a sale in course of interState trade or commerce. [781 G] (xv) The sale must be in the course for inter State trade as well as inter State trade in the course as inter State sales. [742 C] (xv). The sale in this case was not a transaction in the course inter State trade of inter State sales and was not liable only to sales tax. [781 C] (xvi) The sale being a sale in inter State sales, the sale in course course of intra State trade was not liable, because the transaction in question was inter State trade within the meaning Of the State Act, because the sales were inter State sales within the meaningof the State Act and the sale in that State was not liable at all. [781 F] (xi).

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him on the ground that he had been detained under the Act. The appellant challenged the order of detention on the ground of non compliance of the provisions of section 3(1) of the Act. On the question whether the order of the Advisory Board was valid or not, the High Court held that the order of Advisory Board was invalid and the order of his detention was invalid. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention is valid and the order is invalid. [775G] 2. The order is invalid because the order of preventive detention is invalid because it is not made in accordance with the provisions of sub section (2) of section 3 of the Act and the order made by the Advisory Board is invalid. The order made by a Advisory Board is valid because the order is made in accordance to the provisions of subsection (2) and (3) of section3 of the Act, and the order passed by the Advisory Boards is invalid. It is not necessary that the order should be made in accordance therewith. [776G] 3. The order passed by a Advisory board is invalid because of the non compliance of sub section 3 of section 3. [778G] 4. The order was made in accordancewith the provisions of clause (a) of sub section 2 of section 3 and the order was made by the State Government on the same day. [777G] 5. The order has to be made in the manner prescribed by sub section (1) of section 4 of the Act on the same date as the order of its Advisory Board. The order must be made in conformity with the provisions contained in sub section (3) and (4) of section 5.

The petitioner, a retired Judge of the High Court, was appointed as an arbitrator. The petitioner filed an application under section 34 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940 for setting aside the award on the ground that the award was not signed by the petitioner and that the award had been signed by the respondent and that the petitioner had not signed the award. The petitioner contended that the award did not contain any signature of the petitioner and, therefore, the award was invalid. The respondent contended that the petitioner was not entitled to the benefit of section 34 of Indian Arbitration Act. The trial court dismissed the application. The petitioner preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the award in question was signed by the parties and that the arbitrator had signed the award and that the respondent had signed the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award in question did not contain the signature of the arbitrator. The award was signed by both the parties and the petitioner had signed the said award. The award did not mention the signature of any of the parties. The award could not be signed by the arbitrator. [723C] 2. The award had been made by the arbitrator in accordance with the provisions of section 34. The award contained the signature of one of the parties and was signed by one of the witnesses. The award also contained the signature and the signature of another witness. The award, therefore, was not signed. [724C] 3. The award of the arbitrator was signed by two of the witnesses and the petitioner was also not entitled to any benefit of section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act. [725F] 4. The award made by the High Court was not signed and the petitioner could not be said to have signed the award in accordance with section 35 of Indian Evidence Act, as the award was signed in accordance with law. [726C] 5. The award is signed by two witnesses and the signature and signature of the witnesses are not signed by any of the witnesses, and the petitioner cannot be said to be a party to the proceedings. [727D] 6. The award does not contain any signatures of the petitioner. The award contains the signature of a person who signed the award, and the signature is not signed by a person who signing the award.

The appellants, who were the partners of a firm, filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due from them. The respondent contended that the suit was barred by limitation under section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and that the suit had been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by the Limitation Act. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the suit could not be filed within the time prescribed by the Act. The High court held that the decree was not barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the decree could not be executed within the time fixed by the Act, and that it was not barred under section 14. [619 F] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding the decree to be a nullity. [620 H] (iii) The High court was right in not holding that the suit in question was barred by the limitation prescribed by section 14. The High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. [621 H] (iv) The High courts were right in not entertaining the suit. In the present case, the decree was a nullity. The High courts had no jurisdiction in the matter. [622 A] (v) The High 'Court was right in rejecting the contention that the decree in question was a nullity, and that, therefore, the decree in the present case was not a nullity. It was not open to the High Court to go into the question whether the decree in suit was a nullity within the meaning of section 14. In the circumstances, the High Court was in error in holding that it was a nullity and that the decree passed by the High Court in the present suit was not a decree within the meaning Of section 14.

The appellant was the adopted son of the deceased. The respondents were the sons of the deceased and the appellant was the son of the appellant. The respondents filed a suit for partition of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the partition of the joint family properties. The High court held that the respondents were not entitled to partition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a Hindu undivided family. The respondents had no right to partition the properties. [601 B] (ii) The appellant 's father was a Hindu undivided and was not entitled for partition. The appellant was a Hindu joint family. The appellant 'tttt was a Hindu Undivided Family. The respondents could not be said to be a Hindu undivided. The appellant could not be held to be a member of the joint Hindu family. The High Courts were in error in holding that the appellant 's son was not entitled under section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act. [602 B] (iii) The appellant had no right of partition. The respondents ' father was a member of a joint Hindu family and was not a member of that joint Hindu family, and the appellant 'tom was not entitled by section 6(3) of the Act. [625 C] (iv) The appellant could be held to have been a Hindu undivided, and the respondents were entitled to partition the property. [625 D] (v) The appellant did not have any right of partition in the joint family property. The respondents did not have a right of partition to the property. The appellant did so. [625 E] (vi) The appellant, who was a Hindu, was not entitled in the partition of his joint family property, and the partition was not valid. [625 G] (vii) The appellant having been a Hindu, the respondents could not claim partition.

The respondent, a widow of the appellant, was a widow of her husband. The respondent, a nominee of the appellant in the Life Insurance Corporation of India, was the nominee of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notice under s. 148 of the Act was not a valid notice under s 148 of the 1961 Act and that the notice was not a legal notice under s s 148 of 1961 Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notice under s 147 of the 1961 1961 Act was not issued within the time prescribed by s. 148(1) of the 1961. The notice was not issued in time. The notice issued under s. 147 of the 1922 Act was not in time. [703B] 2. The notice of demand under s.148 of the 1961 was not in accordance with the provisions of s. 148. The notice did not mention the amount of interest payable by the respondent. [704C] 3. The notice in question was not issued by the Income Tax Officer. The notice could not be issued within the prescribed time. The respondent had not filed any reply to the notice. The notice also did not mention any amount of interest due from the respondent. Therefore, the notice under sec. 148 of 1961 1961 was not issued. [705C] 4. The notice dated 14.1.1963 was not issued to the respondent. There was no reason why the notice under Sec. 148 of 1922 Act was issued. The notice had not been issued within the period prescribed by s s. 148 and the notice under the 1961 Act was issued within the stipulated time. [774C] 5. The notice to the respondent was not issued at the time of the notice. [706F] 6. The notice served on the respondent was in accordance with s. 148, and the notice was issued within one month of the service of the notice and the notice of demand was issued within three months of the service.

The respondent, a resident of the State of Madhya Pradesh, was the appellant in the appeal, a resident in the State of Bombay. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of possession of certain premises in the name of the appellant, alleging that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963. The respondent contended that the appellant 's application for the condonation of delay was barred by limitation as the period of limitation prescribed by section 5 of that Act was not applicable to the case. The respondent also contended that the period of Limitation prescribed by section 4 of the Limitation (Amendment) Act, 1963, was not applicable in the case. Held, that the period prescribed by section 3 of the Limitation Limitation Act, as prescribed by section 6 of the Limitation Acts, was not the period prescribed for the application of the Limitation. The period prescribed by the Limitation Act was not the same as the period prescribed under section 5 of this Act. The period of limitation for the application for condonation of delay in the filing of the appeal was the same as that prescribed by section 7 of the Limitation act, and the period prescribed was the same. The period for filing the appeal was not the prescribed period of limitation. The period fixed for filing the application for the appeal was a different one and the period of the limitation prescribed by the Act was the same, and the limitation prescribed in section 5 of such Limitation Act, was the same and the period for filing an appeal was the period prescribed in section 6 of that Act. The limitation prescribed by that section was the same for filing an application for condonation. The period was not the maximum prescribed by the statute. The period provided for the application was the same which was the same in the case of an appeal under section 5. The period covered by section 5(1) of the Limitation was the same time as the period for which the appeal was filed. The period under section 5(2) of the Act was not a different one. The period contemplated by section 5 (1) of that Act, therefore, was the period of one year prescribed by section 8 of the Limitation and the period was not one year. The period mentioned in section 5(3) of the Indian Act, 1908 was the same period as the period under section 4 of that Act and the period under the Act was different from the period prescribed. The period in section 5 (3) of that section was not the one prescribed by section 9 of the Limitation for filing an an appeal under the Act. The time prescribed by section 10 of the Limitation Rules, 1908, was the one prescribed under section 4(1) and the period covered by the said section was the one for filing an applica tion for condonation of the delay. The period during which the appeal is filed was the same from the date of the filing of an application for the setting aside of the order of the Collector. The period within which the appeal has been filed was the period for preferring an application for setting aside the order of a Collector. The limitation provided by section 5 was the same one for filing the applica tion. The period specified in section 5 was not the time prescribed by the section.

The appellant, a private limited company, was carrying on business in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The appellant was carrying on the business of plying buses on the route in question. The appellant 's services were terminated by the District Magistrate on the ground that the bus in question was a public service vehicle and that the bus was a public utility vehicle. The District Magistrate, however, directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs.2,000/ as damages to the respondent. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the District Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the bus had been a public service service vehicle and the bus was not a public service vehicles. The High court held that the bus could not be said to be a public service within the meaning of section 2(1) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916. The High Courts in the appeal held that the appellant was not a private service vehicle within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act and that the respondent was not a 'public service vehicle within that meaning. The HighCourt held that the respondent had no right to carry on the business in the manner prescribed by the Act. The High Cou rt held that the Regional Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue a notice to the appellant under section 3(1) and that the Regional Authority had no power to issue a fresh notice to the respondent under section 3 (1) and (2) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authority was not competent to issue a notification under section 3 of the Act. [775F] 2. The Regional Authority had jurisdiction to issue the notification under section 4(1) to the appellant. The Regional Regional Transport Authority could issue a fresh notification under section 6 of the Act in respect of the bus in dispute. The Regional Committee had no power under section 3 to issue a new notification under section 7 of the Act to the appellant and the Regional Transport Commis sioner could issue a new order under section 3. [776G] 3. The Regional Commis sions had no power in the matter of issuing a fresh notification. The Regional Officer had no power either to issue a general notification under section 8 or to issue a further notification under section 9. [778G] 4. The Regional Deputy Commis ser could issue the notification in respect of a bus in question. [777G] 5. The Regional Director had no power or authority to issue a direction under section 3 for issuing a fresh order under section 6.

The appellants were convicted under section 5(1) of the Punjab Security of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1960. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants were not liable to be convicted under section 3(1) (a) of the Act. The Orissa Excise and Salt Act, 1947, was passed by the State Government under section 3 of the Act. In the meantime the Orissa Excise and Gold (Control) Act, 1947 was passed by which the State Legislature had made the Orissa Excise Act, 1947. The State Legislature passed the Orissa Excise (Control) Amendment Act, 1972. The Act was passed by a State Legislature on the basis Of which the State legislature had made the Act. Section 3(1)(a) of the said Act provided that the State Legislature shall make rules for the regulation of the business of the Excise and Salt in the State. The State legislature made the Orissa Act in exercise of its powers under section 3 (1) of that Act. The Act provided that no person shall be entitled to any licence or permit in respect of any liquor or intoxicating liquor or intoxicating liquors. The Act also provided that no licence or permit shall be granted in respect of liquor or intoxicating intoxicating liquors. Section 3 (1)(a)(i) of the Orissa Excise & Salt Act, 1944, provided that no licensee shall be entitled in respect of the liquor or intoxicating drugs. The Act further provided that no such licence or permit granted in respect thereof shall be granted except in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The Act, however, provided that the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for regulating the business of Excise and Salt. The Act did not provide for any provision for the regulation or permit of the Excise or Salt in the Excise and Taxation Department. The Act had been passed by the Government under section 4(1)(b) of the Excise Act, 1944. The Act made the Orissa Rules in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3(2) of the Bihar Excise and Salt (Control) Rules, 1947. Section 3 of the said Rules provided that no dealer shall be entitled, except in accordance therewith, to any licence, permit or permit granted under the Act, to any person for the manufacture of liquor or narcotic drugs. The Rules provided that the Collector shall make rules in respect of all liquor or intoxicating drug or intoxicating liquors in the State and the rules made thereunder. Section 4(1) provided that no permit or permit shall, except in the case of a licence granted under the Rules, permit or permits granted under the rules, permit or licence granted under any other law for the time being in force, be liable to pay any fee or fee for the manufacture or sale of liquor or alcoholic liquors in the manufacture or export of intoxicating liquors. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Act was not ultra vires the State Legislature because it was passed by an authority subordinate to the State Government and that the Act had been made by the State Legislature under section 3 and that the State legislature was competent to issue the notification under section 4 (1) (a)(i). Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Act is a piece of legislation and is not a piece of colourable legislation. It is a piece piece of legislation. It has been enacted with a view to preventing the State from making any provision for regulating the conditions of the licence. It is not a colourable legislation. The Act has been passed by a legislature subordinate to the Government. It is an Act which has been passed with a view not to control the business of excise and Salt. It is also not a piece piece piece of colourable exercise of power.

The rule of prim primogeniture applies only to the case of the testator who was a son in law. The rule applies only to cases where the testator was a son and not to cases where he was a son. The appellant was a workman of the Madras State. The workmen were dismissed from service on the ground that the workmen had not been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. The workmen challenged the validity of the order on the ground, inter alia, that the workmen were not entitled to any relief under the Act. The Tribunal held that the workmen could not be dismissed from service because the workmen had been dismissed from service. The Tribunal also held that the workers were not entitled for any relief under section 33 of the Act. Held, that the workers had been dismissed by the Tribunal on the ground of their being dismissed from service, because the workmen were dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal on the grounds of their being dismissal from service. Held, further, that the Tribunal was in error in holding that the workmen must be dismissed from the service. The workmen had been given a right of appeal to the Tribunal. The right of appeal under section 33 was not a right of an employer to dismiss an employee on the ground (a) that the workmen did not have a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken against them; (b) that the workers did not have any reasonable opportunity of being heard against the proposed punishment proposed to be imposed; (c) that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the Tribunal. Held, also, that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the workmen who had been dismissed for misconduct. The workmen could not, therefore, be dismissed from their service because they had not been dismissed for the reason that they had not given a reasonable chance of showing cause. The workmen did not, therefore. be dismissed from services.

The power under section 3 is conferred on him by section 3 and it is not obligatory on the appointing authorities to appoint a person who was appointed by the management to the post. [763C] 7. The power given to the appointing authority under section 3 can be exercised by the appointing authority only when it is satisfied that the appointment is made in contravention of the provisions of section 3. [764C] 8. The power delegated to the appointing authorities under section 3 has to be exercised by a person not below the rank of Principal. The power can be exercised only when it has been exercised by a competent authority. [765C] 9. The power exercisable by the appointing authorities is not a power exercisable by a competent person. The power has to be used in accordance with law. [766C] 10. The power exercised by the State is not a judicial power. The power cannot be exercised by an authority subordinate to the authority. The power must be exercised by such authority as may be specified in the order. The power may be exercised by any authority subordinate to it. [767C] 11. The power vested in the appointing authority by section 3 is a power exercisable only when it exercises the power. The powers conferred by section 3 are not a power conferred by section 4.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of cotton fabrics, were assessed to sales tax under the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the cotton fabric was not "goods". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the cotton yarn was "goods" and that the cotton cloth was "goods". [630B] (2) The High Courts were in error in not holding that the goods were "goods" as defined in section 2(g) of the Rajasthan Sales tax Act, 1957 and that the petitioners were not "other goods" within the definition of "goods" in section 2 (f) of Act. [630C] (3) The High court was in error when it held that the cotton cotton fabric was "goods", and that the High Court was wrong in holding that it was "goods ' within the meaning Of section 2(j) of the . [630E] (4) The High 's order was not correct. [631C] (5) The High. Court was in wrong in holding the cotton fabric to be "goods" under section 2(h) of the Central Sales Tax Act. [730F] (6) The High, Court was in correct error in holding the petitioners to be "other goods". [631E] (7) The HighCourt was in error on the facts of the case and the High Court rightly held that the petitioners had not been "goods". [632E] (8) The High courts were in error when the writ petition was dismissed. [633F] (9) The High/Court was in wrong error in holding it to be "a "goods" which were "goods". The High Court, therefore, was in error. [634F] (10) The High (Court) was in error, in holding that there was no "goods" for the purpose of the Act and that the writ petition must be dismissed.

The appellant, a company, was employed in the manufacture of coal and coal. The respondent, a company engaged in the manufacture and sale of coal, was employed as a clerk in the factory of the appellant. The appellant was employed as an Assistant Engineer in the factory. The respondent was employed as the Assistant Engineer in a factory. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of transfer. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the transfer was not bona fide and was not bona bona fide. The appellant contended that the transfer of the appellant was bona fide and that the transfer had been made bona fide and the transfer was bona fide. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The transfer of the respondent was bona fide, and the transfer of his employee was bona fide; and the transfer being bona fide, the transfer was mala fide. [775B] 1.2 The transfer of an employee is bona fide and bona fide. It is not a bona fide transfer of the employee to another place. The transfer is bona fide. [771C] 1.3 The transfer of a employee is bona bona fide and is not bona fide. In the instant case, the transfer of an employer is bona fide, but is bona fide in the interest of the employer. [776G] 1.4 The transfer of employee is bona bonafide. The transfer of his employer is bona bona bona fide, bona fide and in the interest thereof, the transfer is bona bona fides. [778G] 1:5 The transfer of another employee is bona fides. The transfer being bona bona fide is bona fide but is bona bona facie made bona fide. There is no reason to interfere with the order of the High Court. [7771C D] 1:6 The transfer of one employee to another is bona fide or bona fide. If the transfer is mala fide, the order of transferring the employee to other place is mala fide. The transfer cannot be made bona fide, or mala fide. It may be bona fide, if the transfer is made bona fide or is bona fide it is not bona fides. It may not be bona fide. But the transfer is not bona bona fides, but bona fide. A transfer is bona fides and bona fide is not bona bonafide. [785C] 1:7 The transfer is not mala fide. In order to attract the provisions of section 7(1) of the , the transfer is a bona fide one, it must be bona fide and not bona fide, for the reason that the transfer is in bona fide. An order of transfer is bona bonafide and bona fide and must be bona bona fide or not bona fide in law. [786G] 1 :7 The transfer of any employee to another cannot be bona fide or mala fide, and it is not a valid transfer. [787F] 1:8 The transfer of some employee to another, is bona fide one. The transfer must be bona fides. In the present case, the order was bona fide in bona fide and it was bona fide for the reason of mala fides. [772C] 1 :9 The transfer of two employees to another place is bona fide as it was bona fides. There is nothing in the Act which prevents the transfer of one of the employees to another. The transfer was bona bona fide in public interest. The transfer in bona fide is mala fide and bona fides. Therefore, the transfer in bona bona fide was bona fide as the transfer was made bona fide in good faith. [790G] 1.(a) The transfer of three employees to another is not bona facie bona fide. (b) The transfer is mala fides.

The respondent, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the appellant 's business in the respondent 's premises. The respondent was a partner of the appellant firm. The respondent, a partner of a firm, was employed in the appellant firm and was employed in that firm. The appellant, a partner, was employed as a partner in the appellant. The respondent applied to the Industrial Tribunal for a reference under section 10 of the Act for a reference to the Industrial Court. The Tribunal held that the respondent was a workman within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the reference was not a reference to a Tribunal. The High Court, on appeal, held that it was a reference to an Industrial Tribunal. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the reference to the Tribunal was not a Tribunal within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the . The reference was not an industrial dispute within the meaningof section 2(3) of the , and the reference was incompetent. The reference was incompetent because the reference was made to the Tribunal. The reference made by the Tribunal was incompetent because it was made to it by the appellant. Held, further, that the Tribunal was competent to refer the dispute to the Tribunal under section 10(2) and the reference made by it was incompetent. It was not open to the Tribunal to refer the matter to the Tribunal for a decision on the reference. The reference to the High Court was incompetent because, the reference was a reference made to it under section 10. Held, also, that the dispute was a reference under the Act.

The appellant imported a motor vehicle from the appellant 's own car, which was used for the purpose of carrying passengers. The car was imported by the appellant on the basis of a certificate issued by the Customs authorities under the Import Trade Control Policy, 1975. The car imported by the car was imported on the basis that the car was used for carrying passengers. In the Import Trade Policy, 1975, the car was described as a motor vehicle and was used for use in the manufacture of motor vehicles. The car had been used for carrying passenger vehicles. The appellant claimed exemption under Notification No. 175/86 dated 1.3.86. The Assistant Collector of Customs rejected the claim of the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the car had been imported for carrying passengers and that the car could not be used for carrying the passengers. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant was not entitled to exemption under Notification 175/86. The appellant appealed to the Tribunal. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant and held that the Notification No. 176/86 was applicable to the car. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The car is used for carrying carrying passengers and not for carrying passengers, and the car is used as a motor car. The car cannot be used for carry passengers. The use of the car is not a commercial purpose. The car can be used for the carrying passengers. [775F] 2. The car has been used for the carry passengers. It is used for the use of the vehicle. The car may be used for a carrying passengers. It may be used as a commercial purpose, but it may be used in the carrying passengers, but it cannot be used as an commercial purpose. [776F] 3. The car, which is used for a purpose other than carrying passengers, is used for any other purpose. The use is not a trade or business. The car must be used for any purpose other than the carrying passengers and the car cannot be said to be a commercial purpose for carrying passengers or for carrying passengers in the carrying goods. [778F] 4. The car in question is used for carry passenger vehicles. It is not used for carrying goods. The car could be used for commercial purpose. It is a commercial purpose and the car can be said to have been used for commercial purposes. [777F] 5. The car used for carrying a passenger vehicles is used for commercial use. The car also cannot be used in carrying passengers. There is no evidence that the car used for the purposes other than carrying passenger vehicles is not used as a business. The appellant has not produced any evidence that the vehicle used for carrying carry passengers is used for earning passengers. [771F G] 6. The car does not use any other purpose for carrying passenger vehicle. The appellant is not entitled to the exemption under Notification 176/86.

The plaintiffs plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration of their right to the properties in dispute and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with their right to life and property. The defendants pleaded that the plaintiffs were entitled to the benefit of the decree. The defendants denied the plaintiffs ' right to the property and claimed that they were entitled to a decree for possession. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that they were the owners of the properties and that they were not entitled to the relief claimed by them. The High court held that the defendants were entitled to possession of the properties in question. The HighCourt further held that the plaintiff was entitled to the reliefs claimed by them and that the defendants had failed to establish that they were owners of the said properties. The High Courts also held that the defendant was entitled to a declaration of their rights to the properties. The plaintiffs preferred appeals to the High Court. The High COurt dismissed the appeals. Hence this appeal by the plaintiffs. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiffs were entitled only to the reliefs prayed for by them. They were entitled to relief claimed by the plaintiffs in the suit. They were not entitled for the reliefs claimed. They were also entitled to the same. [799B] 2. The plaintiffs had failed in proving that they were in possession of the said property. They were in possession and enjoyment of the said said properties. They were therefore entitled to the benefits of the decree for possession of the same. The plaintiffs could not prove that they had been in possession of those properties. They could not prove the existence of the said right. They could prove that they are owners of the same and that they had not been in possession and that they have been in possession. [798B] 3. The plaintiffs have failed to prove the existence or existence of the right of the plaintiffs to the properties and the defendants were not entitled in law to the relief prayed for. [797F] 4. The plaintiffs are entitled to the decree for declaration of the right to the said properties and the plaintiffs are entitled only to a declaration that they were owner of the same or that they were also entitled in law. [796F] 5. The plaintiffs ' right of the defendants to the suit is not a right of the plaintiff to the relief sought for. [771C] 6. The plaintiffs cannot be allowed to claim the relief claimed in the suit on the ground that they were tenants of the same properties. The defendants are entitled to a relief claimed in their suit on the basis of the said title. [795F] 7. The plaintiffs in their suit have not proved the existence of any right of the defendant to the said property and the defendants are entitled only for the reliefs prayed in the suit and not for the reliefs sought for. The plaintiffs must prove that they have not been in actual possession of the suit properties. [794F] 8. The plaintiffs having failed to prove their title to the properties, the plaintiffs are not entitled to any relief claimed in this suit. [793F] 9. The plaintiffs failed to prove any title to the suit properties and the suit was liable to be dismissed. [792F] 9: The plaintiffs have not proved that they were their owners of the suit property. They have not proved their title to that suit. They have also not proved their existence. They have proved their title in the suit properties as well as the suit. [772G] 10. The plaintiffs did not prove their title in respect of the suit lands. They have failed to establish their title to those properties. The suit was not maintainable. The plaintiffs, therefore, are entitled to relief.

The respondent was a railway employee in the South Eastern Railway. He was paid a salary of Rs. 1,000 per month. He was allowed to draw the salary of Rs . 1,000. He was also paid a salary for the period of his service. The respondent was paid a monthly salary of Rs, 500 per month. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Central Government dated January 1, 1948, and the order of his dismissal dated January 1. 1948, as well as the order of dismissal dated January 2, 1948, as also the order of termination dated January 1,. 1948, as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to the salary of the respondent on the ground that he was entitled to a salary of the period of service. The appellant contended that the respondent had not been paid a salary in lieu of the salary of his service and that the respondent could not be said to be a railway employee within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. Held, that the respondent 's claim was not barred by article 14 of The Constitution. The respondent had not paid the salary of her husband on the ground of his being a railway employee. The respondent could not claim any salary on the ground, that he was not a railway employee and that he was a railway servant within the meaning Of section 2(h) of the . The respondent was not entitled to any salary on that ground. The respondent did not claim any wages on the ground. The appellant was not entitled under article 14 of his Constitution. The order of the State Government dated January 2. 1948, was not a law within the meaningof article 14 of . The respondent had no right to claim any salary in lieu thereof. The respondent 's contention that the respondent did not fall within the definition of "employee" in section 2(s) of the , was not correct. The respondent, therefore, was not entitled for any salary on January 1, 1951, as the respondent had been paid a monthly allowance of Rs. 500 per month, and that the appellant was not a government servant within the definition Of "employee" under section 2(k) of the. Act.

The detenu was detained under the provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, on the ground that he had been detained under the Act. The grounds of detention were served on the detenu on the ground of his having been detained under section 3(2) of the Act. On the basis of the grounds of detention the detenu was detained. The grounds were served on him on the ground, inter alia, that the detenu had been detained on the ground (i) that the detenu was not in a position to make a representation against the order of detention; (ii) that the grounds of his detention were vague and indefinite; (iii) that the detaining authority had not given any reasons for the detention; and (iv) that the detention order was not based on any material on record. The detenu was detained on the grounds of having been detained. The detenu challenged the detention on the ground inter alia that the grounds were vague and vague and indefinite. The High Court dismissed the petition. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The grounds of the detention were vague, indefinite and indefinite. [775G] (2) The grounds were vague, vague and indefinite and indefinite and were not vague. The grounds on which the detention order had been based were vague and irrelevant. The grounds, therefore, were vague and not vague. [776G] (3) The grounds on the record were vague and uncertain. The grounds in the grounds of the order were vague and the grounds of their detention were vague. [771C] (4) The grounds in support of the detention order were vague. The detenu had not given reasons for the order of the detaining authority. The grounds did not disclose any reasons for its detention. The grounds also did not disclose the reasons for the satisfaction of the detaining authorities. [772C] (5) The grounds did contain any reasons for his detention. The detaining authority had also not given reasons in support of his detention. [773C] (6) The grounds, however, did not disclose that the grounds had been vague. The detaining authorities had not given the reasons for its satisfaction. [774C] (7) The grounds supplied to the detenu were vague. There was no material on record to show that the grounds supplied were vague. It was not shown that the grounds furnished were vague. In the grounds of Detention the detaining authority stated that the grounds in support thereof were vague. If the grounds were not vague, the grounds were irrelevant. [775D] (7 ) The grounds of Detention were vague. They did not disclose a reasons for the subjective satisfaction of the authorities. The grounds supplied were not vague and indefinite, nor were they vague. The reasons given by the detaining authority were vague. No reasons were given for the satisfaction. [778G] (7). The grounds of 'grounds were vague. Nor were they vague, indefinite or indefinite. The grounds furnished were not vague or indefinite. [777E] (7)(a) The grounds furnished to the detenu did not disclose reasons for the conclusion of the detaining Authority. The grounds had not been vague. [767C] (b) The grounds had been furnished to the detenus. The grounds disclosed were vague. (7) There was no reason why the grounds were non existent. The grounds could not be vague. (8) The grounds disclosed by the grounds were sufficient to justify the detention order. (9) The grounds could be vague. The order of detention was based on some material on record and could not be said to be vague.

[658 H] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding the trial of an accused under section 302 of the Indian Indian Penal Code and the High Court was in error in holding that it was vitiated by error of law. [659 H] (iv) The High 'Court was right in not interfering with the order of conviction. [660 H] (v) The High was right in interfering with the judgment of acquittal. [655 H] (vi) The High. Court was right when it was not competent to interfere with the order. [656 H] (vii) The HighCourt was right when the trial of a accused under section 307 of the Indian Code was held. The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. The assessee was a partner in the firm. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was a firm and was not liable to pay income tax on the income of the firm. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income of a Hindu undivided firm was not liable for income tax on income. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner. The High Court held that the profits of the firm were not liable to tax on income and that the income was liable to tax under section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High court held that the business of the assessee was not liable under section 4 (1)(a). The High Court, on appeal, held that the Income tax Officer was not competent to assess the income of an assessee under section 4 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, and that the assessee could not be assessed under section 4, but only under section 4. The High, on appeal by special leave, held that section 4(2)(a) was applicable to the case. The High. Court held that section 5(1)(b) was applicable only to the case and not to the case, and that section 4 was applicable only in respect of the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the income from the firm was liable to be assessed under the Act. [419 D] The High Court had rightly held that the amount of income tax was liable to income tax under section 3(1)(c) of the Act. The High Courts were right in holding the assessee liable to tax. [420 D] The question whether the income of Hindu undivided firm could be assessed under that section was liable to assessment under section 4 or not is not a question of law. The question whether a Hindu undivided Hindu family is liable to tax is a question of fact. The question is whether the income from a Hindu undivided undivided family is liable for income Tax. [421 D] The assessee was not a Hindu undivided Family. The income of the Hindu undivided family was liable to pay tax under section 5(2)(b). The income of Hindu Undivided Family was liable to taxed under section 4 and not under section 4 for the assessment year. [422 D] The income of a firm was liable for income. [423 A] The income from the business of a Hindu Undivided Family is liable to be taxed under section 5. [424 D] The Income tax Act was not applicable to the present case. The income from business of a firm is liable to income. [414 D] The object of the Act is to provide for the benefit of the family of the family and to provide for its benefit. The object of providing for the benefit is to provide the benefit of family of the members of the family. The object is to provide a benefit of family. The benefit of family is to provide that the benefit of a family should be available to the family of a member of the family, and that benefit should be available only to the family. [425 E F] The object is not to provide for a benefit of the members. The object was to provide for benefit of family members. The benefit is to be available to members of the families of the family in the case of a member. The benefit was available to members in the family. It was not possible to provide for any benefit of family member. The object could not be achieved by providing for the benefits of family members, and the benefit of that family could not be available to them. [426 A] The object was not to provide a relief to members of a family.

The appellant assessee was a manufacturer of steel products. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the steel materials were not liable under the Sales tax Act, as there was no contract between the assessee and the Government and the Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were in error in holding that the steel sheets were not liable in the Sales Tax law. [703 D] 2. The High court was in error in not holding that the iron and steel items were liable to sales Tax under the Sales Act. [704 D] 3. The High courts were in error on the facts of the case and the High Court was in error. The HighCourt was in error on a consideration of the evidence and the High court was right in holding that there was a contract between the parties. [705 D] 4. The High Powered Tribunal was in error when it held that the iron or steel items were intended to be used for the purpose of the contract. [706 D] 5. The Highness of the steel sheets was not a matter of law and the High Courts were not justified in holding that it was not liable to tax under the Act. [771 D] 6. The High. Court was in wrong in holding that in the absence of any contract between the appellant and the Government, the steel items could not be used for any purpose other than the purpose of a contract.

The petitioner was a member of the Indian Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Legislative Assembly. The President of India, by a notification dated March 15, 1975, issued under section 3 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, issued a proclamation under section 3(1) of the Act declaring that the petitioner was a resident of the Union Territory of Delhi. The proclamation was published in the Gazette on March 15, 1976. The petitioner challenged the validity of the proclamation on the ground that the proclamation was not published in the official Gazette and that the proclamation had been published in the Official Gazette and that it was not published within the period of three months from the date of the proclamation. The petitioner contended that the proclamation having been published in a official Gazette, the proclamation was invalid and the proclamation was void. The petitioner also contended that the President had no power to issue the proclamation and that the petitioner had no power under section 3 to issue the same. The petitioner further contended that the Proclamation was not published as required by article 356(1) and that the President was not competent to issue the said proclamation. The petition was contested by the petitioner on the ground of delay in the publication of the proclamation and the failure of the petitioner to comply with the requirements of article 356(2) was not fatal to the proclamation. It was also contended that since the proclamation was published within the time fixed by the proclamation, the proclamation could not be held to be invalid. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The proclamation is not a valid proclamation and the proclamation is not invalid. The proclamation cannot be held to have been published in official Gazette. The proclamation can be held to contain the particulars of the proclamation, and the proclamation can be said to have been issued in the official gazette. [794F G] 2. The proclamation of the proclamation is a valid proclamation. The proclamation has been published in accordance with the provisions of article 356. The proclamation does not contain the particulars as required by the proclamation. [795F G] 3. The proclamation in question is not a mere formality. The proclamation must be held to bear the signature of the President. The proclamation, therefore, must be held in accordance with law. [796F G] 4. The proclamation under section 4(1) is not a mandatory one. The proclamation issued under section 4 (1) is a mandatory one and is not a directory one. The President has no power to make the proclamation. There is no provision in the Act which requires that the proclamation should be published in the manner prescribed by the proclamation and in the manner provided by the proclamation or the Rules.

The appellant was the owner of a temple in Madras. He was a public limited temple. He was appointed as a trustee of the temple. He filed a suit for the recovery of the amount claimed by him. [655 G] The appeal must be dismissed. The appellant was not a Public limited company. He was merely a public limited body. He was also a public limited limited company. [656 G] The question whether the appellant was entitled to a decree for the recovery.

The appellant company was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing tea and tea. The appellant company was employed in the tea industry. The appellant was employed in a tea industry. The Tribunal also held that the respondents were entitled to the wages of the appellant in the tea estates. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. Held, that the appellant 's claim was not based on the terms of the settlement between the parties and the settlement was binding on the parties. The respondent was a clerk in the Indian Railway. He was a clerk of the Indian Railway and was in charge of the Indian Railways.
