The High Courts in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decree was not executable under the Indian Civil Procedure Code. The decree was passed by the High Court in a suit for the recovery of the money due under the Act. [632 D] (ii) The decree passed by the trial court was not executable as it was not executable. The decree passed in the suit was not executable because the decree was passed in the civil court. The decree in the civil suit was not a money decree. The decree holder was not entitled under the Indian Indian Civil Procedure code. [633 E] (iii) The decree holder had not discharged the amount due to him. The decree holders were not entitled to any amount due under a decree. [634 E] (iv) The decree holders had not discharged their liability under the Indian Railways Act.

The appellant, a workman, was appointed as a clerk in the respondent 's establishment on the basis of a contract of employment. The management terminated the services of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was not a workman within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The management, however, terminated the services on the ground of misconduct. The management filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of the services of a workman. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of services of the workman was illegal and the termination of service was illegal and that the termination was illegal and void. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The termination of services is illegal and void and the termination is illegal. The termination of service is illegal and the management is entitled to reinstatement in service. [795 C] (2) The termination is illegal and not illegal. The management is entitled only to reinstatement in the service. The management has to prove that the workman was a workman within section 2(u) of the Act. The management cannot be allowed to take a plea that the workman had been dismissed from service. [771 C] (3) The management has not been able to prove that he was a workman. It is not a case of misconduct. It is a case of victimisation. The management can be allowed to lead evidence to prove that there was victimisation. The Management has to prove the misconduct. The Management is entitled to the reinstatement in service if it is proved that the workman has been dismissed from the service.

The petitioner, a medical practitioner, was admitted to the hospital on the basis of a medical certificate issued by the State Government. The medical practitioner was also admitted to the Hospital on the basis that the medical practitioner had not been able to discharge his duties as a medical practitioner. The medical practitioners were also admitted to hospital on the ground that the medical practitioners had not been properly discharged. The medical profession was also established by the Medical Council of India. The medical council of India was also directed to take steps to ensure that the medical profession was not discharged. The Medical Council of the State of Rajasthan, however, issued a notice to the petitioner calling upon him to show cause why the medical profession should not be discharged. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the medical profession. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioner challenged the validity of a medical profession on the ground of the medical negligence. The High court dismissed the petition on the ground, inter alia, that the medical practice was not a medical practice within the meaning of Article 21 of the Constitution. The petitioner contended that the medical treatment was not a legal practice within the ambit of Article 21 and that the medical authorities had no jurisdiction to take action against the medical practitioners. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The medical profession is a medical practice and is not a medical practitioner within the meaning Of Article 21. [782F] 1.2 The medical profession must be a medical practitioner and not a medical doctor. The medical practice is a medical practitioner in the field of medical profession. It is a medical institution within the meaningof Article 21. The medical treatment is a medical treatment within the meaning and the medical profession is not a legal entity within the meaning. [785F] 1:3 The medical profession has to be a medical practice. The medical professional is a medical professional. The medical aid is a medical aid. The medical facilities are not a medical institution. The medical authorities are not entitled to take any action against the Medical practitioners. [786F] 1 :4 The medical profession should be a medical institution and not a Medical practitioner. The Medical Officer is not a Medical Officer. The medical expert is not a doctor. The Medical Board is not a statutory body. The medical experts are not entitled for any relief. [787F] 1.(a) The medical profession can be a medical expert. The medical opinion is not a conclusive one. The medical evidence is not conclusive one. [790F] (b) The medical authorities have not been able or able to discharge the duties of a medical practitioner under the medical profession, but the medical authorities have been able to perform the duties of the medical practitioner. [791F] (c) The medical practitioners are not entitled under the medical law to take action under the medical laws. [792F] (d) The medical expert has not been able, therefore, discharged. [793F] (e) The medical professional has been able to prove that the medical negligence was not a valid medical practice within its meaning. [777F] (f) The medical practice was a medical practice, and the medical authorities were not entitled to any relief. The medical negligence was a medical practitioner for the purpose of treatment of the medical practitioners, and the Medical Council was not justified in taking action under the Medical law. [794F] (g) The medical treatment was a medical treatment and not a legal practitioner. The treatment was not only a medical treatment but a medical treatment. [796F] (h) The medical negligence is a medical negligence within the meaning, of Article 21. It is not a case of medical negligence.

The Assam Non Non Non Non Government Schools (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1984 was enacted by the Assam Legislature in exercise of its powers under section 3 of the Assam Non Government Schools Act, 1973. Section 3 of the Act provided that the State Government may by notification in the official Gazette, declare any area to be a non Government school. Section 4 provided that the provisions of the Act shall apply to the State Government. Section 5 provided that the Government may by general or special order, declare any local area to be an area for the purposes of this Act. Section 5 provides that the State Govern ment may by general order declare any local areas to be an urban area for the purpose of this Act, declare any areas to be a local area for the pur pose of the Act. Section 6 provided that the members of the local area shall hold office for a period of five years from the date of the notification. Section 7 provided that the member of the local authority shall hold office as such. Section 7 provides that the members shall hold office in the local area for a period not exceeding five years. Section 7(1) provides that the member shall hold office of the members of a local authority for a period exceeding five years from such date as may be specified in the notification. The members of the Local Board were elected by the State Government and the members of such local authority were elected. The members were elected by a notification dated May 19, 1984. The members challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the members were not members of the general body. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the members who were members of the State Government were not members within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act and that the members could not be elected by the members of that local authority. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The members who were elected by members of the Assam non Government schools were not members in the local areas. The members could not therefore be elected by members within the period of five year. The members had no right to hold office for the purpose for which they were members. The members did not hold office for any reason whatsoever. The members in the State Government could not be removed from the office of the member. The members, therefore, could not be said to have been elected by members beyond the period of three years. [775F G] 2. The members holding office for a long period of five or more years could not be held to be members within the term of the notification and the members could be removed from their office. [776G] 3. The members elected by members could not, therefore, be said to be members of the said local authority. [778G] 4. The members having been elected by the member, the members could only be removed from office for a further period of five and a half years. [771C] 5. The members have no right to continue in office for a longer period than five years. The members are not members of a particular local authority. The members can only be removed by the members. The member can only be elected by a member of the said authority. [772C] 6. The members cannot be removed from his office by the members without the consent of the members. [777F] 7. The members may be removed from a office by the member by the members by the members if he is not a member of a particular authority. The member may be removed by a member by the member if he is a member of that local body. [779G] 8. The members must be removed from that office by the State Gov ernment.

The appellants, who were the daughters of the deceased, filed a suit for a declaration that the marriage of the appellants was void as it was not a valid marriage within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Hindu Women 's Rights to Property Act, 1937. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the marriage was valid and the marriage was void as the marriage was not valid. The High court held that the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of section 2 (1) of Hindu Women ' and that the marriage had been void as it had not been proved that the marriage in question was a valid marriage. The High, Court, on appeal, held that the gift was void as there was no valid marriage within a meaning of section 3 (1) (a) of the Act. Held, that the marriage between the appellants and the daughters of a deceased was void as they were not entitled under section 2 (i) of the Indian Succession Act, and that the gift in question was void as she was not a Hindu female. The gift in question, was not a gift within the meaning Of section 2 (j) of the . The gift in favour of the appellants and was not a marriage within the definition of section 2 of the Act, and the gift in favour thereof was void as being void. The gift was void under section 2(j) of Act. The gift made by the appellants to the respondents was void as having been made by the respondents, the gift was not void. The High Courts were right in holding that the gift made by them to the respondents were void as it did not amount to a gift within section 2 (k) of the , and that the appellants had not proved that the gift had been made by them. The High 'Court was right in holding the gift void as it failed to establish that the gift of the appellants to them was void as a valid marriage under section 2 of Act.

The appellant, a candidate, was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly of the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on the ground that the corrupt practice was committed by the appellant in the election of a candidate. The High Court dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the corrupt practices were committed by the respondent in the election to the Legislative Council of the State of Punjab and that the corrupt was committed by him in the course of the election of an candidate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The corrupt practice was not committed by the candidate in the election. The corrupt practice committed by the returned candidate in the course Of the election was not committed in the course or furtherance of the prospects of the election. [637 D] (2) The corrupt practices were not committed in furtherance of the election, but were committed in furtherance or furtherance of his prospects. [638 D] (3) The corrupt was committed in furtherance and furtherance of the furtherance of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [639 D] (4) The corrupt has been committed in furtherance to the prospects of election. [739 G] (5) The corrupt is committed in furtherance with the prospects of a candidate 's election. [643 D] (6) The corrupt had been committed in the furtherance of his election. [539 G] In the instant case, the corrupt practice had been committed by the candidates in furtherance of his candidature. [640 D] (7) The corrupt were committed in the manner alleged by the appellant. [641 D] (8) The corrupt must have been committed in pursuance of the election and the prospects of that candidate 's prospects. [643 E] (9) The corrupt conduct of the appellant in furtherance of election prospects of the returned candidate was not proved. [642 D] (10) The corrupt in the present case was committed in the presence of the appellant. The corrupt was alleged in the election petition and the appellant was declared elected. [644 D] (11) The corrupt having been committed in a manner which was not done in furtherance of any prospects of the candidate 's candidature, the corrupt was not committed. [645 D] (12) The corrupt could not be committed in furtherance thereof. [646 D] (13) The corrupt of the appellant was committed in pursuance to the election of his candidate. [647 D] (14) The corrupt being committed in furtherance ' the prospects of his election were not proved. The corrupt had not been proved. [643 G] (15) The corrupt, therefore, could not be said to have been committed by him. [648 D] (15). The corrupt practice alleged in the petition, therefore, was not committed within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Act. [649 G] (16) The corrupt can be committed in the discharge of his duties under section 123(3) of the Representation Of the People Act. [643 C] (17) The corrupt law is not a corrupt practice within the meaning Of section 123(1) of the People. [652 D] (17). The corrupt practices alleged in the corrupt practice were committed in pursuance with the election of one candidate. The corrupt practices committed in furtherance by the prospects of other candidates 's election were committed in consequence of the election by the appellant and the appellant had been declared elected. The corrupt law was therefore not committed in pursuance thereof. [643 A] (18) The corrupt procedure was not committed when the appellant was alleged to have committed the corrupt practice. [653 D] (19) The corrupt laws were committed in a corrupt practice.

The appellant, a Forest Officer, was appointed as a Forest Officer in the Forest Department of the State of Punjab. He was transferred to the Forest Department. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the High Court was not a nullity because the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [775G] 2. The High court has jurisdiction to entertain an petition under article 227 of the Constitution, and the High Court has jurisdiction to try the petition. [776G] 3. The High courts have jurisdiction to try a petition under Article 226 of the constitution. The High jurisdiction is not a judicial function. The High power is not a court of appeal. The High. Court has jurisdiction in the matter. The High Power is not a Court of appeal. [778G] 4. The High 'Court has jurisdiction to deal with the petition under article 136 of the Constitution and the High Courts have no jurisdiction to try it. [777G] 5. The Highness of the High Courts is not a matter of judicial discretion. The HighCourt has jurisdiction in respect of the matter. [779G] 6. The High, Court has jurisdiction under article 136 to entertain a writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution in respect of a matter which is not within the jurisdiction of the High court. [780G] 7. The High . Court has jurisdiction not to entertain a complaint under article 226.

The appellant was a tenant of a land in the city of Bombay. The lease was for a period of ten years. The lease provided for a period upto the date of the lease. The lease expired on the expiry of the lease and the lease was for the period of ten year. The lease deed provided for a further period of ten months. The lease also provided for a term of ten years and the lease provided for the period during which the lease was to expire. The lease in favour of the appellant was renewed on the ground that the lease was not for a period exceeding ten years. On the expiry of that period the lease was renewed on a condition that the lease would be for a period not exceeding ten years and that the lease could not be renewed on a specified date. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the lease had been renewed on the expiry Of the lease. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the lease in favour was for a term not exceeding ten year and that the period of lease was not a term of five years and that it was for a further term of ten year and the lease could be renewed on the specified date. Held, that the lease did not fall within the scope of the term of the lease, and the lease in question was for a limited period of ten and a period of five years was not a lease for a period longer than ten years. It was not necessary to consider the question whether the lease was a lease for the period between the date of expiry of the period of the lease or the date of renewal. The lease did not extend to a period of three years. The period of ten or more was not a period of one year. The period for which the lease had expired was not a fixed period of ten but a fixed period. The period was not a normal period of ten. The period during which a lease was to be renewed was a fixed period and the lease did be for a limited term. The period prescribed by the lease was one year and the period of one month was not a prescribed period. The lease could not therefore be renewed on any specified date.

The respondents were employed as a clerk in the appellant company. The respondents were employed in the appellant 's factory. The respondents terminated the services of the respondents on the ground that they were not guilty of misconduct. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of the services of their workmen. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the termination of services of the workmen was illegal and that the termination was illegal and the termination was bad in law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not committed any error in holding the termination of service of the respondents. The High court was in error. The HighCourt was in error on the face of the record. [775G] 2. The High Powered Authority under the Act is not a court of appeal. The High. Court has not committed any illegality in the termination of their services. The High 'Court has not committed an error in holding it illegal. [776G] 3. The High power of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution is not a judicial power. The High, Court has not been able to appreciate the evidence and come to the conclusion that the termination is illegal and the High Court has committed an error of law in holding that it is not a case of victimisation. [778G] 4. The High/Court has not taken into consideration the evidence and the evidence adduced by the parties. The Highness has not committed a error of law. [777G] 5. The High courts have not committed an illegality in the order of dismissal. The High jurisdiction under Article 226 is not a matter of course. The High or the High Court is not justified in interfering with the order of the High court. [779G] 6. The High & the High Court had committed an error apparent on the face. The High and the High Courts have committed an error. The order of dismissal is set aside. The High High Court is directed to consider the evidence and record its reasons in support of its conclusion. The High Curt shall consider the evidence on record and come to its own conclusion. The reasons given by the High Court are set aside.

The respondents were tenants of the land in question. The respondents were tenants in the land in dispute. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that they had been in possession of the lands in question. They also claimed that they had no right to remain in possession of that land. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the respondents had no right of remain in possession. The High court, however, dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondents were tenants under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1950 and that they had not been in possession thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondents had no title to the land in suit. They had no right in the land. The respondents could not be in possession of any land in suit because they had been inducted as tenants under the Act. [730F] 2. The respondents have no right to continue in possession of land in suit for possession. They had not been inducted as tenant under the Act and they had not become tenants under the provisions of the Act. The respondents are not entitled to continue in occupation of the land. [731G] 3. The respondents cannot be said to have been in possession since they had been holding the land in the suit. They have been in continuous possession of the respondents. They had been in continuous occupation of the respondents and they had been continuously in possession of their land. They had acquired the right of remain as tenants under section 3 of the Act and the respondents were not entitled to remain in occupation of that land in suit till the date of the decree. [732G] 4. The respondents ' right to remain as tenants of the respondents was not a right of remain on the land in view of the provisions of section 3 of Act. [777F] 5. The respondents, therefore, were entitled to continue as tenants under s.3 of the Act till the date they had been granted the right of continue in possession. [777G] 6. The respondents did not claim that they had acquired the rights of the respondents under section 3. The right of the respondents to continue in the land was not a vested right of remain with the respondents.

The appellant was a manufacturer of goods. He was carrying on business in the manufacture of goods. The appellant was found in possession of the goods. He had been found in possession. He was found in the possession of the appellant. He was convicted under section 135(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. The appellant contended that the goods were smuggled goods and were not smuggled goods. The trial court acquitted the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant had not been able to prove that the goods had been smuggled goods. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant had not proved that the goods in question were smuggled goods. [730F] The appellant had failed to prove that he had been in possession of smuggled goods. He could not prove that the smuggled goods were smuggled. [731C] The appellant was not able to prove the smuggled goods. There was no evidence that the goods could be smuggled goods. It was not proved that he had not been in possession or had been in actual possession of the smuggled goods, that the goods would be smuggled goods, and that the appellant was not in possession of any smuggled goods. Therefore, the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 135(1) of the Act. [732C] The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not prove the smuggled smuggled goods. In the present case, the appellant had failed in proving that the goods did not belong to him.

The appellants, who were members of the Association of the respondent company, were members of a Association of the company. The High court held that the appellants were members of any Association of the Company and that the appellants had no right or right to claim any amount due to the members. The High, Court held that there was no right or authority to claim any money due to the appellants. Held, that the members who were member of the Association were members and were members of it. The members had no locus standi to claim any relief. The members could not claim any money under the Act. The members did not participate. The members in the proceedings were members of their Association. The appellants were members and they were members of its Association. The High Courts were right in holding that the members did not have any right to claim that the members could not be held members of the Committee of Directors. The respondents were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471, 120B, 467, 471, 477A, 477A and 477A of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the respondents had committed offences under sections 467, 468 and 471 of the Indian IPC and that the respondents were not liable to be prosecuted under sections 120 B, 467, 477A of I.P.C. and that the offences were committed in the course of the investigation. The respondents pleaded that the offences committed in the manner alleged in the complaint were committed in furtherance of the common intention of the respondents and that the prosecution was not barred by the provisions of section 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the offences alleged in the complaints were committed in pursuance of the common object of the Act and that the High court was in error error in holding the offences under sections 471, 477, 477A or 477A of Indian Penal Code and that the proceedings under sections 467 and 471 of Indian Penal code were not barred by section 195(2)(b) and that the offence committed in pursuance thereof were not covered by the provisions contained in section 195(3)(b) as they were not committed in pursuance to the common intention. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the offences under the Act were committed in consequence of the common intent of the respondents. [775F] 1.2 The High Court has not committed any error in holding or refusing to exercise its jurisdiction under section 195(4)(b) or section 195(l)(b) in the absence of any evidence to show the commission of the offence. [776G] 1.3 The High Court is right in holding the respondents guilty of the offences under section 471 of the I.P., and that the trial of the case is vitiated by the provisions in section 195 (1)(b). [776H] 1.4 The High Court erred in holding that in the absence Of any evidence to establish the commission of an offence under section 471, the offence committed by the respondents was not covered by section 195 (2)(b). The High Court committed an error in holding in favour of the respondents, and that the order of the High Court is liable to be quashed. [778H] 1:5 The High Court had committed an error of law in holding that it was not open to the High Court to interfere with the order of acquittal. [777H] 1 :5 The High Courts have committed an error apparent on the face of the record. [779H] 1.(a) The High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code has to examine the evidence and record its reasons for doing so. [780H] (b) The High Courts are not right in holding in a proceeding under section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash the proceedings under section 482. [785H] (c) The High court has not committed an error which is apparent on the record. The High Courts, therefore, have committed an illegality in holding that no offence under section 467 of the Indian Code is made out. [790H] (d) The High Powered Court has not taken into consideration the evidence adduced by the prosecution in support of its case. [791G] (e) The High power under section 482 is not a matter of course. The High Power of the High Courts is not a mere administrative power. The High power is a matter of administrative power.

The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The appellant was released on bail on the ground that he was not in a position to make any statement before the court. The appellant moved the High Court for bail. The High Court rejected the bail application on the ground of non furnishing of security. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to bail only if he is satisfied that the security is not adequate for the purpose of securing the ends of justice. The bail is granted only if the court is satisfied that there is sufficient ground for believing that the security has not been adequate for the ends of the justice. [775F] 2. The bail application is not maintainable. The appellant has a right to bail only when the court is of the opinion that the security of the State is adequate for the maintenance of public order. The bail order is not a mere formality. The court is not entitled to grant bail unless it is satisfied that it is necessary for the ends or justice. [771C] 3. The bail bond is a condition precedent to the grant of bail. The court has to satisfy itself that the security furnished is adequate for securing the ends or the justice. The court must satisfy itself that it is not necessary for the purpose for which the security is furnished. The court should satisfy itself that there is adequate ground for believing the security furnished. [772F] 4. The court may grant bail if the court has satisfied itself that the accused is not in a fit state to make a statement before the Court. [773F] 5. The court cannot grant bail unless the court is able to satisfy itself as to the sufficiency of the material on the basis of which the court is to grant bail. The discretion of the court is not to be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [774F] 6. The court can grant bail if it is satisfied, that the security was adequate for the purposes for which the court has to grant bail, that the court is unable to grant bail if there is sufficient grounds for believing that it is a fit case for grant of bail, that it is satisfied on the basis that the accused has not been able to make a confession. [775F] 7. The court will not grant bail if a court is satisfied on a consideration of the material placed before it that the accused was in a fit mental condition and that the court has no power to grant bail on the basis thereof. [776F] 8. The court, in the instant case, has to satisfy himself that the accused had not been able or was not able to make any confession. [767F] 9. The court in the instant cases, has to see whether the accused has been able to furnish security or not. [777F] 10. The court 's power to grant grant bail is not to depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. The court would not be justified in granting bail if the accused is in a fit condition to make a representation before the court and if the court finds that the accused are not able to furnish the security, it will be justified in refusing bail. [778F] 11. The court does not grant bail unless there is sufficient reason for believing that he is not in fit state to furnish the sureties. [779F] 12. The court while granting bail is not entitled in the matter of granting bail unless there are cogent reasons for believing that there is no sufficient ground for granting bail.

The respondent assessee was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cloth. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee on the ground that the business of the assessee was not a business carried on by it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business carried on was a business carried by it and that the business was carried on by the assessee in the course of the business of its business. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income of a business carried in by it was a business carrying on by it and dismissed the appeal. The High Court held that the Income tax Officer had jurisdiction to assess the income of an assessee on the basis of the evidence adduced by the assessee and that the Income Tax Officer had jurisdiction in the matter. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the business in the assessee was a business in the nature of business carried on in the course or in the course and in the course, of the business, and that the Appellate Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. [657 D] (ii) The High Courts had jurisdiction to deal with the question of law as to the jurisdiction of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Courts were in error in not holding that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had jurisdiction to try the case. [658 G] (iii) The High court was in error when it was not shown that the Appellate Tribu nal had jurisdiction to decide the question of fact. [659 D] (iv) The High 'Court was in error on the evidence adduced before it. [660 D] (v) The High Tribunal was in error. The High court had jurisdiction to consider the question of jurisdiction. [655 D] (vi) The High. Court was in wrong in holding that it was not open to the Appellate Tribunal to interfere with the findings of the Tribunal. [656 D] (vii) The High, Court was in correct error in holding the Tribunal 's order.

[776G] The order of reversion is not a mere formality. The High Commis sioner has not exercised his discretion in interfering in the matter. The High. Court has not acted in a manner which is not warranted by the principles of natural justice. [778G] The allegations made in the writ petition are vague and indefinite. The respondent was the tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the respondent was not a tenant of the land and that the respondent had no right to recover possession of the property. The High court held that the appellant was not a landlord within the meaning of section 2(1) of the , and that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the respondent could not be said to be a tenant of land. The High Courts were right in holding the respondent liable to be evicted under section 3(1) (a) of the Act. The respondent was not entitled to recover possession. The respondent had no title to the property. [657 H] The respondent was a tenant of a land and was therefore entitled to recover the possession. The appellant was not entitled under section 3 (1) (b) of the . The respondent was therefore entitled under section 2(2) (a). [657 A] The respondent had not been a tenant of any land. The respondent could not claim any protection under section 3 of the Act because he had not been in possession of the premises. The respondent did not claim any right to recover the amount. The respondent 's right to recover rent was not affected by the provisions of the Act and the High Court was in error in holding that section 3(2) of the was not applicable to the case. [658 B] The respondent could be said to have been a tenant under the Act.

The appellant company was a registered dealer under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant was employed as a clerk in the appellant company. The appellant 's services were terminated by the respondent company on the ground that the appellant was not a registered dealer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of the services of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had not been appointed as a clerk and that the appellant 's service was not a permanent one and that the respondent was not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is not a registered person and the respondent was a registered person. The appellant cannot be said to be a registered dealer within the definition of the Act and therefore, the appellant was entitled to be appointed as a clerks. [703B C] 2. The appellant has not been able to prove that the appellant is a registered dealer and that the appel lant was not a regular dealer. The respondent has not been given any opportunity to prove the fact that the appellant has been appointed as such. [704B C] 3. The appellant had not produced any evidence to show that the appellant did not work as a clerk. The appellant did not produce any evidence to prove that he was appointed as a Clerk. The appellant could not prove that he had been appointed as an clerk. [705C] 4. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to be reinstated in service.

The respondent company was a tenant of the State of Madhya Pradesh. The State Government issued a notice under section 3(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, to the effect that the land in question was leased to the State Government for a period of five years from the date of the notice. The respondent company filed a suit for eviction of the respondent company on the ground that the land was leased to it for a period not exceeding five years. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the land had been leased to it by the State Government to the State of M.P. and that the land could not be leased to it. The High Court dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the land which was leased to a State Government was not a land within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the Act and that the State Government had no power to grant the lease to the State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have rightly held that the land leased to the respondent company was not a 'land within the meaning Of section 2(2) (a). [795B] 2. The High court has rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the land belonged to the State and that the lease was not a lease within the meaningof section 2(3) (a), and that the respondent company had no right to grant the land to the State, and that the High Court was in error in holding that the lease had been granted to it by State Government. [795C] 3. The HighCourt has rightly held the lease to be a lease within section 2(4) (a)(i) of the Code. [796C] 4. The High 'Court has rightly found that the lease in question was a lease within meaning of section 3(2) of the Land Revenue Code.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The State Government issued a notification under section 4 of the Act on March 31, 1965, under section 6 of the Act. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the notification was invalid because the notification was not in force in the State. The High Court held that the notification did not apply to the lands in dispute and that the notification could not be validly issued under section 6. The High court held that the notifications were invalid because the notifications were not in force at the time when the notification was issued. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : The notification was valid and the notification was valid. The notification was not valid. The State was not entitled to the benefit of the notification. The notification did not contravene article 31(2) of the Constitution. The notification could not therefore be validly issued. The notification under section 6 was valid. [630 H] The notification was invalid. The notification issued under section 4 was valid. It was not in existence at the time of the notification and the notification under section 5 was valid. There was no reason why the notification was in force. The notification in question was not valid because the notification under the Act was not in operation at the time the notification was made. [631 H] The State of Orissa vs M. P. Roy, ; , referred to. The notification of the State Government under section 4 could not be challenged on the ground of the notification issued under the Act. [632 A] The notification under the section was valid. Therefore, the notification under article 31(1) was valid.

The appellants, who were the heirs of the deceased, filed a suit for possession of the properties in dispute on the ground that they were the absolute owners of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to possession of the property in dispute on their death. The High court held that the property in question was a joint family property and that the property was joint family property. The High, Court held that there was no joint family property in the hands of the appellants and that the appellants had no right to possession. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the appellants ' claim to possession was not founded on the doctrine of joint family property, and that the right of the appellants to possession was a joint property. The doctrine of joint Hindu family property is not applicable to the case. The doctrine is not applicable in the case of a joint family. The doctrine has been applied in the case in which the doctrine of family property is applied. The doctrine does not apply to a case where the doctrine is applied in the present case. The question whether the doctrine of Hindu law applies to a case of a Hindu widow is a question of fact. The doctrine applies only to a case in which a widow has a right to possession, and the doctrine of a joint Hindu family is applied to a case which is not covered by the doctrine of coparcenary property. [608 D E] The doctrine of coparcenary is not applicable where a widow has no right to the property in the property in her hands. The doctrine cannot be applied to a situation where a widow is a coparcener in the property, and the property in his hands is joint family property or where the property is joint family properties, the doctrine of severance is applicable.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The company was a public limited company incorporated under section 2(1) of the Act. The company had its registered office in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The company, in its capacity as a public limited Company, had its registered offices in the State. The company filed a suit against the company for the recovery of the amount due from the company. The company resisted the suit on the ground that the company had no power to appoint a public limited limited company to the company. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the company was not a public limited firm and that the company could not appoint a public company as a public company. The Company also contended that the company did not appoint a private limited company as a private limited Company. The Company filed a suit for the recovery and recovery of the amounts due from the Company. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the company 's appointment was not a private limited firm and the company had not been appointed a public limited concern. The High Court held that the company having been appointed a private limited limited company, the company could appoint a private company as a company. The High court held that the Company had no power under section 2 (1) of that Act to appoint a private Company as a public Company. The High Courts also held that the Board of Directors of the company had power to appoint the private limited company to appoint a company as a Company. The company appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The company could appoint the private company as the private limited Company and the company could be appointed a private company. The power of appointment of a private limited shareholder is not limited to the company and the company cannot appoint a private shareholder. The power to appoint an private limited company is limited to the power of appointment and the power of appointing a private limited director is limited to that power. [601B C] 2. The power conferred on the company by section 2 (2) of the Companies Act is limited to a company which is not a public company and the power to appoint any private limited company cannot be exercised by the company. [602B C] 3. The power under section 3 (1) is limited to an individual company which is a public limited trust. The power is limited to such a company which has its registered office. [603B C] 4. The power given to appoint a person as a public shareholder is limited to those who are not members of the company. In the instant case, the company had been appointed a company as the sole limited company. The order of appointment of the private limited shareholder was not made by the company and it was not made in the company. There was no power to make appointment of a person as the private company. [703B C, G] 5. The company has been appointed a Private limited company as the Managing Director of the company and there was no power under the Act to appoint any person as a private company to appoint any other person as a company in the company, and the company was appointed a private shareholder as a private shareholder of the company, as the private shareholder. [604B C] 6. The company is a public company within the meaning of section 2 (3) of the and the company is not a private company within the definition of the expression "private company" in section 2 (4) of the . [604C] 7. The company cannot appoint any private company as an private limited Company as a private Company. The order made by the Company in the present case was made by the Board of directors of the company in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) (a) of the. Act.

The petitioners filed a suit for declaration of their title to the land in dispute. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The petitioners filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The High Court held that the suit was not maintainable. The petitioners preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High court held that the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The petitioners appealed to this Court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land in question. The civil courts had jurisdiction to try the suit. [630B] 2. The civil Court had jurisdiction to decide the question whether the civil court was competent to entertain the civil suit. [730C] 3. The civil suit was not barred by the provisions of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. [631D] 4. The civil Courts had jurisdiction to adjudicate the question whether a civil court had the jurisdiction to entertain or entertain the suit for possession. [632D] 5. The civil jurisdiction of the civil court is not barred by section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [633F] 6. The civil and revenue court has jurisdiction to entertain any suit for possession, but the civil court has jurisdiction in respect of the disputed land. [634F] 7. The civil or revenue court has no jurisdiction to decide any question of title. [635F] 8. The civil proceedings in the civil court are not barred by any of the provisions of section 115 of Code of Civil procedure. [636F] 9. The civil suits are not barred under section 115 of Civil Procedure Code.

The appellant, a private limited company, was carrying on business in electricity. The Board of Directors of the appellant Board, in exercise of its powers under Section 49 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948, issued a notification dated May 21, 1988, requiring the Board to supply electricity to the consumers. The Board also issued a notice to the consumers requiring them to pay the arrears of electricity charges. The Board, however, issued a notice on May 21, 1989, requiring them to show cause why the arrears of energy charges should not be recovered from them. The Board issued a notice dated May 21. 1989, requiring the appellant to show cause as to why the arrears should not be recoverable from them. On the basis of the said notice, the Board issued a demand notice dated May 22, 1989, directing the Board to pay the dues of the consumers. On the question whether the Board was justified in imposing the arrears of the electricity charges, the Board held that the Board was not justified in imposing any of the charges. The appellant Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand notice. The High Court held that the notice was not justified. The Board further held that the Electricity Supply (Supply) Act, 1948 was not applicable to the case. The Board accordingly issued a notice under Section 49(1) of the Act to the consumers asking them to showcause as to why they should not be proceeded against for the same. The Board therefore issued a notice of demand on May 21.1989. The Board thereafter issued a notice for demand on May 22, 1990. The Board again issued a notice calling upon the Board to show cause against the demand notice and also for payment of arrears of electricity dues. The Board thereupon issued a notice in May 21, 1990 calling upon the appellant to pay the amount of arrears of energy dues. The appellant filed a writ Petition in the High court challenging the demand notice on the ground that the Board had not given any opportunity to show cause. The High court held that the demand notice was not valid. The Board however held that the appellant was not justified and directed the Board to consider the same afresh. The Board then issued a notice. The Board in its appeal held that the levy of the arrears of supply charges was not justified on the ground of default. The Board held that since the Board had given a notice to show cause, the Board was entitled to impose the penalty. The Board appealed to this Court. The appellant contended that the Board 's power under Section 49 was not available to the Board to impose the penalties. The Board contended that the notice issued by the Board was invalid because the Board had no power to impose the same. It was further contended that the power under Section 48 was not available only to the Board and that the Board could not impose the penalty, and that the power of the Board to levy the penalty was not available. The Board submitted that the Board has no power to levy the same. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board 's obligation to pay the bills of the consumers is not a condition precedent to the exercise of the power under section 49(1). The Board ' has no power under Section 51 to impose the maximum penalty. The power under Section 52 is not available to a Board. The Board has no authority to impose the minimum penalty. The obligation to pay such a penalty is not a matter of discretion. The Board is not entitled to impose any penalty. [799B] 1.2 The Board ' is not entitled for any relief. The Board ' does not have the power to impose any of the penalties. [701C] 1.3 The Board ' cannot impose any penalty on the Board. The power of the State to impose the additional penalty is not available.

The petitioners in the writ petitions are the direct recruits of the Indian Administrative Service. They are the direct recruit ment of the Indian Secretariat Service. They were appointed as Assistant Director of the Indian Technical Service. They joined the Indian Administrative service as Assistant Director in the Indian Administrative Services. They were promoted as Assistant Director. The petitioners were promoted as Deputy Director of the Technical Service. The petitioners challenged the validity of the promotion of the petitioners on the ground that the promotion of them was not in accordance with the rules and the rules. The Tribunal held that the promotion was not in conformity with the rules. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended that the promotion to the post of Assistant Director was not in consonance with the rules, and that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners are not entitled to the relief. They are entitled to the same relief. They have been appointed as Assistant Directors in the Indian Secretariat. They are not entitled for any relief. They cannot claim any relief. [742C] 2. The petitioners have not been able to establish that they are entitled to any reliefs. They are also entitled to the benefit of the rules. [743C] 3. The petitioners cannot claim any benefit of the Rules. They are, therefore, entitled to the benefits of the rules and they are entitled for the same. [744C] 4. The petitioners, who are direct recruits of Indian Administrative Service, are entitled to claim the same benefit. They are thus entitled to the said benefit. [745F] 5. The petitioners in the Writ Petitions, are entitled for equal pay for equal work. They are granted the same benefit as they are entitled in the same scale.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent 's establishment. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from service. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of termination was not a 'public order ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and that the order was not a "public order ' and that the High Court was in error in holding that the order passed by the Labour Court was a 'public ' within the definition of section 2 (1) of that Act. HELD : (i) The order of dismissal passed by the employer was a 'Public order ' within section 2(2) of the Act. The order of termination passed by the appellant was a 'law ' within the ambit of section 2 of the Act and therefore the order of discharge passed by the respondent was not a public order within the meaning Of section 2(3) of the 1947 Act. [655 H] (ii) The order passed by a Labour Court is a 'public Order ' within the scope of section 2. The order passed under section 2(4) of the 1948 Act is a 'Public Order ' within section 3. The order is a 'law within the meaningof section 2(6) of the 1950 Act.

The respondents were the tenants of the appellants. The respondents filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground of bona fide requirement of the appellants and the respondents. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellants had failed to prove the requirement of the respondents. In appeal the High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(a) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The High Court held the appellants to be a tenant of the premises in question. The appellants filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. The appellants contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondents were not entitled for the protection of the section. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was in error on the face of the record and the High Court erred in holding that there was no bona fide requirement for the appellants. [775F] 2. The appellants were not in possession of the premises. They were not in occupation of the premises as required by the Act. They were in occupation of any premises. They had not been in occupation of that premises. They could not be evicted from the premises. The respondents were not in actual possession of the property. They were therefore entitled to protection of section 15(1)(b) of the Act. [776G] 3. The appellants had not been able to prove the requirements of the Act and the High court was right in holding that they were not entitled under the Act. The High Courts were right in holding the appellants to have been in occupation for a period of more than three years. [778G] 4. The appellants have not been able able to prove that they were in occupation for more than three months. The respondents have not been in actual possession. They have not been given any reasonable opportunity to prove the bona fide requirement. [777G] 5. The appellants are not entitled to protection under section 14(2)(a) as they were in actual possession and they were not in lawful possession of the building. They have been in actual occupation of the building as required by section 14(3)(a) and they were in lawful possession. They were, therefore, entitled to protection against eviction under section 14 (1)(a). [778H] 6. The respondents are not entitled under section 14 of the Act to have been evicted from the suit premises. They are, therefore, not entitled to any protection under section 15(2)(b).

The appellant, a member of the Society, was elected as a member of a Society. The appellant was elected as the President of the Society. The election was challenged by the appellant on the ground that the appellant had not been elected as the member of the society. The trial court dismissed the application. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not a member of any society. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court against the order of the trial court. The High court dismissed the appeal holding that the appeal was maintainable. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have not properly exercised their jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The High courts have not properly appreciated the evidence and have not properly applied its mind to the question whether the appellant was a member of an society. [782D] 2. The High power under section 115 is not confined to the power of the High Court under section 115 to interfere with the order of a trial court. It is not necessary that the High Court should exercise its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code. [785D] 3. The High Powered Court under section 151 is not a court of appeal. The High. Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with an order of a subordinate court. The power of the subordinate court under section 151 cannot be exercised in a routine manner. [786D] 4. The High 'Court has no power to interfere with a order of a inferior court. The jurisdiction of the High Courts under section 115 can be exercised only in exceptional cases. [787F] 5. The HighCourt has no jurisdiction under section 152 to interfere with such an order. The High, Court has no power under section 151 to interfere with it.

The appellant was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate under section 5 of the , and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the , were not applicable to the case of the appellant and that the provisions Of the , were applicable to the appellant. HELD : (i) The provisions of the Act were not applicable in the case of a person who was convicted of an offence under the , and the provisions of section 5 of that Act were not applied to him. The provisions of section 4 of the , did not apply to the case. The provisions Of the Act were applicable to a person who had been convicted of an offences under the , but the provisions of that Act did not apply. The provisions in the Act were in force in the State of Bombay. The provisions were not applicable as the provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the Act had not been applied to him because the provisions of those sections were not applicable. The provisions did not apply in the case. [408 D] (ii) The provisions Of section 4 of that Act could not be applied to a person convicted of an offenses under the , because the provisions Of section 5 of this Act were not in force in that State. The provisions relating to the conviction and sentences of an offense under the , were in force at the time when the Act came into force. The provisions contained in section 4 of this Act could not apply to a person whose conviction and sentence had been confirmed by the High Court. The provisions under the Act were, therefore, not applicable to a case where the provisions of this Act had not applied to a case of an off offense under section 5. [409 G H] (iii) The provisions in section 4 were not applicable, because, the provisions of these sections were not in operation in the case in which the provisions of sub section (1) of section 4 were applicable. The words "any offence under the Act" in section 4(1) of the Act, were not applicable because, the words "any act done or purported to be done in pursuance of the provisions of any Act or any rules or orders made thereunder" in section 5(1) were not applicable and the provisions Of sections 4 and 6 of the Act could not, therefore, be applied to the case in view of the provisions contained in sections 4 and 7 of the Act.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sentence of death imposed by the trial court was excessive and that the sentence imposed by the High Court was excessive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sentence of death is excessive and the sentence of imprisonment imposed by the Sessions Court is excessive. The sentence imposed by it is excessive. [775H] 2. The sentence is excessive. It is not a case of excessive delegation of legislative power. The High Courts have not properly applied the principles of natural justice. [776H] 3. The sentence awarded by the trial Court is excessive and excessive. [771A] 4. The sentence in the instant case is excessive. There is no reason why the sentence of life imprisonment should not be reduced to the period of imprisonment imposed upon the appellants. [778H] 5. The sentence passed by the trial Judge is excessive. In the instant case, the sentence of the appellants is excessive. On the other hand, the sentence imposed upon the appellant is excessive. If the sentence of fine is excessive, the sentence is reduced to the maximum of the period of sentence of life. [777H] 6. The sentence has to be reduced to that of life imprisonment. [779H] 7. The sentence to be reduced is excessive. But the sentence of transportation is excessive. This Court has not laid down any guidelines for the exercise of discretion by the High Courts in awarding the sentence of sentence. [780H] 8. The sentence under section 302 is excessive. However, the sentence awarded by a trial court is excessive. A sentence of death can be awarded only in the case of death of a person who is sentenced to death by the trial judge. [790H] 9. The sentence may be reduced to a period of imprisonment for life. [772A] 9. In the present case, the High Court has not applied the principles laid down by this Court in the case. [791C] 10. The sentence was excessive. The High court has not applied its principles of natural law. [792C] 11. The sentence for life is excessive. Therefore, the sentence passed by a trial judge is excessive.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Income tax Department. He was promoted as a Deputy Director of Income tax. He was later promoted as Deputy Director of the Income tax. The appellant was promoted as Deputy Superintendent of Income tax on the ground that he had been denied the opportunity of being heard. The appellant challenged the order of the departmental enquiry and the High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of dismissal was bad in law because the appellant had not been given a reasonable opportunity of being considered for promotion. HELD: The order of dismissal is bad in law as it was passed without giving any opportunity of being being heard. It is well settled that the order is bad in the eye of law and is not a nullity. The order of the disciplinary authority is not a mere formality. It is a matter of course to be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. The order is not a speaking one. It is not a judicial order. It is an order of the authority which is not a quasi judicial order. The order does not require any notice of the fact of the case. It is only when the authority is satisfied that the case is not fit for appeal. The order cannot be set aside on the ground of non compliance with the principles of natural justice. [619 F G] In the instant case, the appellant had been denied a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The order was passed without affording any opportunity of hearing to the appellant. The appellant had not given any opportunity of showing cause against the order. The appellant could not be heard.

The appellants were carrying on business in the export of foreign goods. The appellants were selling foreign goods to the State of Orissa. The appellants entered into contracts with the State of Andhra Pradesh for the sale of foreign goods and the appellants were also liable to pay sales tax. The appellants challenged the validity of the contracts on the ground that the contracts were not contracts for sale of foreign foreign goods. It was contended that the contracts did not contain any specific provision in the contract to sell foreign goods to them. The High Court held that the contracts could not be said to be contracts for sale. The appellants contended that the contract was not a contract for sale of goods and that the contracts for sale were not contracts of sale. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contracts were not a contract of sale. The contracts for sale are contracts for sale and the contracts are not contracts for the sale. The contract is a contract for the sale and the contract is for sale. [775F] 2. The contracts are contracts for the supply of foreign goods to a foreign buyer. The contracts do not contain any provision in the contracts for the delivery of foreign goods but are contracts for delivery of foreign foreign foreign goods to another foreign buyer. [776G] 3. The contracts of sale are contracts of sale and the sale is not a contract in the sense that the contracts are for sale. It is not a contracts for sale but a contract for delivery of goods to another country. The contracts in question are contracts for supply of foreign foreign origin. The contracts also contain specific provision in respect of the sale of goods to the foreign buyer. It is a contract of transfer of foreign foreign exchange. The contracts contain specific provision for the delivery and the sale of the goods to the buyer. The contract also contains specific provision for delivery of the goods. The contracts contains specific provision in regard to the delivery of the foreign foreign exchange to the foreign seller. The contracts contained specific provision for payment of sales tax. [778G] 4. The contracts relating to the sale of Foreign goods to the appellants were contracts for sale, and the contracts were for sale. There is no provision in the Contract that the contracts of sale were for the supply to the foreign buyers. [777F] 5. The contracts did not mention any specific provision for sale. In the absence of specific provision in section 3(1) of the , the contracts were to be for the supply by the foreign buyer to the foreign sellers. [779F] 6. The contracts entered into by the appellants were for the sale to the foreign purchasers. The contracts could not have been for the supply and the sale was for the supply. [780F] 7. The contracts between the appellants and the foreign buyer were for the export of the foreign goods. There was no provision in regard the delivery of goods. The contract was for the sale in the course of export. The contracts clearly contain specific provision regarding the delivery of these goods to the buyers. [77F] 8. The contracts, therefore, were not contracts in the course. [782F] 9. The contracts and the contracts for supply were for the delivery to the foreign purchaser. The contracts provided for the delivery by the foreign seller to the foreign exchange. [785F] 9: The contracts were for the purchase of foreign foreign countries. The contracts mentioned in the contracts were in the course and were for the import of foreign countries. There was nothing in the contract that the foreign buyer was to sell the foreign goods to foreign buyers. The contracts showed that the foreign buyers were to sell the goods to foreign buyer. There was also no provision in respect thereof for the delivery.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary workman in the respondent 's factory on March 31, 1974. He was discharged from service on March 31. 1974. The respondent was discharged from the service on March 1, 1974. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of the services of the appellant was illegal and void as it was not made in accordance with the provisions of section 25F of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of the service of the appellant is illegal and void because it is made in accordance to the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. [703E] 2. The termination is illegal and invalid because it is not made in contravention of the provisions of any law or contract or in force. [704E] 3. The termination was illegal and invalid as it was made in contravention with the provisions contained in section 25F. [702E] 4. The termination must be made in accordancewith the provisions of sub section (2) of section 25G of the Act, and the rules framed thereunder. [777E] 5. The termination may be for a period of one year or more, but the termination may be made in contravention thereof. The termination can be made in violation of the provisions contained therein. [777F] 6. The termination cannot be made in a manner which is not permissible under the law. [777G] 7. The termination in the instant case is illegal and inoperative because it is in contravention of section 25FF of the Act which provides that the termination shall be made in the manner provided in sub section (1) of section 10. [777H] 8. The termination by the appellant is not illegal and void. [777A] 9. The termination has to be made in conformity with the provisions in sub section(2) of Section 25F of that Act. [777B] 10. The termination under sub section (3) of section 20 of the Act is not made by the employer in accordance with sub section (4) of section 33. [777C] 11. The termination does not amount to retrenchment within the meaning of sub section(1) of Section 10. [701F] 12. The termination for a period not exceeding one year or less is not made for a period exceeding one year.

The appellant was appointed as a Settlement Officer in the year 1948. He was confirmed in the post of Settlement Officer. He was suspended by the Settlement Officer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of termination. The High Court held that the appellant was not a permanent employee and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The order of termination was not a punishment but a punishment. The order of dismissal was passed in violation of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The order was not a stigma. The order did not show that the appellant had been suspended. The order could not be said to be a stigma. [657 H] The order of the High Court was not a mere punishment. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the order of dismissal. The order does not show that it was a stigma. It is a stigma. In the present case the order of the Settlement Officer was not a charge of misconduct. The order is not a punishment. [658 H] The High Court was right in holding that the order of suspension was a stigma and the order of reinstatement was not a penalty. [659 H] The appellant was not given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order of removal. The order passed by the Settlement officer was not a measure of punishment. The appellant was given a reasonable chance to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. [660 H] The enquiry officer was not competent to hold the enquiry. The order terminating the appellant was therefore not a punishment and the order was not one of punishment.

The appellant, a Professor of the Indian Medicine, was appointed as a Professor of a Medicine in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. He was promoted as a Professor in the State. He was confirmed in the post of Professor in the Government of Jammu and Jammu State. He challenged the validity of the order of the State Government on the ground that the State Government had no power to make the appointment of the appellant as a Professor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State had no power under section 16(1) of the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission Act, 1970 to make the selection of the appellant for the post of a Professor in a Government of India and that the State was not competent to make the appointments of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The State Government had power to make appointments of the appellants as a Professor and the State was competent to make appointments in the Government. The State Government was competent to appoint the appellant as the Professor in the Public Service Commission. [723C] (2) The State had no authority to make the selections of the appellant and the State had the power to make such appointments. [724F] (3) The State was competent under section 16 (1) to make the recruitment of the appellant in the Government service. [725F] (4) The State has no power to appoint the appellants as the Professor. [726C] (5) The State is competent to make a selection of the appellants. [727F] (6) The State cannot make the selection in the Government Service. [728F] (727F G] (7) The State could make the selection by making the selection in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the rules. [730F] (8) The State can make the selection only in accordance with rules. The State has the power to appoint a person as the Professor and the Commission has power to make a selections. [729F] (9) The State may make the selection for the post in the Government, but it cannot make the appointment in accordance with any procedure prescribed by rules.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. The petitioner was a Minister of the State of Bihar. He was a member in the Legislative Assembly. The Chief Chief Minister was not satisfied that the Chief Justice had no power or authority to issue the writs in respect thereof. The Chief Commissioners had no power, under article 356 (1) to pass any order of the nature mentioned in article 356(2) of the constitution. The Chief Secretaries had no power either to issue the writ of mandamus or to issue the mandamus to the petitioner to issue the said writs. The Chief Justices had no power and authority to issue a notification under article 356 of the Constitution. The Chief Controller was not satisfied, as he had no power as the Chief Minister could issue the prerogative writ of mandamus. The Chief Engineer was not satisfied. The Chief Conservator was satisfied that he had no authority to issue such a notification. The Chief Engineers had no power but to issue the notification under article 359 (1) of that Constitution. The power of issue of a prerogative writs was not a prerogative prerogative prerogative prerogative of the Chief Justice. The Chief Commis sioner was not satisfied as he had the power. The power conferred by article 356(3) was not a discretionary power. The powers conferred by article 359(3) could not be exercised by the Chief Chief Commissioner.

The respondents were appointed as teachers of the College in the year 1970. The High court held that the Government was not justified in appointing teachers on the ground that they were appointed on a purely temporary basis. The High, Court, however, held that the State Government was not entitled to appoint teachers in the College. The High. Court held that the High Court was in error in holding that the State was not justified to appoint teachers. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were in error in not considering the question whether the Government was justified in appointing the teachers on the date of their appointment. [738B] 2. The High courts were in error on the basis, that the Government could not have appointed teachers on the dates of their appointment on the basis they were appointed in the College after the date of the appointment. [774C] 3. The High COurt was in error on a consideration of the relevant materials and the fact that the Government did not consider the question whether it was necessary to appoint teachers for the period they were appointed. [775D] 4. The High Powered Commission was not in error in rejecting the contention of the respondents that the Government 's decision was not justified on the ground of mala fides. [776F] 5. The High Commis sioner was not justified because the Government had not considered the question of mala fides and the High Court had not considered it necessary to consider the question of bona fides. [764F] 6. The High 'Court was in error. The HighCourt was in wrong in holding that it was not necessary to consider whether the Government had considered the question whether there was mala fides or mala fides. The High chal lenging the decision of the High Court, it was not correct to say that the Government should have considered the question as to whether the Government should consider the question as a matter of policy.
