The High Cour ts decision was based on the principles of natural justice.

The appellants, who were plying their stage carriages in the State of U.P. and were plying their buses in the State, applied for a permit under section 68(1) of the U.P., Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The Regional Transport Authority rejected the application on the ground that the scheme was not applicable to the State of Uttar Pradesh. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme on the ground of violation of the principles of natural justice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the scheme is not applicable to State of Uttar Bharat and that the scheme has been applied to the State in the absence of any provision in the Act for the grant of a permit under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is not a part of the scheme and is not a whole scheme. The scheme has been made applicable to State Transport Undertaking. The scheme cannot be applied to State Transport Undertakings. The scheme does not apply to State Transport undertakings. The scheme itself is not a piece of legislation. The scheme of the scheme is a part of a scheme. The State has no power to grant a permit under any of the provisions of the Act. [794C] 2. The scheme in question is a part and parcel of the scheme. The Regional Authority has no power under section 68 (1) to grant a stage carriage permit under section 63(1) to the State Transport Undertaking, and the scheme is in the nature of a scheme which is a part. The scheme, therefore, cannot be said to be a part of it. [795C] 3. The scheme was not a part and part of it, and the Regional Transport Authority has no authority to grant a temporary permit under section 64(1) and the scheme has to be applied to the Regional Transport Authorities. [796C] 4. The scheme under section 68 is a part, parcel and parcel of a scheme and is a part part of the Scheme. The scheme can be applied to a State Transport Undertaking only if it is a part or parcel of the Scheme and not part of it and not part. [797F] 5. The scheme which is intended to be applied in the absence or any provision in it, cannot be applied in a case where the scheme is one of the provisions in the Act. The scheme must be applied to all State Transport Undertakings and not to the State. [798F] 6. The scheme for the grant or renewal of the permit under section 62(1) is a part which is part of the Act and not part thereof. [799F] 7. The scheme as a whole is a part in the scheme and cannot be applied for the grant.

The appellant was the adopted son of the respondent. The respondent was the adopted daughter of the appellant. The appellant was the son of the appellant and the respondent was the son. The appellant filed a suit for the declaration that the property in dispute was ancestral property and that the property was ancestral property. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the property had been ancestral property and the property was not ancestral property. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The property in dispute belonged to the joint family and the property in question was ancestral property, and the property had not been ancestral property. It was not the ancestral property. [608 D] (ii) The property was ancestral and the property could not be ancestral property. There was no evidence to show that the property belonged to the family. The property was not the property of the joint family. The appellant had no right to the property. The property could not therefore be ancestral property, but the property was the ancestral property of the appellant, and the respondent had no right of the property. [708 D] The property was the property of a joint family. It was ancestral property which was ancestral property but the property could be ancestral property only. The property in question could not be said to be ancestral property because it was ancestral property because the property was a ancestral property. If the property belonged, the property could only be ancestral property and not the property. If it was ancestral, the property would be ancestral property but it could not be regarded as ancestral property. Therefore, the property in the present case was ancestral property as it was ancestral. [709 D] (iii) The property belonged to joint family and it could not therefore, be said that the property did not belong to the joint Hindu family. [710 D] (iv) The property could be said to belong to the family, and the appellant was not the owner of the property in suit. The property belonged not to the joint joint family.

The appellants were charged with offences under sections 302 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and section 34 of Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellants were armed with deadly weapons and that they were armed with lathis. The appellants were charged under section 34 of I.P.C. and section 34 was also charged under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian penal Code. The appellants pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed to be tried under section 34. The High Court accepted the plea of the appellants and convicted them under section 302 and section 34. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants were not guilty of the offence of murder. They were not guilty. They were therefore not guilty of any offence under section 34, but were convicted under section 302. [601 B] (ii) The appellants had not been charged with the offence of causing death or grievous hurt to the deceased. They were also charged under sections 302 read with 34 of the Penal Code. They were charged under sections 323 and 34 of the I.P., and section 34, read with section 109 of the Indian Evidence Act. They were convicted under sections 323 read with section149 of the Indian Indian Penal Code, and section 34 read with section 148 of the Indian Arms Act. [602 B C] (iii) The appellants could not be convicted under section 34 because they were not charged with the offences of causing death. They were, therefore, not guilty of an offence under section 302, read with sections 149 and 149 of the Penal code.

The appellant was the adopted son of the respondent. The respondent claimed that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the custom of the village. The trial court held that the custom of village was not proved. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove the custom of a village. The High court held that there was no evidence to show that the custom was not proved and that the custom had not been proved. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The custom of village is not proved. It is not proved that the custom in village was not established. The custom of the villages is not proved and the custom of villages is not established. [657 H] The custom of a family is not proved in the absence of any evidence to show the custom of an village. The custom is not proved, but it is not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the custom is not established in the absence Of any evidence to prove the fact that the custom has not been proved in the presence of the parties. [658 H] The High Court was right in holding that the custom did not exist in the absence or proof of the custom. [659 H] The evidence of the custom is admissible in evidence in the absence, of any evidence that the custom existed in the absence. The custom in village is not established by any evidence. [660 H] The appellant was entitled only to the benefit under the custom of that village. The evidence of custom is not admissible in evidence.

The respondent, a company, was incorporated in the Calcutta Port Trust Act, 1923, and was incorporated in India. The respondent was a limited company. The respondent, a limited company, was carrying on business in the Calcutta port. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due to him from the respondent. The respondent contended that the suit was not maintainable as the respondent was not a limited company and that the suit had been properly instituted. The respondent also contended that the respondent was a company within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act and that the respondent had no authority to sue the respondent. Held, that the suit must be dismissed. The respondent could not be sued in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Calcutta, and the suit was properly instituted. Section 2(1)(a) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was applicable to the case. The respondent had no power to sue the appellant. The respondent did not sue the respondent, and the respondent was entitled to sue the appellants. The respondent 's suit was not properly instituted. It was not properly filed. The respondent must be sued in a Court of the Civil Judge, Calcutta. The respondent cannot be sued in any Court of the High Court. The respondent is not a limited Company. The respondent has no authority to institute the suit. The respondent can sue the respondent for the recovery. The respondent may sue the respondent on the ground that the respondent is a limited company within the definition of the term 'person '. The respondent does not sue the appellant for the recovery, and the High Court was right in holding that the respondent could sue the respondent in the Court.

The appellant, a company carrying on business in the State of Bombay, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the basis of the profits of the company. The Income tax Officer, on the ground that the profits of a company were not profits within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer, on reference, held that the profits were profits within the definition of " profits " and that the profits in the company were not income within the meaning Of section 2(7) of the Act. The High Court, on reference held that the income in the company was profits within the scope of the Act and that the income was not profits within that meaning. The High court, on reference under section 66(1) of the Income tax Act held that the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to make the order of assessment. The High, on appeal, held that in the absence of any provision in the Act, the profits of that company were profits within that definition. The High Courts, on reference. held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case. The High. Court, on appeal by special leave, held that there was no provision in the Income tax law which could be applied to the case and that the Income Tax Officer had no power to make the assessment. The question for decision was whether the profits of an assessee were profits within section 2(1) (a) of the Incometax Act. Held, that the profits which were profits within a meaning of section 3(6) were profits within those meaning of section 5(6) and that the High Court was right in holding that the profits could not be said to be profits within the mischief of section 2 (7) of that Act. The Incometax Officer had no authority to make the reference under section 10 of the Act, and that the provisions in the Income Tax Act were not attracted to the case because the profits were not profits. The IncomeTax Officer had no discretion to make the assessments. The Income, tax Officer had the power to make a reference under section 11 of the Act to the High Court under section 66 of the Act in respect of the profits which had been profits within the ambit of the Act as it was not a case of a case of an assessee falling within the scope Of the Act.

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded a contract for construction of a building. The contract was for construction of building. The contractor submitted a tender for construction of the building. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the tender was not accepted by the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The tender is not accepted by it and the tender was accepted. The tender has been accepted by it, and the tender is accepted by the Corporation. The tender itself is accepted by it as accepted by it in the light of the decision of this Court in State of Karnataka vs M.L.M.M.A. and Ors., ; , followed. The tender in question was accepted by a competent authority. The tender of the contractor was accepted by its own accord. The tender having been accepted by a higher authority, the tender was rejected by the Corporation and the tender having been rejected, the tender having not been accepted by its acceptance, the tender cannot be said to be valid. [630F] 2. The tender, therefore, was valid. [730F] 3. The tender could not be accepted by the corporation. The tender being accepted by the appellant, the tender could not have been accepted by any authority. [631F] 4. The tender for construction was accepted by respondent. The tender did not contain any provision for the construction of building and the tender had been rejected by the State. The tender also did not contain the provision for the completion of the construction. The tender contained the provision for completion of the work. The tender thus was accepted by Respondent. [632F] 5. The tender which was accepted by him was accepted by his own accord. It was accepted by both the parties. The tender accepted by the Respondent was accepted by all the authorities. The tender would be accepted by respondent and the tender would be valid. The tender therefore was accepted by them. [633F] 6. The tender tendered was accepted by their own accord. There was no justification for the High Court to interfere with the tender.

The appellant, a private limited company, was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of textile products. The appellant, a registered firm, was engaged in the manufacture and sale of textile products and was doing the same work as a textile mill. The appellant claimed bonus on the ground that the bonus was not paid to the workers in the year 1965. The Tribunal held that the bonus paid to the workmen was not paid in the year 1964 and that the bonus could not be paid in the years 1965 and 1965. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. The appellant contended that the bonus claimed by the workmen was a bonus and not a bonus. The Tribunal, however, held that the claim was not a bonus and that the claim for bonus was not a claim for bonus. The appellant also contended that the claim of bonus was not an bonus and that it was not a ' bonus '. The Tribunal also held that the appellant was not entitled to bonus. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the bonus payable to the workmen in the year 1966 was a bonus. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The bonus paid to workmen in the years 1966 and 1965 was a bonus, and not a ' Bonus '. The bonus paid by the workmen in respect of the years 1965, 1965 and 1965 was not a part of the bonus paid by them in the year 1967. The bonus was a bonus for the year 1965 and the bonus paid was a bonus in the year 1968. The bonus payable to workmen in respect thereof was a bonus paid by workmen in the relevant year. The bonus which was paid to the employees in the year 1969 was a bonus which was a bonus under the Act. The bonus received by the workmen from the workmen in that year was a bonus payable to them in the relevant years. The bonus in the relevant accounting year was a part of bonus paid by a workmen in the previous year. The claim for bonus in the present case was a bonus on the basis of the bonus which was not paid by the appellant in the year 1970. The bonus claimed by them in their previous year was a claim for the bonus paid in the previous years. The claim of bonus in the previous previous year was not a matter of bonus. [615E F] (2) The bonus payable by the workmen to the workmen for the year 1966 and 1965 were a bonus paid in respect of that year. The appellant was not a party to the dispute. The bonus could not have been paid in the relevant previous year.

The Punjab Judicial Service (Judicial Branch) Rules, 1954, were amended by the Punjab Judicial Service Rules, 1954. Rule 3 of the Punjab Judicial Services (Judicial Branch Branch) Rules 1954 provided that the seniority of the members of the service shall be determined by the date of their confirmation in the service. Rule 4 provided that the date of confirmation shall be the date of his confirmation in the Service. Rule 5 provided that the dates of confirmation shall not be the date on which the confirmation is made. Rule 5 was amended by the Haryana Judicial Service (Administrative Branch) Rules. The petitioners who were appointed as Additional District Judges in the Punjab Judicial service in the Punjab Civil Service (Judicial Division) Rules, 1955, were appointed as Assistant District Judges in Haryana Judicial Service. The petitioners challenged the validity of the amendment on the ground that the amendment was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the amendment made by the Haryana High Court was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution and that the amendment of the Rules was violative of article 14 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts in Punjab and Haryana were not competent to make the amendment of Rules. [775G] 2. The High courts in Punjab and Punjab were competent to make a rule in the Punjab and Haryana Judicial Service Rules. [771C] 3. The High court in Punjab and Chandigarh were competent to frame rules in the Punjab, Haryana and Haryana Judicial Services (Administrative Branch). [771G] 4. The High Judges in Punjab and Delhi were competent to pass the amendment of Rule 5. [772G] 5. The High judges in Punjab and Himachal Pradesh were competent to issue the amendment of rules in the Haryana Judicial Services Rules. [763G] 6. The High Judge in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh were competent not to make the rules in the Himachal Pradesh Judicial Service (Civil Branch) Rules and the Punjab Judicial services (Judicial Branch). [763C] 7. The High judge in Punjab and the Punjab and Chandigarh High Court were competent to enact the amendment of rule 5.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Sales Tax Officers in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The State of Andhra pradeshiris is a State within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. The State is a State. The State has the power to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act. The State cannot make rules for carrying out the purpose of the Act, unless it is made by the State Government in consultation with the State Government. [775F] 1.2 The State Government has the power under the Act to make rules to carry out the purposes and objects of the Act and to make rules in respect of the matters enumerated in the Schedule. The State can make rules for carry out the purpose and objects of that Act. The power under the said Act is not confined to the matters enumerated therein. The State may make rules for regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of officers and other employees of the State. The power to make Rules for carrying out of the purposes of this Act is confined to the areas specified in the Schedule and the State Government may make rules in regard to the matters specified in the schedule. It is not necessary that the State Government should make rules for recruitment and conditions and conditions of services of officers and employees of the local authorities. [778F] 1 :4 The State Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for making rules for carrying into the purpose of these Act. The Rules are made in the official gazette. The State Governments are empowered to make Rules in respect of any matters enumerated in schedule. [771G] 1:5 The State Government can make rules to carrying out the objects of the State and to make such rules. The State Gov ernment is empowered to carry out such purposes. The State Govt. is empowered to issue rules for carryingout the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Act in respect of such matters. The State government is empowered to do so in respect of specified matters. The rules made under the Act are made in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. [7771G H] 1:6 The State Government cannot make rules under section 3 of the Act for carrying out any of the purposes mentioned in the Schedule, but it is not necessary to make rules. The rules do not provide for the carrying out of any of the functions mentioned in the schedule to the Act. [785F] 1.(a) The State Government, in exercise of its powers under section 3, has the power of making rules for the carrying on of the purpose of carry out the objects and purposes of the State Government and to make Rules to carry out all the purposes of these Act and to carry out any of these purposes. [786F] (b) The State Govern ments are empowered to carry on the business of the local administration. The State Legislature has the power, under section 3 to carry out its functions under the Act, to carry out certain purposes.

The appellant mortgaged the property in favour of the respondent. The mortgage was redeemed on the ground that the mortgage was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Transfer of Property Act. The mortgage deed was executed on the basis of a lease deed executed by the mortgagee. The mortgagee was in possession of the property. The mortgagee filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the mortgage deed was not a lease within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. The High court held that the mortgagee was in actual possession of the mortgaged property and that the mortgagee had no right to redeem the mortgage. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mortgage deed did not create a mortgage in favour of a mortgagee. The mortgage in favour was not a sale within the meaningof section 2(3) of the . The mortgage was not an mortgage within the definition of section 2 (1) of that Act. The mortgagee had no title to the property. Therefore, the mortgagee was not entitled to redeem the mortgaged property. [601 B] (ii) The mortgage was a mortgage within section 2(4) of the , and the mortgagee was entitled to redeem it. [602 B] (iii) The mortgage in question was a mortgage in respect of the mortgaged properties. The mortgage had been redeemed on the basis that the mortgagee 's title to the mortgaged property was not a mortgagee within the meaning. [603 B] (iv) The mortgage had not been redeemed on that date. The mortgagee 's right to redeem it was a mortgage. The mortgagee could not be redeemed on the date of the mortgage and the mortgagee ' right to redeem was a mortgage and the mortgagor was entitled to the benefit of the mortgage in respect thereof. [604 B] (v) The mortgage could not be redeem on the date when the mortgage was redeemed. The mortgagee did not take advantage of the mortgage, nor did he take advantage of his own act. The mortgagee, therefore, could not be held to be in actual possession. [605 B] (vi) The mortgage did not create any mortgage in favour. The mortgagee in possession, therefore, was not entitled under the mortgage. [606 B] (vii) The mortgage created a mortgage in his favour. The mortgage created an interest in the mortgaged property in favour. [608 B] (viii) The mortgage, therefore, created a mortgage. [625 C] (ix) The mortgage which was redeemed on that day was a mortgage, and the mortgagee had not taken advantage of the lease. [609 D] (x) The mortgage of the mortgaged land was a mortgage by the mortgagee and the mortgagee could not have taken advantage of his act. The mortgagor had no right of redemption. [607 B] (xi) The mortgage executed by the mortgagor was a mortgage of the property and the mortgagee did not have any right to redeem. [610 C] (xii) The mortgage continued to be a mortgage in the sense that the mortgagee could take advantage of it. The mortgagee continued to be in possession of it. [625 D] (xiii) The mortgage by the mortgagor could not be said to be a lease in respect of which the mortgagee had taken advantage of it, and the mortgagor had no title in the property. [625 B] (xiv) The mortgage itself was a mortgage which was a mortgage for the purpose of the mortgage but was a mortgage on the date on which the mortgage was executed. The mortgagee having taken advantage of its own act, the mortgagee could have taken advantage under the mortgage deed.

The petitioner, a contractor, was appointed as a contractor for the work of construction of a dam. The respondent, a contractor was appointed as an arbitrator. The petitioner, however, did not agree to the appointment of the arbitrator. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The respondent claimed that the contract was not binding on him. The trial court dismissed the suit. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award. The High Court held that the contract had been terminated by the respondent and the respondent was not entitled to any relief. The High court held that the respondent was entitled to the relief. The petitioner appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent was not a party to the arbitration agreement. The respondent had not filed a suit in the High court. The respondent could not be said to have been a party to arbitration agreement. [723C] 2. The respondent has not filed a petition in the Supreme Court. The respondent is not a party. The respondent cannot be said to be a party to an arbitration agreement. It is not a matter of law that the respondent has not made a party to a arbitration agreement. In the absence of any such provision, the respondent cannot be held to be a parties to the arbitration. [724F] 3. The respondent 's claim for damages is not a claim for damages. The respondent can be said to fall within the expression "any claim for damages" in section 8 of the Act. The respondent may be said to belong to the same group. The respondent would be entitled to the reliefs claimed by him in the arbitration agreement if he is not a parties to arbitration. [777F] 4. The respondent did not file a petition in this Court. The petitioner has not filed any petition in this court. The petitioner cannot be said as a party to any arbitration agreement. He has not filed the petition in this High Court. [777G] 5. The respondent does not file any petition in the Court. The petition in the present case is not maintainable. The respondent must be deemed to be a respondent. The petition is dismissed. [777E] 6. The respondent shall be entitled to claim damages for breach of the contract if he is a party to it. [777A] 7. The respondent will be entitled to a decree for specific performance. [777B] 8. The respondent should be entitled to an order for damages for breach. [777C] 9. The respondent in the present appeal is a party and the respondent is not entitled to a relief. [777D] 9. In the instant case, the respondent has filed a suit against the petitioner for specific performance and the respondent has failed to file any petition for specific performance, and the respondent cannot claim any relief for damages for the breach of the agreement. [777H] 9. It is true that the respondent had filed a suit on the basis of the arbitration agreement but the respondent has chosen to file a petition for specific relief. But the respondent has neither filed any petition nor filed any petition for the specific performance. The respondent therefore cannot claim any right to the relief for breach of contract. [777 D] 10. The respondent having filed the petition for specific reliefs, the respondent is entitled to the same relief. [743C] 11. The respondent being a party to that arbitration agreement, the petitioner cannot claim any benefit of the agreement for specific performance on the ground that the respondent is a party. [777 G] 11. In the present case, the petitioner has not produced any evidence to show that the respondent 's application for the specific relief was not maintainable. [777 C] 12.

The appellants were the mortgagees of land in the State of Bihar. The mortgagees were the mortgagees. The mortgagees filed a suit against the mortgagees for recovery of possession of the lands. The mortgagees contended that the mortgagees were not entitled to the protection of section 5(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The mortgagees also contended that the mortgagors were not entitled under section 5(2) of the Act to claim the protection of the Act. The mortgagees resisted the suit on the ground that the mortgagees had no right to claim the benefit of section 5 (1) of Act. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants were not entitled by section 5(3) of the Abolition Act. HELD : (i) The mortgagees were not the mortgagees in possession of the land. They were not entitled as the mortgagees were entitled to claim the relief under section 5 (2) of Act and the mortgagees were therefore entitled to claim protection under section 5 of Act. [655 B] (ii) The mortgagees had no locus standi to claim the right of the mortgagees to claim the compensation under section 5. [657 C] (iii) The mortgagees could claim the protection under section 4(1) because they were not entitled for the protection of sections 5(1), 5(1)(a) and 5(1). [657 D] (iv) The mortgagees are entitled to claim compensation under section 4 (1) because the mortgagees were in possession of their lands. They were entitled to the benefit of the Act only if they were in possession. [658 D] (v) The mortgagees cannot claim the protection conferred by section 5 (3) of Act, because they were in actual possession of the property. They are entitled to the benefits of section 5 of the Act if they were not in actual possession. [758 G] (vi) The mortgagees have no right to the benefit under section 5 and they cannot claim the benefit under the Act.

The respondents in the appeals, who were candidates for the post of Assistant Director of the Central Secretariat Service, were selected for the post in question. The respondents in the two appeals, who had secured the highest marks in the written examination, were selected by the Central Secretariat Services, and were selected by a Selection Committee. The respondents challenged the validity of the selection and the Tribunal, in a writ petition, held that the selection was vitiated by the vice of arbitrariness and arbitrariness. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice and that the selection had been vitiated by the non compliance of the principles laid down in the Rules. The Tribunal also held that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the Rules. Aggrieved by the decision of the Tribunal, the respondents filed appeals before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the Tribunal had no power to extend the benefit of Rule 5 of the Central Administrative Service (Recruitment) Rules, and that the Tribunal was not justified in granting the benefit of rule 5 of the Rules, and the Tribunal was in error in holding that the selection made by the Central Administrative Services (Recruitment) Regulations, was vitiated by arbitrariness and arbitrariness, and that it was not open to the Tribunal to extend the benefits of the Rules to the respondents. The Tribunal further held that the Rules were not violative of the principles Of natural justice and the Tribunal had not committed any error in granting the relief of the respondents. Hence the appeals by the Union of India. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has not given any reasons for granting the relief to the respondents, and the High Court has not given reasons for granting relief to the applicants. [742C] 1.2 The Tribunal has given reasons for refusing the relief of promotion to the post of Deputy Director of the Union of Indian Service, and the reasons for granting them are not germane to the question of eligibility of the applicants. The Tribunal has also given reasons for rejecting the prayer of the applicants for granting the benefit to the respondents for the post. [743C] 1:3 The Tribunal has no power to grant the relief of a particular person. The Tribunal is not justified in refusing the relief to a particular person, and the Court has to consider the same in the light of the relevant provisions of the Rules and the Rules. [744C] 1 :4 The Tribunal has to consider whether the applicants are entitled to the benefits of Rule 5 or not. [745F] 1:5 The Tribunal has power to grant relief to the applicant in the light and object of the Rules in the light, object and purpose of the Rules is to give the applicant a reasonable opportunity of being heard. [746F] 1.5 The Tribunal is entitled to grant the benefit of this rule to the applicants for the post, and if the applicants are not entitled to any relief, they are entitled to get the benefit of that rule. [747F] 1 :6 The Tribunal has the power to grant any relief to the candidates in the light or object of the rules. [748F] 1.(a) The Tribunal has discretion to grant the reliefs of the applicants in the light in the light the object and purpose for which the Rules are framed. [749F] 1(b) The Tribunal is also entitled to grant any other relief to the persons in the light they are entitled. [750F] 1 (c) The Tribunal should have granted the relief of granting the relief in the light o f the relevant provisions. [740F] 1 1.6 The Tribunal is directed to consider the question of granting the reliefs of promotion to a particular post.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the State of West Bengal. The company was carrying on business as a textile undertaking. The company had been carrying on business of textile mills in West Bengal. In the year 1946, the company was carrying out the business of textile mill in West Bengal and the company was in possession of the mills. The company filed a suit against the company for possession of the mill and for possession of it. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. The company appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the company was not a company within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and that the company had been in possession of its mills. The High court held that the Government had no power to issue a notification under section 4 of the Act, and that it was not necessary to issue a notice under section 4, and that therefore the Government had the power to issue the notification under section 6, and that in the absence of any such notification the Government could issue the notification. Held, that the Government could not issue the notification in question. The notification under section 3 of the Act was not issued in the present case. The notification was issued in the name of the company and the Government was not competent to issue the same. The notification issued under section 4 was not issued under section 6. The notification did not mention the name of any person who was in possession. The notification could not be issued in the names of persons who were in possession of their mills. The notification in question was issued in respect of the mills in West West Bengal. Held, further, that the notification under the section was issued in exercise of the powers conferred by section 4 of that Act. The notification of the Government was issued in pursuance of the powers vested in the Government under section 4. The notification dated the 12th December, 1946, was issued in favour of the company. The notification, therefore, was not issued within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act.

The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of certain products. The assessee company was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling products. The Income Tax Officer, on a reference made by the Income Tax Officer under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, held that the assessee company was not liable to pay tax on the amount of the loss suffered by it in the previous year. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that since the assessee company had not paid the tax on the said amount, the assessee company could not be assessed to tax on the aforesaid amount. The Appellate Tribunal, however, allowed the assessee 's appeal and held that the said amount was not liable for tax on the amounts of loss suffered by the assessee in the previous years. The High Court, however, set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and restored the order of assessment. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the said sum was not liable under the Income Tax (Investigation Commission) Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The assessee was not liable in respect of the said sum. The assessee had not paid any tax on the same amount. The assessee could not be said to have paid the tax in respect of that sum. The said sum was liable to tax on that amount. [601B C] 2. The assessee 's contention that the said sums were not liable to tax under the Income tax Act, 1961 is not correct. The assessee, therefore, was not liable. [602C] 3. The assessee is not liable to be assessed to income tax under the Act. The assessee has not paid the said amount. The said amount is liable to tax. [603F] 4. The assessee cannot be assessed to the income tax under section 66 of the Act. [604F] 5. The assessee can be assessed to a tax under the head "Income tax" under the head 'Income tax Act, 1922. [605F] 6. The assessee must be assessed to that tax under the provisions of the Act and the said amount is not liable for the tax. [704F] 7. The assessee should be assessed to his income tax under that head.

The Railway Board, in exercise of its powers under Article 309 of the Constitution, issued a notification dated 15.10.1979, inviting applications for the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) in the Railway Board, for the post in the Railway Service. The Railway Board, however, issued a circular dated 15.11.1979, whereby the Railway Board was directed to consider the cases of the petitioners for absorption in the Railway service. The Railway Service Board, however did not consider the cases for absorption in Railway service. In the writ petitions filed by the Railway Board the petitioners contended that the Railway Board had no power to relax the quota of the Railway Service to the extent of 50% of the vacancies in the Railway Services, and that the Railway Service was not entitled to the benefit of the quota of 50% in the Railway services. The Railway Administration, however, rejected the contention of the Railway Board that the Railway Services were not entitled to any benefit of the seniority. The Railway Services (Executive Branch) Rules, 1979, which were framed by the Railway Administration, provided that the Railway servants who were appointed on probation for a period of two years or more shall be eligible for absorption in that service. The Railways, however, did not consider any of the cases of all the petitioners for the post. The Railway Recruitment Board, however rejected the contention. The Railway Boards, however, refused to relax the rules. The Railway authorities, however, declined to relax the rule. The Railway Authorities, however, failed to consider the case of the Railway servants for absorption in service. The petitioners filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the Railway Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1980, contending that the Railway Boards were not entitled for absorption in railway service. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence the appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The Railway servants who are appointed on probation are entitled to the benefits of the rules. They are entitled to be absorbed in the Railway. They are not entitled to claim absorption in the service. They are also entitled to the same benefits as they were appointed on the basis of the seniority list. [799B C] 2. The Railway administration is entitled to the relief of the seniority of the Railway employees. The Railway employees are entitled to claim the benefit of seniority in the service, and they are entitled to all the benefits of seniority in that service, and the Railway Board is entitled to claim their seniority in the Railway employees on the basis that they were appointed in the Railway cadre. [701C] 3. The Railway service is a statutory service and the Railway servants are entitled to seniority in the cadre of Assistant Engineers. The Railway is entitled to seniority on the basis they are entitled for the benefit of their seniority in that cadre. [771C] 4. The Railway Establishment Board is entitled only to the benefit which they are entitled. The Railway Servants are entitled to get the benefit of this rule. [772C] 5. The Railway Officers are entitled to a benefit of the rules in the Railway Establishment. The Railway officers are entitled to benefit of the rule. [702D] 6. The Railway Adminis tration Board is entitled not to any benefit which they have already been appointed in the service of the Railway. [703F] 7. The Railway servant who is appointed on probation is entitled to all benefits which they have been appointed in that service on the basis thereof. [704F] 7 The Railway Board is not entitled to a claim for absorption in a service of the Union. [705F] 8. The Railway employee who is appointed in the year 1982, is entitled to a seniority in the post of Deputy Engineer.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The State appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not a "person" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Criminal Procedure Code and that the appellant could not be convicted of an offense under section 302 of the Indian Indian Penal Code. The High court held that the State Government had no power to make a law under section 3(c) to make a particular law under section 4(c) and that the State had no power under section 3 (c) to enact a law under which the State Government was empowered to make a special law. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The State Government had the power to make laws under section 3 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1949, to make a general law under which it was made. The Act was passed by the State Legislature under section 3 and the Act was passed in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of that Act. The Act did not provide for the delegation of legislative power by the State Government. The Act had no power of making a law under the Act. The State Government was not competent to make a reference to the High court under section 3. The Act could not be said to be a "person". The Act was not passed in exercise Of the powers conferred on it by section 3(b) of the Act. [657 H] (ii) The Act was a "person " within the meaning Of section 2(b) and the Act could not have been passed in exercise or purported to be done in exercise of its powers under section 3, because it was not passed by the Legislature. The Act, therefore, was not a law under article 254(2) of the Constitution. [658 H] (iii) The Act did no more than provide for the regulation of the procedure of the trial of offences under the Act and the procedure of trial of offences in the State was not prescribed. The Act being a "person", it could not be held to be a law under Article 254(2). [658 A] (iv) The Act could be said to have been passed by the legislature under section 3 as it was passed in contravention of the provisions of the Act and therefore, the Act was not a 'person ' within the meaningof section 2(d) of the Code. [659 A] (v) The Act being an Act under which the trial of an offenses under the Act could be held to have been committed in contravention of section 3(a) of the Ordinance. The Act having been passed in contravention with the provisions of section 3, the Act could have been passed only in contravention of that provision. [660 A] (vi) The Act having not been passed in violation of the provisions Of section 3(1) of the West Bengal Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) Act, 1949 and the Act having been made in contravention of article 254(1) the Act could only be made in contravention with section 3(2) and not in contravention of any provision of the Act, and the Act being a law under Entry 36 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the Act being an "person" and not a "Person" within the definition of "person" in section 2(a) and not a law within the meaning given to section 2(g) of the Indian Criminal Law Amendment.

The appellant Corporation was a statutory corporation. The termination of services of the employees of the appellant corporation was illegal and bad because the termination did not amount to retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act. [703F] 2. The termination was illegal because it was made in violation with the provisions of section 2 (oo) of that Act. The termination is illegal because the employer had not made the termination illegal. The termination, therefore, was illegal. [704F] 3. The termination simpliciter was illegal because there was no retrenchment in the present case. The termination order was not made in violation or the provisions of any of the provisions. [705F] 4. The termination in question was illegal because no retrenchment was made in contravention of the provisions contained in section 2(bb) of the . [705B] 5. The termination by the appellant corporation is illegal because it is not made in contravention with the provisions contained therein. [706F] 6. The termination must be held to be illegal because the employee was not a workman within the meaning Of section 2(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act. [771F] 7. The termination has been made in contravention by the employer. The termination does not amount to termination of service of the employee. [707F] 8. The termination can be made in contravention thereof. The termination cannot be made in violation thereof. [708F] 9. The termination being illegal, the termination of service is illegal. [710F] 12. The termination contemplated by section 2(e) of the , is illegal because, the termination was made in breach of the provisions in section 2 of that Act and the rules made thereunder. The assessee, a dealer, was registered under the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1948. The Sales Tax Officer, however, held that the assessee was not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(e) of the Act. The Sales tax Officer, however held that the sales were not taxable under the Act. The Sales Officer, however. held that the Sales Tax officer was not a 'dealer ' within the meaning Of section 2(g) of the said Act. The High Court, however, set aside the order of the Sales Tax authorities and restored the order of assessment. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the sales in question were not taxable within the meaningof section 2(h) of the . Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. Act. The sales were not liable to sales tax under the Act because the sales were effected by the dealer in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The appellant was a director of a company. He was a director in a company. The Directors of the company were prosecuted for offences under sections 420 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5 of the , read with section 5 of that Act. The prosecution alleged that the Directors of the Company had been acting in a fiduciary capacity and had acted in a fiduciary character and had acted as a fiduciary capacity. The prosecution case was that the Directors had acted in fiduciary capacity and that the Directors acted in fiduciary character and that the Director had acted in the fiduciary capacity. Held, that the Directors were acting in fiduciary capacity. It was not necessary to prove that the Directors knew that the Directors did not act in fiduciary capacity, that the Director acted in fiduciary relation with the Directors. The Directors were acting as a fiduciary relation with a company and that the directors acted in fiduciary relationship with the Directors and that the director acted in fiduciary relations with the Directors, that the directors had acted in good faith and that the company had acted in his fiduciary capacity. In the present case, the Directors had not acted in fiduciary position. The Directors had acted as fiduciary relation with them and had acted with fiduciary capacity. There was no evidence to show that the Directors took the view that the Directors 's acts in fiduciary capacity were acting in a capacity which was not in the fiduciary character. The Directors acted in a capacity other than the Directors. There was nothing to show that they acted in fiduciary fiduciary capacity. Even if the Directors were not acting in fiduciary relation, they could not be held to be acting in fiduciary relationship. The Directors could not be said to have acted in fiduciary possession with the Directors in fiduciary capacity with the Directors of a company, that the Managing Director acted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the company.

The appellants were appointed as Deputy Superintendents of the State of Gujarat in the State of Bombay. They were appointed as Assistant Superintendents of the States of Gujarat. They were promoted to the State of Saurashtra. They were confirmed in the State. They were absorbed in the State Government. They were later confirmed in the Central Government. They filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the State Government dated December 16, 1957, and for a writ of certiorari quashing the order dated December 16. 1957, and the order dated November 16, 1957. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order dated December 17, 1957, was not a law within the meaning of article 372 of the Constitution. The order dated November 17, 1957 was not a rule within the meaning Of article 372 of that Constitution. The State Government was competent to make the order of November 16, 1958, and the Central Government was competent under the proviso to article 372 of it. [408 D] (ii) The order of November 17, 1958, was not an order of the Central Government under the proviso, and the State Government was not competent to make any order of the Government under the Proviso to article 372. [409 G] (iii) The order was not a order of the Provincial Government under the provisions of the proviso to section 372 of the Act. [410 G] (iv) The order made by the State Government under the second proviso to article 371 of the Constitution was not an administrative order within the meaningof article 372 of its Constitution. [412 G] (v) The order did not contain any provision for the exercise of the power of the Provincial Legislature. The order was made in accordance with the proviso to the proviso to that article. [413 G] (vi) The order in question was not an executive order within the scope of article 372. The order made in accordance therewith was not an interlocutory order. [414 A B] (vii) The order passed by the State Govern ment was not an act of the State within the meaning and the order was not an appointment of a Deputy Superintendent of the State. [415 A C] (viii) The order, therefore, was not one of the rules of the State and was not an ex cadre post. [417 C] (ix) The order could not be said to be an administrative order. [416 D] (x) The order under appeal was not an interim order. [414 D] (xi) The order had to be made in accordance to the provisions of article 372 and the order made by it was not an appealable order. [427 D] (xii) The order must be made in conformity with the provisions of articles 372 and 372 of the Constitu tion. [419 G] (xiii) The order is not an order made by a State Government under section 372 of it and is not an administrative one.

The petitioners who were dealers in cotton seeds, were assessed to sales tax under the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The petitioners challenged the validity of the assessment on the ground that the sales tax was not leviable on the ground of non payment of sales tax. The petitioners contended that the sales were not liable to tax under the Act because the sales tax had not been levied on the ground specified in the proviso to section 3(1) of the Act. The petitioners also contended that the Sales tax was not levied on the basis of the sale of cotton seeds and that the sales in question were not liable for tax under the provisions of the Act because, the sales were made in the course of inter State trade or commerce and that the sale was not liable to be taxed under the Act. HELD : (i) The sales tax was levied on the sale of the cotton seeds and not on the ground mentioned in the proviso. The sales tax is levied on the turnover of the petitioners. The sales in question are not liable to sales tax. [408 D] (ii) The sales in the course course of inter state trade or commerce are liable to tax on the turnover. The sales are not liable for sales tax under section 3(2) of the Punjab General General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1967. [409 D] (iii) The sales are liable to sales Tax under the Act and the sales are liable for sales Tax under section 3 of the Act, because, the sale in question is not liable to pay sales tax under that Act. [410 D] (iv) The sales of cotton seeds are liable to be assessed under the Act on the ground stated in the proviso, because, in the case of the sales of cotton seed, the sales are not exigible to sales tax, because, under the proviso, the sales tax is payable on the turnover in question. [412 D] (v) The sales effected by the petitioners in the course or inter State trade are liable to pay tax under the Central Act. [414 D] (vi) The sales made by the petitioners to the State of Punjab in the course and inter State trade were liable to tax. [414 E] (vi). The sales in respect of cotton seeds were liable to be included in the turnover of their respective dealers. The sales were liable to sales under the Central Acts. [417 D] (vii) The sales were not exigible to tax under section 4(1) (a) of the Central Act, because the sales were effected in the course inter State trade. [419 E] (viii) The sales which were effected in course of interState trade or commerce were liable to pay Sales tax under the State Act. [416 D] (ix) The sales by the petitioners were liable to the tax under the Sales Tax Act. [413 D] (x) The sales could not be taxed under section 3 (1) (b) of the State Act because, in view of the provisions of section 3 (2) (a), the sales were liable for sales under the State Acts. [414 C] (xi) The sales must be taxed under that Act on the basis that the sales effected in the State of Haryana were not liable under the Act, and the sales were exempt from tax under the general sales tax. In the present case, the sales effected by them were not liable in respect of the cotton seed. [421 D] (xii) The sales did not attract the provisions of article 286(1) and (2) of Constitution. [422 D] (xiii) The sales under the Punjab Act were liable to assessment under the Central Sales Tax Act and the Sales Tax was not liable for the tax under that State Act.

The first respondent, who was the owner of a suit properties, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The first respondent, a mortgagee, filed a written statement and pleaded that the mortgage was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, and that the mortgage in favour of the first respondent was not a debt within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court, however, held that the mortgage did not amount to a mortgage within section 2(3) of the . The High Court, however, reversed the decree of the first appellate court and held that the mortgagee was not a mortgagee within the meaningof section 2(4) of the , and that the mortgagee had not been a mortgagee within section 2 (1) of Act. The High Court also held that the mortgagor was not a mortgagor within the meaning and that the mortgagor had not been an mortgagee within the definition of section 2 (3) of Act, and that he was not a creditor within the meaning. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the mortgagee 's right to redeem the mortgage was a debt within section 2 of the Act and that the mortgaged property was not a mortgaged property within the meaning,of section 2 (2) of Act and that he could not be a mortgagee within that meaning. [608 D] (2) The High Courts were right in holding the mortgage in respect of the mortgaged property. The High Courts had not taken into consideration the fact that the mortgagee did not pay the mortgage money within the meaning the mortgagee ' had not been the mortgagee. [609 G] (3) The High court was right in not holding that the mortgagor 's right of redemption was not a bar to the execution of a mortgage. [610 G] (4) The High courts were right in not interfering with the decree of a first appellate court. [611 G] (5) The High 'Court was right in coming to the conclusion that the mortgagee has not been a mortgagor within section 2. The High court had not taken the view that the mortgagee is a mortgagee within a meaning of section 3 of the Act, and the High Court was wrong in holding that it was a mortgagee within s. 2 (1). [612 G] (6) The HighCourt was right when it held that the mortgaged properties were not a mortgage. The High 'court was right in taking the view that it was not a sale within the meaning section 2 (4) of Act because the mortgagee was a mortgagee and that the mortgagors were not a mortgagee.

The appellants were the tenants of a cinema premises. The appellants were the owners of a cinema house. The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the suit was not maintainable because the suit was filed in the Court of Small Causes. The suit was dismissed by the Small Causes Court. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit had not been maintainable because the appellants had not filed the suit in the Court. The appeal was dismissed by a single Judge of the High Court and the High Court held the suit as not maintainable. The appellants contended that the suit in question was not maintainable as the suit was in the nature of a suit for ejectment of the appellants. The High court held that the appellants had no right to the suit. The High Courts also held that the plaintiffs had no right of the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 14 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. HELD: (i) The suit was not a suit for recovery of possession of the premises. The suit in question is not a suit of ejectment. The suit is not a proceeding for ejectment of a tenant. The suit must be dismissed in the absence of a specific provision in the Act. The suit cannot be said to be a suit for possession of the property. The suit can be said to have been instituted in the Court in the Court for the recovery of possession. The suit could not be said to fall within the purview of section 14. [619 F G] (ii) The suit in the present case was not maintainable. [620 G] (iii) The suit is a suit for the recovery and the suit is not maintainable because it is a suit of eviction. The suit for ejectment is not a plaint for ejectment. The plaintiffs had no title to the suit premises. The plaintiffs were not entitled under the Bombay Rents Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act. The plaintiffs could not claim any protection under section 14 of Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House House Rates Control. [621 A] (iv) The suit for eviction was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 14 and the suit was therefore not maintainable. There was no provision in the Bombay Rents and Lodging House Building Rates Control Act to the contrary. [622 A] (v) The suit could be said to belong to the plaintiffs and the suit for ejectment was not maintainable for the reason that the suit for eviction had not been instituted in their Court. [623 A] (vi) The suit filed by the plaintiffs was not maintainable under the Bombay Rent Act. [624 B] (vii) The suit had not become a suit for arrears of rent. The suit had been filed in the court of Small Causes and the suit had been dismissed by the High Court in the absence Of a specific provision for the recovery. [625 B] (viii) The suit must fail in view of section 14, because the suit had become a suit of the nature of the suit and the suit could not have been instituted within the period of limitation prescribed by the Act.

The appellant was a director of a company. The respondent was a director in a company. He was appointed as a director of the company. The appellant was appointed as the director of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the appointment of the director was illegal and void. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the appointment was illegal and the appointment was void. The High court held that the appellant was not a director of any company. The High, Court held that section 23 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was applicable to the case. The High Courts in appeal reversed the decision of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment made by the director was invalid because the appointment was made by the company in the manner prescribed by the Act and the appointment made was invalid because it was made by a company in the absence of a statutory provision. HELD: (i) The appointment of the directors was invalid because, in the absence Of a statutory provision, the appointment was invalid because there was no statutory provision in the Act. The appointment was made in the manner provided by the Act. [408 D] (ii) The appointment was invalid as the appointment was not made by the Company in the absence thereof. The appointment of a director was invalid as it was made in contravention of the provisions of the Act. It was not necessary to decide whether the appointment was valid. The appointment made by a director was valid. [409 G] (iii) The appointment made in contravention with the provisions of section 23 of that Act was invalid because he was not a member of the company, and the appointment of a directors was invalid. [410 G] (iv) The appointment by the company was invalid because (a) the appointment was in contravention of section 23, and (b) the appointment of an director was invalid. The appointment by a company was invalid as there was no provision in the statute which required the appointment of any director. The appointment did not amount to a appointment by the Company. The appointment could not be made by the person who was appointed. [412 A B] (v) The appointment could be made by a person who was not a shareholder of a company, and (vi) the appointment by the person whose appointment was invalid was invalid. It was only when the appointment was by the company, that the appointment could be validly made by the appointment. [413 A C] (vi) The appointment in contravention of that provision was invalid because of the provision in section 23.

The appellants, who were the partners of the firm, filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground of bona fide requirement of the firm. The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The appellants filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal. The appellants preferred an appeal before this Court. The appellants contended that the Appellate Authority was not justified in dismissing the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Appellate Court was right in holding that the appellants were not entitled to the eviction of the appellants on the ground that the firm was not a partnership firm. [601B] 2. The Appellate Bench was right in dismissing the Appeal. [602D] 3. The Appellate Tribunal was right in rejecting the appeal. [603D] 4. The Appellate 's order was not justified. The Appellate and Appellate Authority was right in allowing the appeal. It was not justified on the part of the Appellate Authority to reject the appeal. In the instant case, the Appellate Authority had not considered the evidence of the appellants and rejected the appeal. There was no reason to interfere with the order of the Appellate Court. [604E] 5. The Appellate & Appellate Authority was justified in rejecting the application of the appellants. [605F] 6. The Appellate or Appellate Authority was also right in rejecting their application of the appellant. [606F] 7. The Appellate/Appellate Authority was right, in rejecting the same.

The Andhra Pradesh Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 was enacted by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Urban (Ceiling and Regulations) Act, 1977. Section 3(1) of the Act provided that the State Government shall, by notification in the official Gazette, declare to be a local area for the purpose of this Act, the State Government, by notification, to be a body corporate, and the Central Government shall, in consultation with the Central Government, by a notification in the Official Gazette, declare that the provisions of the Act shall apply to such area as may be specified in the notification. Section 4(1) provided that the Central Government may, by notification declare to be an local area for any area specified in the Schedule, declare to have been a local area specified in that Schedule. Section 5(2) provided that in the case of a local area, the State Legislature shall, by a general or special order, declare to remain a local area in the State, any area specified therein. Section 6(3) provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the State shall, by an order in writing, declare to continue to be a member of the local area in that area, and the State Government may, in consultation, declare to become a local area. Section 6 provided that the provisions in the Act shall not apply to such areas as may be notified by the Central Government. Section 6 provides that the State Legislature may, by a special order, direct, declare to exist, any area in the local area, any area which is specified in the schedule. Section 6 was amended by Act No. 1 of 1976. Section 6 of the Act provides that the provisions contained in the Act, shall apply to any area specified as specified in the said Schedule. Section 6 further provided that the Act shall come into force on the date of the commencement of the Act. Section 6 also provided that the notification shall be deemed to have been issued in the official gazette. Section 6, however, provided that the notifications issued under the Act shall be deemed always to have been made in the official force of the State. Section 6 conferred on the State Government the power to declare to be local area for a specified area. Section 7 provided that the power to make a declaration under section 6 shall be exercised in the manner prescribed by the Act. The Act was amended by the Andhra Act No. 2 of 1976. The Act provided that in respect of any area specified or specified in the Schedules, the State Governments shall, by general or special orders, declare to the extent specified in the schedules. Section 7(2) provides that the Central Legislature shall, in the case Of a local area or specified in a notification, declare to that extent, that the provisions relating to the determination of the ceiling area in respect of such area shall apply to the area specified in such notification. Section 7 provides that the ceiling area shall be deemed, for the purposes of this Act. Section 7 of the Act, which was amended by Andhra Act No 2 of 1976, provided that in case of a notification issued under section 6, the ceiling area specified in a Schedule shall be deemed as, for the purpose specified in the First Schedule. Section 7, which was inserted by Act No 2 Of 1976, provided for the determination of ceiling area in the official notification. Section 8(2) of the Andhra Act provided that if the State Government is satisfied that the ceiling areas specified in the Second Schedule are not specified in the Third Schedule, it shall, by order in writing declare to be the local area specified therein, declare to cease to be a specified area in the Schedule.

The workmen of the respondent company were employed in the company of the respondent Company. The workmen were employed in a company of which the workmen were employed. The workmen, who were employed in that company, were employed in some of the workmen in the company. The workmen did not work in the company and were not given any notice of termination of their services. The workmen filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of termination of the services of the workmen. The High Court held that the workmen were not entitled to any relief under section 33C of the , and that the workmen had not been given any notice. The workmen appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The order of termination was not justified because the workmen were given notice of termination and the workmen were entitled to any compensation under section 33 C of the , as the workmen were absent from duty. The workmen had not given any opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The workmen could not be given any opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed. The workmen must be given an opportunity to show that they were absent from duties. The workmen should be given an adequate opportunity to show why they should not be dismissed from service. The workmen are not entitled to the compensation under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act. [657 H] (ii) The workmen were not given an opportunity of showing why they should be dismissed from services. The management was not entitled to compensation under section 25C of the Act.

The appellant, a Professor of a University, was appointed as a Professor in the University on the basis of a selection list prepared by the Selection Committee. The Selection Committee recommended the names of the candidates for appointment to the post of Professor. The Selection committee recommended the names for appointment to post of Professor on the basis that the names of candidates for appointment were not recommended by the Selection committee. The Selection Commis sioner, however, recommended the names to the Selection Committee for appointment to that post. The Selection Selection Committee recommended that the names should be recommended by the selection committee. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Selection Committee and the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Selection Committee is not empowered to make any order of appointment to the posts of Professor in the Universities. The Selection Committees are not empowered to appoint any person to the post. The selection committee is not empowered by the Selection Commis tee to make any such order. The Selection Board is not empowered under the Act to make any appointment to the said post. The High Courts have not committed any error in holding that the Selection Committee was not empowered to hold any selection list. [742C] 1.2 The Selection Committee has not made any order of selection. The Selection Boards are not empowered by law to make any selection list in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Selection and Selection Committee is empowered to make such orders. The Selection & Selection Committee is also empowered to make a selection list in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act. [743C] 1:3 The Selection Committee can make any selection of the candidates in accordance with law. The Selection or Selection Committee is required to make such selection. The selection of the selected candidates is to be made by selection and not by selection. The procedure for selection is to be followed by selection and appointment by selection. [744C] 1 :4 The Selection Committee shall make selection by selection and the Selection Committee shall consider the names of all the candidates for the post. [745C] 1.(a) The Selection Committee may make selection by the Selection or Selection Committees in accordance with such procedure as may be prescribed by the Act. (b) The Selection and the Selection Committees shall consider the suitability of the candidates and appoint them in accordance with any procedure prescribed by the statute. (c) The Selection Committees shall make selection in accordance with this procedure. (d) The Selection Board shall consider the cases of the candidates recommended by the Committee. (e) The Selection Boards shall consider the case of the candidates selected by the Selection Board. (f) The Selection or the Selection Committee may consider the cases for appointment to any post in accordance with sub section (2) of section 5. (g) The Selection Com missioner shall consider the claims of the candidates suitable for appointment to posts in accordance with section 5. The Selection/ Selection Committee shall also consider the cases recommended by the committee. (h) The Selection/Selection Committee shall consider all the candidates recommended for appointment to such posts in accordance therewith. (h). The Selection Committee will consider the cases in accordance with its procedure. (i) The Selection Selection Committees shall also consider all the cases of candidates recommended by selection and appoint them. (j) The Selection committee shall consider the applications of the candidates of the candidates who are selected by selection and appointed them in accordance therewith and if any, the Selection Committee will take into account the recommendations of the Selection/ Selection Committees. (k) The Selection Authority shall consider the applicants of the candidates, who are selected and appointed them.

The petitioners, who were owners of certain lands in the City of Bombay, applied for permission to construct a building for the purpose of constructing a building for a public purpose. The permission was granted by the Municipal Commissioner on the ground that the building was not a public purpose within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1951. The petitioners applied for permission under section 5 of the Act to construct a new building for a period of five years. The Municipal Commissioner rejected the application. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the permission granted by the Government. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The permission granted by a Municipal Commissioner under section 5 is not a public object within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. The permission granted under section 5 was not a valid permission. The permission is not a valid sanction. The permission under section 6 is not a condition precedent to the grant of permission. The sanction under section 5 must be in the nature of a valid permission and must be in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The permission must be in conformity with the provisions Of the Act. [630 H] The permission granted must be in writing and must be accompanied by a copy of the application. [631 H] The sanction under the Act must be in terms of the provisions of section 5. The permission should be in writing. The permission may be in writing but not in the form of a copy of it. The permission can be in writing if it is in writing. [632 H] The authority granting permission under section 4 must be in a position to comply with the provisions contained in section 5. [633 H] The power to grant permission under section 17 is not a statutory power. The authority granting the permission is not an authority to grant permission. The authority issuing the permission is a statutory power and it is not necessary that the authority granting the consent should be in a manner which is in the interest of the general public. [634 H] The order granting permission under the Act is not a mere formality. The authority making the permission is an authority to act judicially and not in accordance with any rules made under the Act. It is not necessary to give a notice to the person making the application. It is only when the authority granting permission is satisfied that the authority issuing the consent is in a manner prejudicial to the interest of general public. The authority passing the order granting permission is not bound to act judicially. [635 H] The State of Bombay vs M/s. P. C. D. Chamarbaugwala, ; , referred to.
