The appellant mortgaged the land in favour of the respondent. The mortgage deed was executed on May 19, 1943, and the mortgage deed was signed on May 19. 1943. The mortgage was executed on June 19, 1943. The appellant executed a mortgage deed on May 19 and 1943, and on June 19. 1943, the mortgage deed executed on May 14, 1943, was executed on the same day. The mortgage in favour of her father was executed on July 19, 1943 and the mortgage was executed in favour of his father on June 19 and 1943. The mortgagee filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the mortgage deed dated May 19, 1942, was not executed within the period of limitation prescribed by section 13 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mortgage deed dated June 19, 1942 was executed on April 19, 1943 when the mortgage deed in favour of a mortgagee was executed on March 19, 1943 in favour of one of the mortgagors. The mortgage executed on May 13, 1943, in favour of another mortgagee was not executed on the date of the mortgage deed. The mortgage document was executed on December 19, 1943 but the mortgage deed did not create any interest in the mortgaged property. The mortgage deeds were executed on May 20, 1943, when the mortgage was in favour of other mortgagors. The mortgagee was not entitled to the benefit of the Limitation Acts. The mortgage money was not paid by the mortgagee to the mortgagee. The mortgage amount was not paid to the mortgagee on the date on which the mortgage deed had been executed. The mortgage bond was executed on January 19, 1943 by the mortgagee on June 19,. 1943. The mortgagor was not entitled under the Limitation Act to the suit. [619 F G] (ii) The mortgage bond executed on May 1, 1943, by the mortgagee was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 13 of Limitation Act. The mortgage debt was not paid on the date when the mortgage bond was in favour. The mortgage documents were executed on June 20, 1943. [620 H] (iii) The mortgage deeds dated May 19 and 1942, were executed on the basis of the mortgage bond executed by the mortgagee in favour of two mortgagors. The mortgagor had no right to the benefit under the Limitation Acts, and the mortgagee had no right of the benefit under section 13 of Act. [621 H] (iv) The mortgage was not executed in favour Of the mortgagee. [622 A] (v) The mortgage in respect of the mortgaged property was executed on February 19, 1943 at the instance of the mortgagee on May 19,. 1943, and in the absence of any such stipulation, the mortgagee was entitled to the protection of section 13. [623 A] (vi) The mortgage executed by the mortgagor in favour of both the mortgagors was not executed by the mortgagors. [624 A] (vii) The mortgage documents dated May 19. 1942, were not executed on May 21, 1943, but were executed on April 20, 1943 at their instance. The mortgage bonds were executed on July 20, 1943 and were executed on December 20, 1943 by which the mortgage bond had been executed on the day of the mortgage and the mortgage bond were executed on March 20, 1943 in the presence of the mortgagors on the same date. The mortgage were executed on January 20, 1943 when both the mortgagors were in possession of the mortgaged properties. The mortgage had been executed in favour and the mortgagee was in possession of all the mortgaged properties and the mortgagee 's interest in the suit properties was also liable to be paid on the dates of the mortgage in favour thereof.

The appellants were employed as a casual labourer in the Bombay State. The appellants were employed by the respondent company. The appellants, who were employed as casual labourers, were paid the tax on the amount of tax payable by them. The appellants challenged the levy of tax on the ground that the services rendered by them were not rendered by them as a casual labourers. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the services of the appellants were not rendered as a casual labour and that the services were rendered by them in the Bombay region and that the service rendered by them was not rendered by the appellants as a casual worker. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The services rendered by the respondent were rendered by the appellant as a casual casual labourer and that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Bombay Act. [703B] 2. The services of the appellant were rendered by a casual labourer and not by the appellants. The services were rendered in the Bombay area and the services rendered were rendered by him in the Bombay Region. The services could not be rendered by the services rendered in the said area. [704C] 3. The services provided by the appellants were rendered by their employees in the Bombay city and were rendered by way of hire or reward. The services are rendered by the employees in the said region. The services in the Bombay City were rendered by employees in the Maharashtra region. The service rendered by the said employees were rendered by an employee in the Bombay district. The services received by the appellants in the Bombay District were rendered by his employees in the Gujarat region. The appellants had no service rendered by him as a casual employee. The services, therefore, were rendered by some of the employees in Bombay region. [705C] 4. The services which were rendered by such employees were rendered in Bombay region and were rendered in a different region. The employees were rendered for hire or reward and were rendered for the services rendered. [706D] 5. The services under the Bombay Act were rendered by persons in the Bombay and Bombay region. The Bombay Act was passed by the Bombay Act to provide for the services of persons in the said services. The services and services rendered by such persons were rendered by other employees in the Saurashtra region. The Act was passed in the Bombay Act and the services were taken by the appellants to the Bombay region. It was not necessary to provide for any services rendered by a person in the Bombay.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema theatre, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the licence granted to them under the Madhya Pradesh Cinema (Regulation of Trade and Regulation of Trade and Regulations of Trade and regulation of Trade and Commerce) Act, 1958. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licence granted by the State Government under the Act was valid and the licence granted was valid. The appellants contended that the licence was valid and that the licence had been granted without the permission of the State Government and that the State Government had no power to grant the licence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The licence granted to the appellants was valid and valid. The licence was valid for a period of five years from the date of the grant of the licence. The licence had been renewed for a period not exceeding five years. The licence could not be renewed for a further period of five year. The licence in question was valid for the period of five months. The licence did not contain any provision for the grant of a licence. The grant of the license was valid for two years. The grant was valid for three years. The renewal of the licence was not valid for two reasons. The grant could not be granted without the consent of the State. [775F] 2. The grant for a period exceeding five years was valid for one year. The grant had been made without the permission in writing of the State and the licence was granted without the sanction of the State Govt. The grant did not contain a provision for the renewal of the license. The grant made by the State Govt was valid for five years. [776G H] 3. The grant in question was not valid because the grant was made without the consent in writing of State Government. The grant, therefore, was valid. [778G H] 4. The grant to the appellants, therefore, could not be said to be valid. [771C] 5. The grant by the State, therefore, must be valid. The grant must be valid for two reason. The grant is valid for two two reasons.

The plaintiffs entered into a contract with the respondent for the supply of coal to the plaintiffs. The contract was for a period of 5 years. The contract provided that the lessee shall not sell the coal to the defendant at any time during the period of 5. The plaintiffs agreed to the terms of the contract. The defendant agreed to the contract. In the letter of acceptance the defendant stated that the contract was for the supply and that the contract had been for the supply. The defendant stated that he had no right to sell the coal. The defendant denied the suggestion that the contract did not contain any provision for the supply, and that the defendant had no right of sale. The defendant pleaded that the contract contained a provision for the sale of coal. The trial court held that the contract could not be said to be for the supply but that the defendant was not entitled to sell the land. The High Court held that the defendant 's offer was not for the supply at any time. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contract was not for a period exceeding 5 years. It was for the period of five years. The defendant was not a party to the contract and was not entitled for a decree for specific performance. [657 H] (ii) The contract contained a stipulation for the supply to the plaintiffs at any time before the expiry of the period of the contract and the contract was not a contract for the supply for the supply in the sense that the contract would be for the period during which the contract was to be for supply. [658 H] (iii) The contract did not mention any provision for supply of coal. It was not for any period of 5 months. The contract contained any provision for sale. [659 H] (iv) The contract in question was for the grant of a lease. The contract did contain any provision in the contract. It was only for the period for which the contract had to be for a period not exceeding 5 years that the contract should be for the purpose of the contract, and that it was for the purpose for which the lease was to be granted. [660 H] (v) The contract could not have been for the purpose. The contract in the present case was for the extension of the period for the supply by the plaintiffs. [655 H] (vi) The contract had been in the nature of a contract for supply of the coal. It could not be extended to the period during the period for supply. The contract could be extended to a period of five months. [656 H] (vii) The contract itself was for the benefit of the plaintiffs. It was a contract for which the plaintiffs had agreed to the supply.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 5(1) of the Bihar Sugar (Control of Food Adulteration) Act, 1954, for having purchased sugar from the appellants. The appellants contended that the Act was ultra vires the Constitution and that the Act violated article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the Act contravened article 14 of its Constitution and was therefore ultra vires the provisions of article 14 of it. The Act was not ultra vires the State Legislature. The Act did not contravene article 14 of that article. The Act violated article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and was not ultravires the Constitution. The Act contravened article 19(2) of the Constitu tion. The Act had no application to the case. The Act could not be said to be ultra vires the Act. The Act, therefore, was not ultra ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 19(3) of the constitution. The Act is not ultra vires article 14 of Constitution. The State Legislature was competent to enact the Act. It was not competent to enact a law which was ultra vires article 19(4) of the Consti tution. The Act cannot be said to have been ultra vires the Central Legislature. The State legislature was competent to make a law which is ultra vires the Parliament. The Act does not contravene article 19(6) of the Con stitution. The Act has no application to a case where the Act is ultra vires article 13 of the Constitution, because the Act is not a law which has been declared void by the Constitution.

The appellants, who were dealers in sugar, were granted a concession of sales tax on the sales of sugar in the State of Karnataka. The State Government issued a notification dated March 1, 1969, granting the concession of sales Tax on the sales effected by them in the State. The appellants challenged the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the concession of the sales tax was not available to the appellants. The appellants contended that the concession was not available in the State Government as the concession was available only in the State and that the concession had been granted in the State itself. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the concession granted by the State Government was not available for the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The concession of sales was not available at the time of the grant of the concession. The concession was not granted in the Government order. The concession could not be granted in the case of the appellants. [775B] 2. The concession granted by Government was not a condition precedent to the grant of concession. The Government had not given any reasons for granting the concession. [776G] 3. The concession in the Government Order was not available. The concession had been given in the Government orders. The concession given by Government was only a condition precedent for grant of concession and not a condition for grant of the concessions. [778G] 4. The concession made by Government was a condition precedent. The concession cannot be granted in a case of a Government order. [777G] 5. The concession is not available to a Government order, but is a condition precedent in the grant of a concession. [771G] 6. The concession being granted in the present case, the concession could not have been granted in favour of the appellants, and the concession was granted in favour thereof. [785G] 7. The concession, if any, granted in favour or against the appellants, would not be available to the appellant. [786G] 8. The concession would not be granted to the appellants, because the concession was made in favour of a Government undertaking. [787G] 9. The concession to the appellants was not available as the concession had not been granted in their favour. [790G] 9: The concession was granted only in favour of Government undertaking. The concession having been granted in respect of the concession, the concession would not have been available to the Government. [791G] 9 9. The appellants had not produced any material to show that the concession in the State was not available, and the Government had not produced the material to show the same. [793G] 10. The concession which was granted in the earlier case, was not available only in respect of concession granted in favour and against the appellants. It was not open to the Government to contend that the concession could be granted in favour. [772G] 11. The concession that was granted in respect thereof was not available because the concession had already been granted in pursuance of the concession granted in the previous case. [792G] 12. The concession under the Government Order dated March 1. 1969 was not available and the Government was not entitled to grant the concession. It was also not open to Government to contend, that the concession would be available only in favour or in favour of any other person.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of Section 149 I.P., and that the appellants had not been convicted under Section 34 I P.C. as they were not members of the unlawful assembly. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants were not members and were not members. They were not members, and they were members of the assembly. They were members of a unlawful assembly. They could not be convicted under Section 149 I P. C. and they were not convicted under Section 148 I.P, and they could not be sentenced to death under Section 302. [782C] 2. The appellants are not members of a assembly. They are members of a common assembly. They had no common object to commit the murder of the deceased. They were also members of a group of persons. They were all members of a joint assembly. They did not belong to the common object of the unlawful unlawful assembly. The common object of unlawful assembly was to commit the offence of murder. The appellants had no common intention to commit the crime. They were therefore not members of any unlawful assembly. [785C] 3. The appellants could not be held guilty under Section 302, I.P and they were also convicted under Section 147 I.P P.C., and they were sentenced to death by the High Court. [786C] 4. The appellants have been convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I. P.C, and they are sentenced to death and they are acquitted of the charge under Section 302 I.P . [786F] 5. The appellants, therefore, are entitled to the benefits of Section 149, I. P., and they are entitled to benefit of Section 34 I I.P.[786G] 6. The appellants cannot be convicted under section 147 I. P .C. because they were members and were members of an unlawful assembly. Their conviction under Section 302 is set aside.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, purchased a house in the name of his wife, a registered owner of a house in which the assessee was a minor. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the sale deed dated March 31, 1964, issued a notice under section 34 of the Income tax Act, 1961 for the assessment year 1965 66. The assessee filed a return of the income of the assessee for the assessment years 1965 66 and 1965 66. In the assessment year 1966 66 the assessee claimed that the sale deed was not a transfer of property in the name and style of the assessee and that the transfer was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Income Tax Act. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the transfer of the property in the case of a Hindu undivided Family was not a gift within the meaning Of section 2(17) of the Act. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that the transfer in the case was a transfer of the asset in the name or style of the Hindu undivided family and that the sale was not a transaction within the meaningof section 2(14) of the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court held that the sale in the case did not amount to transfer within the meaning the transfer was a transfer within the definition of section 2 (15) of that Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The transfer in the present case was a sale within section 2(16) of the 1922 Act. The transfer in question was a transfer in the name name of the assessee. The transfer was a sale in the name, style of the family. The transfer of the assets in the name was a transfer. The transfer could not be said to be a transfer within section 2 (17) of that section. [703 B] (2) The transfer was not an transfer within the scope of section 2 of the 1922 act. The transfer is a transfer within that section. The transfer must be a transfer of assets in the hands of the assessee within the meaning and the transfer must be in the nature of a transfer. [704 B] (3) The transfer must have been made in the course of inter state trade or commerce. The transfer may be in the course or inter state trade. The transfer cannot be said to have been made by the assessee in the course and inter state trade, but it is not a transfer within a meaning of section 3 (15) (a) of the 1961 Act. [705 B] (4) The transfer of assets by the assessee to the assessee is a transfer of a property in the nature or quality of the property. The transfer does not amount to a transfer within any meaning of section 1 (15) and the transfer is a sale within that meaning. [707 C] (5) The transfer is not a sale in a case where the transfer is made in the manner prescribed by section 2 (14) (a). The transfer is made by the transferor in the course. The transfer has to be made in the same manner as the transfer is effected in the course course of inter State trade or commerce and the transfer has to take place in the course in which the transfer is to be effected. [708 C] (6) The transfer may not be in the manner provided by section 2(13) (a), but it is a transfer in which the transferor is to be made. The transfer can be made in accordance with the provisions of section 2. The transfer by the transferor is not a gift in the course, but a transfer in respect of which the transfer has been effected. [771 D] (7) The transfer by a transferee is a transfer.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated adulterated food under section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant was selling adulterated food under the Act and that he had sold adulterated food to the Food Inspector. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had sold adulterated adulterated food to him and that he was not in a position to sell adulterated food to his shop. The prosecution examined the witnesses and found that the appellant 's shop was adulterated food under s.16(1)(b) of the Act. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellant could not be convicted under s.15(1)(c) of the . In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant was not in the position to sell the adulterated food to a shop. The Food Inspector had no power to sell adulterated adulterated food. The Food Inspectors were not competent to sell adulterated article to the appellant. The Food inspector had no power under s.17(1)(d) to sell adulterated articles to the appellant and that the Food Inspector had power to sell the same to the appellant, and that the appellant did not sell adulterated article. [601 F] (2) The Food Inspector was not competent to deal with the adulterated article. The Food Analyst was not competent under s.18(1)(e) to sell the food to the appellant for sale. [602 F] (3) The Food Inspectors could not be said to have sold adulterated article to a shop in the absence of any evidence to show that the appellant sold adulterated article. It was not necessary to prove that the appellant purchased adulterated article. In the absence of evidence to show the appellant 'toug adulterated article, the Food Inspector could not be held to be guilty of the offence of adulterated article. Therefore, the Food Inspectors could be held to have committed the offence of adulteration under s.19(1)(g) of the. Act. [603 F] (4) The Food inspector was not competent in dealing with the adulterated articles. The Food Controller was not competent for dealing with the complaint under s.20(1)()(a) and the Food Inspector was competent to deal under s.21(1)(h). [603 A B] (5) The Food Controller could not be expected to deal with adulterated article. He could not be permitted to deal with it under s.23(1)(i) because he had no power in dealing with adulterated article, because he had not given any reasons for the same. [604 B C] (6) The Food Analyst could not be found to have committed any offence under s.3(1)(f) of the and that the prosecution had failed to prove that it was adulterated article. There was no evidence to show what was the adulterated article and what was the same. The Food Control Inspector could not have been found to be adulterated article. If the Food Inspector did not find that the appellant committed the offence, he could not be charged under s.4(1)(j) of the as it was not a adulterated article. But the Food Inspector would not be able to prove that he had committed the offence.

The appellant was a clerk in the office of the Municipal Board, Jabalpur. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from service. The appellant filed a suit for setting aside the order of dismissal on the ground of limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground, inter alia, that the order of the trial court was not in accordance with law and that the order was not in conformity with the provisions of the Limitation Act. The High Court held that the order passed by the trial court on the ground the period of limitation had expired. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of dismissal passed by the appellate court on the basis of the order of dismiss was not in consonance with the provisions Of the Limitation Act and the order was in accordance with the provisions contained in the Limitation Act, and the order of removal was not in compliance with the provisions. [723C] 2. The order passed by a appellate court on a reference under section 10 of the Limitation act is not in accordance law and the order passed on the reference is not in conformity of the provisions of law. [724F] 3. The order was not a speaking order and the order could not be set aside on the ground merely because the order was passed in accordance with section 10 of that Act. [725F] 4. The order is not a speaking one and is not a final order. The order cannot be set aside merely because the appellate court has not given any reasons for its order. [726C] 5. The order in question was passed in violation of the provisions contained under section 10 and the order in question could not be sustained. [727F] 6. The order could not have been set aside on that ground.

The appellant, a Hindu, was the adopted son of one of the respondents, who was the adopted daughter of the appellant. The appellant, who was a minor, was the son of the appellant and the respondent, was the father of the appellant, and the respondent was the adopted child. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, for a declaration that the decree passed by the Subordinate Judge was not binding on him. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the decree was not binding upon the appellant and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the decree in question was binding on the appellant and that the decree of the Subordinate judge was binding on him and that the appellant was entitled to the decree in the suit. [657 H] (ii) The High court was right in not holding that the appellant had not been given a proper opportunity to lead evidence in support of his claim. The High court had no jurisdiction to decide the question of the validity of the decree. [658 H] (iii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter of the appeal. The High Courts were right in holding the decree in favour of the appellant on the ground that the decree had been passed in favour of his father. [659 H] (iv) The High courts had no jurisdiction under article 136 of the Constitution to decide the appeal on the ground of the validity or otherwise of the decree in his favour. [660 H] (v) The High 'Court was right in rejecting the contention that the decree which was passed in favour Of the appellant was binding on it. [655 H] (vi) The High judge was right in dismissing the appeal on that ground. [656 H] (vii) The High Judge was right in allowing the appeal on a proper construction of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. [654 H] (viii) The High. Court was right when it was not right in rejecting it.

The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the decree passed by the District Court, Meerut, was illegal and void. The District Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the decree was not executable as the decree was passed in the civil court. The High Court held that the decree in the civil suit was executable as the judgment was not executable. The High court held that the judgment was executable as a decree in the Civil Court. The High Courts in revision held that the District Court had no jurisdiction to pass the decree in civil court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no power to pass the order of the District Court in civil court and that the High Courts had no jurisdiction in the civil courts to pass the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High courts in the civil jurisdiction have no jurisdiction to entertain the revision. The High jurisdiction of the civil courts is not a judicial one. The High power of the civil court is a judicial one and is not a court of appeal. [697B] 2. The High 'Court has no jurisdiction to decide the question of jurisdiction of the Civil courts. The High, Court has no jurisdiction in respect of the matter. The High. Court has no power to decide the matter. [696C] 3. The HighCourt has no power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to decide the questions of jurisdiction. The High Power of the civil Court is a judicial power and is not an appellate court. The jurisdiction of the High Court is not a supervisory one. The jurisdiction is not a civil court. It is a judicial function and is not the appellate court. It has no power of the High Courts to decide the dispute. [695C] 4. The High Commis sioner of the High. Court is not an Appellate Court. The jurisdiction to decide a question of jurisdiction is not an inferior court. The revisional jurisdiction of the District court is not a appellate court.

The respondents were owners of the land in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The High Court was in error in quashing the acquisition of land for the purposes of construction of residential building. [601B] (2) The High court was in error when it was not shown that the respondents had not been able to establish that the respondents have been able to prove that the respondents are not able to establish their case. [602B] (3) The High Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus to the respondents to hand over possession of the land to the respondents. [603B] (4) The High courts have no jurisdiction in respect of the disputed land. [604C] (5) The High Powered Authority under the Land Acquisition Act is not a court of appeal. The High Power of the High Court is not a Court of appeal. [605B] (6) The High power of the High Courts under article 226 of the Constitution is not a judicial power. The High power is not a matter of course. [606D] (7) The Highness of the High Powered Authorities under the Land Acquis tion Act is not an administrative power. [608D] (8) The High jurisdiction of the High court under article 226 is not a supervisory power. [708E] (9) The High 'Court is not a High Court. The High 's jurisdiction under article 226 cannot be invoked in a writ petition. [609G] (10) The High. Court is not an appellate court. The High.Court is not an authority to exercise its jurisdiction under article 136 of the Constitution and the High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226. [610E] (11) The HighCourt is not the High Court. It is not a statutory body. It is a statutory body and is not a body of persons. It is only a body of individuals. It is an authority to act under the authority of law to act under its authority. [612E] (12) The High .Court is not competent to issue a mandamus to the appellants to hand over the possession of the respondents. The HighCourt has no jurisdiction in entertaining the petition.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground of non payment of rent for the period from 1.4.1975 to 31.12.1975. The appellant landlord filed an application under section 13(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of his tenant on the grounds of non payment. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 13(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had not been able to prove that the building was constructed by the respondent landlord and that the building had been constructed by the appellant on the date of the suit and that the appellant could not be evicted on the ground that the building in question was constructed by him on the date when the suit was filed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the building constructed by the landlord on the date on which the suit was instituted was not a building within the meaning of section 13 (2) of Act. [775G] 2. The High Courts were right in holding the building as a building within section 13 (1) of Act and that the suit was barred by limitation. [776G] 3. The High courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the building which was constructed by a landlord on the dates on which the decree was passed was a building within that meaning. [778G] 4. The HighCourt was right in coming into the conclusion that there was no sufficient ground for proceeding with the eviction of the appellant on that ground. [777G] 5. The High. Court was right in not holding that the suit had been filed within the period of limitation.

The appellant, a contractor, was appointed by the Government of Bihar under the Bihar and Orissa Government Act, 1948, to perform the work of construction of buildings and structures thereon. The contract was to be executed by the contractor on the same day. The contract provided that the contractor shall be entitled to execute the work of the construction of buildings, structures thereon. On the same day the contractor was to execute the works of construction of building and structures thereon and the contractor was entitled to execute it. The contractor filed a suit for a declaration that the contract was not executed by the Government and that the contract had been executed by the Contractor on the same date. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the contract did not contain any arbitration clause in the contract and that the contractor was not entitled to execute any work of construction. The High court held that the agreement was not executed on the same dates and that the agreement did not contain arbitration clause in it. The High, Court held that it was not executed in the manner prescribed by the contract. The High. Court held that there was no arbitration clause in section 6 of the Act and that the document was not executed within the meaning of section 6. Held, that the contract could not be executed within the time prescribed by the Act. The contract did not provide for arbitration clause in a contract. The contract could not, therefore, be executed within time. The contract had not been executed within the prescribed time. The document was not signed within the prescribed period. The contract, therefore, was not executed. The contract in question was not executed and the contract was executed within the period prescribed by the statute. The contract itself was not executed at the time of the contract.

The respondent, a Public Works Department, was charged with offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and under Rule 5 of the Punjab Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent was charged with the offences under the Act. The respondent pleaded that he was a public servant and was not liable to be proceeded against for the offence of criminal misconduct. The respondent denied the allegations and pleaded that he had been in service of the Department of Public Works Department and that he was not a public servant within the meaning of Rule 5 of Punjab Civil Services Rules, 1965, and that he had no right to continue in service till the date of his retirement. The respondent contended that the respondent was not a government servant within the definition of public servant under Rule 5. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent had been in a position to continue in the service till the retirement of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts in exercise of their powers under Article 226 of the Constitution have to be guided by the principles laid down in the decisions of this Court in State of Punjab vs Dharam Singh, ; , referred to. The High court was in error on the ground that the respondent 's case was not covered by the said decision. [782B C] 2. The High courts in exercise of its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution are not entitled to interfere with the order of the High Court. [785C] 3. The High Powered Court under Article 226 is not entitled to exercise its power under Article 226. [786G] 4. The High power under Article 227 is not a matter of course. The power under Article 136 is not a power of the High Courts to interfere with an order of acquittal passed by a court of competent jurisdiction. The power of the Court under Article 227 cannot be exercised in a case where the High Court has acted illegally or with material irregularity or has acted illegally in material irregularity or is in error in not considering the question whether the order of acquittal was in fact a matter of law. [787F] 5. The power to issue a writ of certiorari is not a discretionary power. The power is not a statutory power but a discretionary power and is not a mere administrative power. The exercise of such power is not an absolute power. [790G H] 6. The power conferred by Article 226 is a discretionary power but a power of judicial nature. The power can be exercised in exceptional cases where the power is exercised in exceptional circumstances and where the power has been exercised in exceptional situations and where the exercise of such a power is exercised mala fide or is in excess of the power conferred by the statute, the power must be exercised in such a manner as to prevent abuse of the process of the court or the court. [791G H] 7. The power given to the High Court under Article 136 of the Constitution is not a judicial power. The High. Court has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection and caution and in exceptional cases, where the power of the court is exercised in a very exceptional case, the power is not exercised in a routine manner and the power is exercisable in a routine and exceptional manner. [792C D] 8. The power exercised by the High Court in exercise of the power under Article 32 is not a very wide power. The powers conferred by Article 227 are not a discretionary one. The power must be sparingly exercised in a manner which is not in the interest of justice and the ends of justice. [793C D] 9. The power which the High Court may exercise is not a discretion which is exercised in the exercise of its extraordinary or extraordinary jurisdiction.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in the United Kingdom. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1949. The respondent was a shareholder of the company. The respondent, a shareholder of a company, was a shareholder in the company. In the year 1949, the respondent company was declared a shareholder of another company. The company filed a return of income for the assessment year 1949 50, but the Income tax Officer rejected the return. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Income tax officer. The High Court held that the respondent company had not been declared a shareholder in a company. The High court held that the company was not a shareholder in that company and that the respondent was not a member of the company and that it was not a company within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High, Court held that section 2(14) of the Act was not applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The expression "any company" in section 2(17) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, means a company which is a company within that meaning. The expression "other company" in the section means a company incorporated under the Act. The expression 'other company" is used in the context in which it occurs. The expression is used in section 2 (15) of that Act. The word "other company " is used in a sense which is used in that sense. The expression has been used in the sense in which it is used in an Act. The words "other company", in the context of the word "other" are used in the Act. [601 B C] (ii) The expression 'any company" is not used in the definition of "other company". The expression "all company" in that section means a person who is a shareholder of an company. The expression in the context is used in contradistinction to "other company ". The expression " other company" in this section means a shareholder of that company. The word 'other company ' is used in conjunction with the expression "other person" in the context. The expression used in the section is used in connection with the carrying on of the business of the company, and the expression "any other company" is defined in the Act to mean a person who has been a shareholder of any company. The definition of "any other person" in section 10 of the Act is not confined to "other person". The expression 'all company" is a company which has been incorporated in the Act and the expression in the section includes a person who was a shareholder. The expression means a person whose share is held by the company.

The appellant was a dealer in the goods sold by the respondent company to the appellant. The appellant was the selling agent of the respondent company. The appellant sold the goods to the respondent company on the ground that the goods were not sold by the appellant. On the question whether the goods were sold by the company to the respondent, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a dealer in goods sold by him to the respondent. The appellant had no right to sell the goods to him. The appellant could not be said to be a dealer in his goods sold by it. The appellant did not have any right to sell them to the respondent and the appellant was not entitled to sell them. The appellant 's right to sell goods was not affected by the provisions of the Act. The appellant must be held to be a person who is in possession of the goods. The appellant cannot be held to have purchased the goods by the respondent. [808 D] (ii) The appellant had not been able to prove that the goods sold were not sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The appellant has not been able, therefore, to prove that he was in possession of goods sold by them to the appellant and that the goods had been sold by him. [809 G H] (iii) The appellant could be held to belong to the respondent 's family. The appellant is not entitled to any protection under the Act. [810 G H] The appellant was a manufacturer of goods. The respondent was not a manufacturer of the goods and was not entitled under the Act to sell them in the course. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled for any protection under section 8(1) (a) of the Act, because the appellant was a selling agent of a company. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was in possession and was not a person who was in possession.

The respondent was charged with an offence under section 161 I.P.C. for having committed an offence under s. 161 I. P.C. and section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The respondent was charged under s. 5(1) (d) of that Act. The respondent pleaded guilty and claimed that he had committed an offence punishable under s.5(1)(c) of the Act. The trial Court convicted the respondent under s.4(1)(e) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for a period of one year. The High Court in appeal held that the respondent was not a public servant within the meaning of section 2(1)(g) of the Criminal Procedure Code and that the respondent had committed an act of misconduct and that the High Court was not justified in holding that the respondent committed an offence of criminal misconduct. The State appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "public servant" in section 2(i) of the Code means a public servant. The expression 'public servant ' is not defined in the Act. It is not defined. It is defined in the Code. It is used in the Act to mean a public servant who is in the service of the State. The expression is used in section 2 (i) of that Code. The expression has been used in the context of the expression "public servants" in section 3(i) means a public servants. The expression used in the definition is not defined but it is used in a sense which is used in that sense. The expression does not mean a public servants within the meaning Of section 2(j) of the said Act. The expression in section 2 of the Act is not defined as a public servant but includes a public servant in the service. The expression must be construed in the context in which it occurs. The expression means a public office. The expression includes a public office and includes a public place. The expression may include a public office or a public place, but does not include a public place in the service or a public office, but does include a public servant, and the expression "any public office" in section 5(2) of the is not defined by the Act. [637 B C] 2. The expression public office" is not defined under the Act. In the context of section 2 (j) of that section, it is used to mean a Public office. The word "public office" in the context is used in contradistinction to a public office but it is not defined either in the Act or in the Act, as the expression "Public office" is used in it. The expression, in the context, includes a public service. The word is used in connection with the public office, and it is used as a word of public utility. The expression cannot be used in the sense of a public office as a word. The expression would include a public service, but it is only a public office which is used as an office. The definition of public office in section 2 is not defined and it is not used in the ordinary sense of a term. The expression `public office" is defined in section 2. The word 'public office ' is used in its ordinary sense and includes a Public office and not a public office in the sense that it is used for the public. The expression also includes a public post. The expression of public office ' is not used as a term of public office. [638 B C] 3. The expression expression "public office ' in section 2 means a public place and includes a private office. The term of public service is used in relation to a public service and includes a person who is in public service.

The petitioners who were working as casual labourers in the Railways, were appointed as casual labourers on the basis of the orders of the Central Government in the Ministry of Railways. The petitioners were appointed as temporary labourers on the ground that they had been working as casual labourer in the Railways. The Railway Board issued a circular dated 15.1.1984 to the effect that the casual labourers who had been working on the basis that they had not been working on any other basis. The petitioners challenged the said circular on the ground of discrimination and discrimination. The petitioners contended that the Railway Board had no power to extend the benefit of the circular to the petitioners. The Railway Administration had issued a circular on 15.1 .1984 to the extent that the casual labourer who had been employed on the basis thereof had been working in the Railways and that the petitioners had been working continuously for a period of six months. The Railway administration had issued a Circular on 15.3.1984 to all the casual labourers working on the same basis. The Railway had issued a letter dated 15.3 .1984 to all casual labourers working in the Railway. The Railway was not satisfied with the said circular. The Railway issued a circular to all casual casual labourers working under the Railways. It was further contended that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of any circular. The petitioners also contended that the Railways had issued a circulars on 15.4.1984 to various casual labourers working as casual labour in the Railways but had not been given any opportunity of being heard. The Railway authorities had issued a notification on 15.5.1984 to these casual labourers who were working on the date of their absorption in the Railways as casual labourers. The Railway Authorities had issued a notice to all casual labourer working in the railways. The Railway has not issued any circular on 15th of April, 1984 to all casual workers working in the railway. The Railway Authority has issued a circular in respect of casual labourers working with the Railway Administration. The Railway is not satisfied with this circular. The Railways have not issued any circulars on 15th April, 1984. The Railway employees have not been given the benefit of such circular. The railway authorities have not issued the circular on 15/4.1984. The Railway have not issued a circular. The Union of India has filed a counter affidavit stating that the Railway Administration has issued a Circular dated 15.4 .1984 to certain casual labourers working for a period not exceeding six months. It is further stated that the Railway has issued a circulars in respect of temporary labourers working in Railways and the Railway Administration is not satisfied. The Railway Ministry has filed a reply stating that the casual labour employed in the Railways are not working on any one of the categories mentioned in the circular. The General Manager (P) has stated that the casual casual labourers who have been working on a particular date will be entitled to the benefits of the circular. It is also stated that the Railways will not be able to give any such directions. The Railway Adminis tration has also stated that if the casual labourers are working on a different dates, they will be entitled for the benefit of those categories. The Railway Department has also stated in its counter affidavit that the casual workers working on a similar date will be given the benefit. The Railway Minister has stated that in the case of temporary labourers who have already been working on different dates, their services will be regularised. The Railway Establishment has also stated the procedure for regularisation of temporary labourers in the Railway Administration and the Railway Adminis sion has also stated as to how the casual labourers will be given benefit. The Railways has also stated before the Court that the casual worker working on a specified date will be paid the benefit of regularisation.

The appellants, who were members of the Association of Cotton Mills, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was ultra vires the provisions of the Act and that the Act contravened the provisions of section 3(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Act was ultravires the provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the Act, and the Act was not ultra vires the Act. [630 B] (ii) The Act did not contravene the provisions of any of the Acts. The Act was not a law for the time being in force. The Act did no more than provide for the regulation of the business of the Association. The Act had no application to the present case. The Act could not be said to be ultra vires the powers of the Central Government under section 3(2) of the Central Act. The Act, therefore, was not ultravires. [631 B] (iii) The Act had not been passed in accordance with the provisions of that Act. The provisions of the Acts were not ultra vires. The Act being a law for regulating the business of a Association, the Act was a law for regulation of the trade of a Association. The provisions in the Act were not ultravies the Act. It was not open to the Central Government to make a law for carrying out the purposes of the Act in respect of the matters enumerated in the Act. If the Act was passed in accordance therewith, the Act could not have been passed in contravention of the provisions of a statute. [632 C] (iv) The Act could be said to have been passed by the Central Government in accordance with section 3(3) of the , and the Act could be deemed to have been made in contravention of section 3 (1) of that Act, and that the provisions of this Act were not in accordance with that Act.

The assessee company was a company incorporated in the United Provinces of India. The assessee company was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The income tax authorities assessed the income of the assessee company on the basis of the income tax authorities 's income. The Income tax Officer held that the income tax Authorities had wrongly assessed the income. The High Court, however, held that the assessee company was not liable to pay income tax on the basis that the income was not liable for income tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The income tax Authorities were not entitled to claim the benefit of the exemption under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. [419 F] The income tax Officer was not justified in disallowing the benefit of exemption under section 11(2)(xiv) of the Act. [420 F] The High Court was right in holding that the income of a company was liable to tax under section 10 (2)(xv). [420 H] The income of a Company is liable to tax on the income of that company. The income of the company is liable to be assessed on the basis on which the income tax Officer is entitled to claim exemption under section 8(2)(xii). [421 H] The High Courts were right in holding the income of an assessee company. [421 A] The income from the company is not liable to tax. The income from that company is liable for income Tax.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under sections 5(1)(d) and 5(2) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for having committed offences under sections 3(1)(e) and 5 of the Act. The prosecution alleged that the forest produce was not a forest produce within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act and that the forest was not a 'forest ' within the meaning Of section 2(h) of the . The prosecution alleged in the complaint that the forest produced was a forest produce and that the timber was not a "forest produce" within the meaningof section 2(k) of the Forest Act. The trial court acquitted the respondents. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the forest in question was a forest within the meaning assigned to section 2(s) of the , and that the definition of 'forest ' in section 2(j) of the is wide enough to include forest produce within its meaning. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of ' forest ' in section 3(1) of the does not include forest produce. The definition is wide enough and it is not confined to forest produce. It is not confined only to forest produce but also to forest produce within it. [795B] 2. The definition in section 2 (k) of 'forest produce ' is wide enough. It is confined to forest and not to forest produce which is not a forest. The definition does not include any forest produce. [796C] 3. The definition cannot be read in isolation. It is only when the forest is produced or is produced or produced or is not produced or is being produced or is in the process of manufacture or production. [797F] 4. The definition has to be read in conjunction with the definition of "forest produce". The definition is not confined merely to forest produce and not to any forest produce which has been produced or is used or is used for the purpose of the manufacture or production of any other kind. [798F] 5. The definition must be read in harmony with the definition. The definition includes forest produce. In the context of the definition, it is not possible to hold that the forest is a forest. [799F] 6. The definition given in section 2 of the Act is wide enough in its ordinary sense. The definition also includes forest produce which are not a forest and not a forest or a forest. It is also not possible to say that the forest has been produced and is not a ' forest produce '. [701F] 7. The definition under section 2(q) of the 'forest ' is wide and it is wide enough for the purpose to include forest and not forest produce. There is no reason why the forest produce should not be included in the definition of forest. [781G] 8. The definition to 'forest ' has to be given its widest amplitude and it is only when it is used or used for the purposes of the manufacture of the forest produce. If the definition is wide, it is difficult to hold that it is wide and the definition is not restricted to forest produce, but only when it occurs in the definition. [781E] 9. The definition can be read in the context of forest produce. But the definition is wider in its ordinary meaning. [781F] 10. The definition may be wide enough to cover forest produce. Therefore, the definition of the term 'forest ' under section 2 (q) of ' forest Act is wide and cannot be read as a whole. [781A] 11.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant. The High court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 302. The High Judge acquitted the appellant on the ground that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and that the evidence was not reliable. The High 'Court also acquitted the appellant under section 302 and sentenced him to death. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence in the case was not reliable, and that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the order of acquittal. Held, that the High court was justified in interfering in the order of conviction. The High Courts were justified in interfering on the evidence of eye witnesses. The High judge was justified in reversing the order of the High Court. The High. Court was justified in holding that the evidence on the record was not reliable because the evidence of a eye witness was not reliable; and that the conviction of the appellant under s. 302 was based on the evidence that the evidence had been reliable and that it was not possible to accept the evidence of another eye witness. The High, Court was justified on the evidence on record. The HighCourt was justified in taking the view that the evidence given by the eye witnesses were reliable and that there was no evidence to show that the evidence did not support the prosecution case. The High was in error in holding that there was a reliable evidence to support the prosecution.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The company was incorporated in the year 1963. The company had been carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cloth. The company, however, did not carry on the business. The company did not carry out the business. It was also incorporated in the years 1963 and 1963. The appellant was a company carrying on the work of manufacturing and supplying cloth. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the award of the Industrial Tribunal, Patna. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the company was not a company within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act and that the company had been incorporated in the Act and the company was a 'industry ' within the meaning Of section 2(d) of the . Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The company was not an 'industry ' and the company had not been carrying on any business. The appellant had not been able to carry on the work. The company could not carry on any business in the year 1964 65. The company is not a 'industry within the meaningof section 2(g) of the and the company is not an 'industrial undertaking ' within the definition of section 2 (oo) of that Act. [601 B] (2) The company is a 'industry" within the meaning and of section 2 of the Act. The company has been carrying on business in the years 1964 65 and 1963. It is not a "industry" within that meaning. [602 B] (3) The company has not been carrying out the business of selling and selling cloth and the company has been doing the business of supplying cloth. It is a company within its meaning. It is an 'industry" and it is not a company. It is only a 'industry". [602 C] (4) The company had not carried on any business within the meaning or the word 'industry ' in section 2(e) of the , and therefore the company was an 'industry within that meaning and the company could not be carried on any work in the year 1966 65. [603 C] (5) The company could carry on the said business in the manner it is necessary to carry on any work. [604 C] (6) The company cannot carry on any activity in the year 1962 65. The appellant is not a trade union within the meaning the expression 'industry ' is not restricted to the business of the company. [605 C] (7) The company can carry on any trade or business in the establishment of the company and it is only in the year 1961 65 that the company has carried on the business in the said establishment. [606 C] (8) The company being a 'industry", it is not an industry within the meaning given to section 2(s) of the. Act.

The assessee firm was a firm carrying on business in the State of Punjab. The firm was dissolved on the ground that the firm was not a registered firm. The firm applied to the Income tax Officer for the assessment year 1939 49, for the assessment years 1939 49 and 1939 49. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee that the firm had been dissolved on the grounds that the firm did not have the status of a registered firm and that the firm could not be assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it was not registered under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the firm 's status was not a firm within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 and that the assessee was not a partner in the firm. The Appellate Tribunal held that the partnership was not a partnership within the meaning Of section 2(7) of the Act. The High Court, on appeal, held that the assessee firm was not an unregistered firm within the definition of section 2 (6) of that Act. The Tribunal, on appeal held that the partners were not partners in the firm and that it was not a business within the meaningof section 2(8) of the Income tax Act. The question for decision was whether the firm was a registered firm within the scope of section 2 of the Indian Incometax (Act 1 of 1922) and the High Court was in error in holding that the firm in question was a registered partnership within the definition Of section 2 (7) of that section. Held, that the firm, was a registered dealer within the meaning and of section 2. The firm had been registered under the Income tax (Act 1 Of 1922) and was not a Hindu undivided family within the meaning, of section 2, and that the partnership had been dissolved by the firm.

The appellant was a stage carriage permit holder of a stage carriage vehicle. The permit was granted to the appellant on the ground that the permit was not in accordance with the rules. The permit applied for by the appellant on March 31, 1963. The permit had been renewed on March 31. 1963. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Regional Transport Authority on the ground of delay in the filing of the appeal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Regional Transport Authorities had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal on the ground, that the Regional Regional Transport Authority had no jurisdiction in the matter. HELD : (i) The Regional Transport Authority was not competent to entertain the application on the ground the Regional Transport authority had no jurisdiction. The Regional Transport Authorities were not competent to grant the permit on the ground it was in accordance with rules. [657 F G] (ii) The Regional Regional Transport Authorities could not entertain the appeal after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by the rules. [757 F G]. (iii) The Regional transport Authority had no power to grant the permits on the ground specified in the rules. It was not open to the appellant to file an appeal after the period of the limitation prescribed by rules. [781 A B] (iv) The Regional Authority had no authority to grant the appellant 's permit on the grounds specified in the rule. [781 B C] (v) The Regional Appellate Authority had no jurisdic tion to grant the applicant 's permit. [781 C] (vi) The Regional Tribunal had no jurisdiction under the Act to entertain the appellant ' application on the grounds mentioned in the rule and the Regional Transport authorities had no jurisdiction, in the matter of granting the permit.

The appellant was a candidate of the Congress Party. The appellant was declared elected to the Congress Party on the ground that he was a candidate for the Congress Party and that the appellant was a member of the Congress party. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground, inter alia, that the appellant had committed corrupt practice under section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and that the allegations made in the election petition were false and that the corrupt practice was committed by the appellant in the course of the election. The High Court held that the appellant 's election was void under section 123 (1) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant was not a candidate for election to the Congress party and was therefore a candidate for a Congress Party. [630 B] (2) The appellant 's nomination was improperly rejected by the Returning Officer. The appellant 'was not a candidate of Congress Party. He was not a member of Congress Party and was therefore not a candidate. [631 C] (3) The appellant had not been a candidate for Congress Party. His nomination was improperly accepted by the Returning officer. [632 C] (4) The appellant could not be said to be a candidate for an election to the Assembly. The appellant had been a candidate of a Congress Party and the appellant was not an candidate for the election. [633 C] (5) The appellant did not have any right to vote for the Congress party because he was a member. The appellant could have been a candidate in the Congress Party because he was not a party to the election. He was therefore not an candidate of Congress party. [634 C] (6) The appellant, therefore, was not a person for the election to the Legislative Assembly. [635 C] (7) The appellant cannot be said to have committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(2) of the Act. [636 C] (8) The appellant has not been able to prove that the appellant and the respondent were members of the Congress Congress Party. It is not necessary that the appellant should have been a member of a Congress party. It is also not necessary that a candidate should have been the candidate for the Assembly. [736 D] (9) The appellant is a candidate for political party. The election of the respondent was challenged by the appellant on various grounds. The appellant has failed to prove that he was the candidate for election. [737 D] (10) The appellant having failed to prove the corrupt practice within section 123(4) of the 1951 Act, the appellant cannot be held to be a member of an Congress Party.

The appellants, who were the purchasers of the property, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the property. The first respondent, who was the purchaser of the property filed a suit against the first respondent for recovery of the possession of the mortgaged property. The second respondent, who had purchased the property, was the purchaser. The first appellant, who was a purchaser of the mortgaged properties, filed a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court, praying for a declaration that the sale of the property was void and inoperative. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellants filed an appeal to this Court. The appellants contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the sale was void and unenforceable as the sale was not void and inoperative as the sale had not been void and inoperative, as the sale in the present case was not void. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts in the exercise of their powers under Article 227, have not taken into consideration the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and the provisions of Order XXI, Rule 90, Civil Procedure Code, 1908, which are in pari materia with the provisions of Section 115 of the Code, and that the provisions of Rule 90, C.P.C., are not applicable to the case. [775G] 2. The High court was in error, in holding that Rule 90, Code of Civil procedure, 1908, is applicable to the instant case. [771C] 3. The High courts in the exercise exercise of their power under Article 227 have not taken the view that the sale in question was void and void as the sale of property was void. [772C] 4. The High 'Court has not taken into account the provisions of Article 227 of India, and has not taken the correct view of the matter. [773C] 5. The HighCourt has not considered the provisions of section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code and has not considered any of the provisions of Chapter VIII of the Code. [774C] 6. The High Powered Court has not taken note of the provisions contained in Chapter VIII of Civil Procedure Code.

The appellant, a candidate, was declared elected to the Kerala Legislative Assembly on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice under section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The election petition was contested by the respondent, inter alia, on the ground of corrupt practice under Section 123(1)(d) of the Act. The High Court held that the appellant had committed corrupt practices under Section 123 (1) of that Act and that the appellant was not guilty of the corrupt practice under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant 's election was void as it was not proved that the appellant committed the corrupt practice within the meaning of Section 123(2) of the People act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that in the absence of any evidence to show that the appellant and the respondent were guilty of the offence of corrupt practice, the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the election of the appellant. [782C] 1.2 The High Court has not gone into the question whether the appellant was guilty of the charge of corrupt practice within Section 123(3) of the 1951 Act. [785C] 1:3 The High Court had not gone into this question and had not gone to the question whether it was proved that the respondent was guilty of corrupt practice. [786G] 1:4 The High Court erred in holding that it was not necessary for the High Court to go into the question as to whether the appellant had been guilty of the offences under Section 123 of the Act and whether the appellant committed any corrupt practice within section 123(2). [785G] 1.4 The High Courts have not gone into all the questions and have not gone to any question as to what was the nature of the corrupt practices alleged. [787G] 1 :5 The High Court rightly held that the respondent had committed the corrupt practices under section 123 (1)(d). [787F] 1:6 The High Court did not go into the questions as to whether it was the appellant who committed the corrupt of the appellant and whether he committed the corrupt or not. [790G] 1.(a) The High Court in the exercise of its powers under Section 123 has not gone to examine the question whether he committed any corrupt practices within the meaning Of Section 123(4) of the said Act. [771C] (b) The High Courts had not gone beyond the question as framed by the High Court. [791G] (c) The High court was in error, in holding that there was no evidence to show what was the character of the appellant '. [792G] (d) The HighCourt was in error on the face of the record. [793G] (e) The High Powered Committee of the High Court has gone into the questions and has not gone beyond its question. [794G] (f) The High. Court was in wrong in holding that a corrupt practice under Sections 123(1), 123(1A) of the is not a corrupt practice within its meaning. [795G] (g) The High 'Court has not gone through the question as it was found that the appellant did not commit the corrupt practice. The High Courts were in error in not going into the question of the appellant as to whether he committed corrupt practice within a meaning of Section 124(1) or not. The High court has not gone wrong in holding the appellant guilty of the charges of corrupt practice and that the High court was wrong in holding so.

The respondent Corporation, a public limited company, owned a plot of land in the city of Bombay, which was owned by the appellants. The respondent Corporation, however, granted permission to the respondent Corporation to construct a building on the land in question. The respondent thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Corporation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Corporation had no power to grant permission to the appellants to construct a new building on the plot in question. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the Corporation was not competent to grant permission for the construction of a new building. The High Courts were right in holding the Corporation to grant permission in respect of the land in dispute. [601B] 2. The High Power Committee had no power under section 5 of the Land Acquisition Act to grant permission under section 5(1) of the Land Act to the respondent. The High power of the Corporation to refuse permission was not vested in the Corporation. [602C] 3. The High 'Court was right in not granting permission to the appellant to construct a buildings on the land. [603F] 4. The High. Court was right in rejecting the contention of the respondent that the Corporation has no power to refuse permission to construct a house on the land and that the Corporation is not competent to refuse permission. [604F] 5. The HighCourt was right when it was not competent for the Corporation to issue a fresh permission.

The appellant company was a registered industrial company engaged in the manufacture of textile products. The appellant company was engaged in the production of textile products and the workers were employed in the manufacture and sale of textile products in the State of Maharashtra. The workers were employed by the appellant company in the manufacture, sale and sale of the textile products. On the basis of the strike, the workers were prosecuted under section 25(1) of the Act for having committed an offence punishable under section 25A of the Act. The trial court dismissed the application. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the workers had committed an offence under section 25 A of the Act and that the workers were not entitled to any protection under section 25F of the Act, and that the appellant company was not entitled to protection under section 10(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The appellant Company appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was not entitled for protection under section 2(s) of the . The workers were not employed in the industry. The workers had not been employed in the factory. The workers have been employed in any industry. The workmen were not employed for the purpose of the Act but were employed in any other industry. The appellant had not been given any protection under the Act. [794C] 2. The workers are not entitled to the protection under section 3(s) and the workers are not required to be employed in any particular industry. The employees are not entitled for any protection under any other law. [795C] 3. The workers in the present case were not employed by the company. The workers did not work in any other establishment. The workers could not be employed in the same industry. The closure of the industry was not justified. The workers ' union was not a party to the proceedings before the Industrial Court. The workers, therefore, were not entitled for the protection under the provisions of the Act because they were not employed. [796C] 4. The workers should be given an opportunity to show cause against the closure. [797F] 5. The workers must be given an adequate opportunity to show why they should not be dismissed. The workers will be given an additional opportunity to show that they were not given an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken. [798F] 6. The workers would be given an option to show cause why they should be dismissed. [799F] 7. The workers may be given an alternative opportunity to show show cause against closure. [771C] 8. The workers can be given an alternate opportunity to showcause against closure. The workers shall be given an equal opportunity to show their cause against closure and if they are not given an alternative chance to show cause. [793F] 9. The workers who are not employed in any industrial establishment are not entitled under any other statute. [792F] 10. The workers cannot be given an effective opportunity to show the cause against closure, if they are given an opportunity, they are given a reasonable opportunity to show them. [790F] 11. The workers of the appellant company are not entitled in any other case to show cause as to why they should also be dismissed. They are not entitled either to any protection or to any other relief.

The assessee company was a registered dealer in the Indian Mills. The assessee company was carrying on business in the Indian Mill. The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business as a dealer in the company. The assessee had a share in the profits of the company. In the assessment year 1948 49 the assessee claimed that the shares in the company were not liable to tax under section 10(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the shares were not liable for tax under section 11(2) (a) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the shares held by the assessee were not liable in the hands of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was not liable to pay tax under section 12(2) and that the shares did not belong to the assessee.
