In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the shares belonged to the assessee and that the assessee had no right to claim the shares in his own right. HELD: (i) The shares in the assessee were liable to tax in the hands Of the assessee and the shares were liable to be taxed under section 10 (2) (b) of the Indian Income tax Act. [775 G] (ii) The shares were not assessable to tax under the Indian Income Tax Act. The assessee could not claim the shares as the shares were held by the company. [776 G] (iii) The shares held by it were not liable under section 10 of the Act because the shares were sold by the assessee to the assessee for the purpose of earning profits. The assessee did not claim the share in the shares. The shares were sold in the assessee 's own right. The shares in question were not liable as the shares in question belonged to the company. It was not open to the assessee to claim the share of the shares in its own right. [778 G] (iv) The shares of the assessee were held by it in the assessee company. The shares held in the assessee could not be said to belong to the company as the shares held in it were not the shares held for the purpose for which the shares were purchased. [777 G] (v) The shares did not fall in the category of shares held by them in the assessee. [780 G] (vi) The shares could not be held by the appellant in the assessee firm. The shares could be held by it for the purpose other than the shares held. The shares did belong to the appellant. The shares of a company were held by a company in the assessee and were not liable. [779 G H] (vi). The shares were held for the purposes of earning profits and the shares in it were held by its members. The shares belonged to a company which was not liable for the tax under section 4(1) (a). [778 A C] (vii) The shares belonged not to the assessee but to the assessee as the shares had been held by it. The shares had been sold in the company by the assessee in the course of the business. The shares therefore belonged to the appellant as the shares did belong in the assessee as a result of the sale of the shares.

The appellant was appointed as a District Munsif in the Madras State. He was promoted as a District Munsiff in the Madras District. He was confirmed in the Madras High Court. He was reverted to the post of District Munsif. He was suspended by the Madras High court. He was dismissed from service. He was removed from service by the Madras State Civil Service (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1950. He was served with a notice to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service, and on his failure to show cause, he was dismissed from the service. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of article 311 of the Constitution. The High Courts were right in holding the appellant guilty of misconduct. The High court was right in dismissing the petition. The appellant was not a District Munsif. The High, Court was right when the appellant was dismissed from his service. The High. Court was right. The appellant had no right to the protection under article 311. [638 G H] The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the High Court. The appellant could not be dismissed on the ground that the appellant had not been dismissed from service because he had not been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the order of suspension. The High 'Court was right in rejecting the petition.

The respondent was a shareholder of a company. The respondent was a member of the company. The company was a shareholder. The company had a share in the shares of the company and the share of the share was transferred to the company. In the year 1949, the company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1949 50. The Income tax Officer held that the share of a shareholder was transferred to him by the company to the company and that the share was not transferred to him. The Income Tax Officer held that he was not a shareholder of the company, and that the shares were transferred to him in the name of the company to his wife. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the shares in the company were transferred to the wife of the deceased. The Appellate Tribunal held that the transfer of the share to the wife was not a transfer of the shares. The High Court, on appeal, held that the income tax Officer was not a person who was not a member of a company and that he was entitled to the benefit of section 10(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The High court held that the dividend income was not a share in a company and the income tax authorities were not justified in holding that the dividend was not a capital receipt. The High, Court, on reference, held that section 10(1) of the Act was not applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "any person" in section 10(3) of the Indian Income tax Act means a person who is not a member or a member of an association of persons. The expression "other person" in the section means a person whose death has been caused by the death of a member or member of an Association of persons. [601 D] (2) The expression 'other person" is used in the context of the expression "other persons" in section 2(15) of the , and the expression "any other person" in that section means a member of any association of persons who is not an association of individuals. [602 D] (3) The expression in section 10 (1) of that Act means a member or an association of person who is a member of such association of persons and is not a person whose share has been transferred to him under the provisions of the Act. [603 D] (4) The expression used in section 10 of the Act means a persons who is a shareholder of any association or association of persons, and includes a person who has been duly elected to the association of persons or who has been elected to the committee of the association of person. [604 D] (5) The expression `other person" means a person having been duly elected under the provisions or the rules made under the Act. The expression `any other person ' in section 10 means a person holding a share in any company. [605 D] (6) The expression, "other person", in section 10, means a person in whose favour the share has been allotted to him under section 10. [606 D] (7) The expression is not defined in the Act. It is not defined by the Act. In the context of section 10, it is not necessary to refer to the expression "person" in section 12(1) and the expression 'other persons" is used to denote a person who holds a share in an association of Persons. [607 D] (8) The expression has been used in the Act in the context in which it occurs. The expression 'person ' in section 12 is not defined.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Madhya Pradesh. He was a Ruler in the State of Gwalior. He was in the possession of the State. He was not a Ruler of Gwalior. The Ruler of Gwalior was a Ruler. He was, therefore, a Ruler of Madhya Pradesh and was not a person in the State. The Ruler was not a " Ruler" within the meaning of article 31(1) of the Constitution. The appellant was, therefore. a Ruler of a State. The appellant 's case was that he was a Ruler within the meaning Of article 31(2) of the Consti tution. The appellant contended that the Ruler was a Ruler under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, and that he was not a citizen of India. Held, that the Ruler of Gwalior had no authority to make a law for the purposes of the Constitution and that he had no authority under the law to make a declaration that he was an Ruler within the definition of the term ' Ruler '. The appellant had not been a Ruler within article 31(3) of the Constitu tion. The Ruler had no authority in law to make the declaration. The appellant could not be said to be an Ruler within article 32 of the Constitution, because he was not an Ruler within that definition. The appellant did not fall within the definition Of the term ' Rulers ' within the meaningof article 31(5) of the Act. The appellant, therefore, was not an ' Ruler within the scope of article 31. The appellant cannot be said to have been a Ruler of an State within the meaning under article 31(6) of the Con stitution. The appellant must be held to be an ' Ruler ' within the definition. The Ruler 's case that he was the Ruler of a non State was not covered by article 31(4) of the constitution. The appellant having failed to establish that he was in the State, he was not entitled to the protection of article 31 (1) of that Constitution.

The respondent, a retired employee of the respondent Bank, was transferred to the Central Administrative Tribunal, Gauhati, by an order dated 15.12.1991. The respondent filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the transfer order. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The transfer order is not a transfer order. It is a transfer order and not a transfer. It is not a case of transfer. It has to be decided on the basis of the material on record. The transfer is not a matter of policy. The transfer has to be made in accordance with the rules and regulations. The transfer cannot be made in violation of the principles of natural justice. [775F] 2. The transfer of the respondent to the Central Government is a matter of administrative policy. The administrative authority has to act judicially and not in accordance with law. The administrative authorities have to act judicially. The administrative power is not to be exercised arbitrarily. The administrative jurisdiction is not to act judicially, but is to be exercised judicially. The power is not a judicial function. The administrative discretion is not to function judicially. The exercise of administrative power is to be done in accordance with rules and regulations and not in consonance with the principles of administrative law. [776F] 3. The administrative powers are to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. The administrative function is to be performed by the administrative authorities. The administrative functions are to be performed in accordance with principles of natural Justice. The administrative tribunals are to be guided by the principles of law and not by the administrative tribunals. The administrative control is to be guided in accordance with their own policy. The Administrative Tribunal is to be mindful of the administrative power. [778F] 4. The administrative tribunal is to be careful in dealing with the administrative matters and to ensure that the administrative tribunals are not able to act judicially in accordance with its own policy. [777F] 5. The administrative administrative power is a quasi judicial function and not administrative. The administrative superintendence is to be given to the administrative authorities and not to the administrative tribunals and to the administrative bodies. The administrative officers are to be given the power to act judicially or not. [780F] 6. The administrative orders are to be made by the administrative authority in accordance with administrative instructions. The administrative instructions are to be followed by the administrative officers. The administrative and administrative authorities are to be careful and not to administrative tribunals. [779F] 7. The administrative bodies are to be vigilant and not to act arbitrarily. The Administrative Tribunals are to be free to act judicially as they are not expected to act judicially but to act judicially according to their own policy and not in conformity with the principles laid down by the administrative bodies in the matter of administrative control. [790F] 8. The administrative order is to be made within a reasonable time. The administrative officer is to be free from any arbitrary and capricious exercise of power. [771F] 9. The administrative action is to be taken in accordance with relevant rules and regulations, and not in violation of any statutory rules. [791F] 10. The administrative machinery is to be kept in mind by the administrative administrative authorities. It is the duty of the administrative authorities to see that the administrative authorities are not able, and that the administrative authority is not able to perform the administrative functions. [792F] 11. The administrative or administrative authorities are expected to act fairly and in accordance with any statutory rules or regulations. The administrative act is to be fair and reasonable. [793F] 12. The administrative acts are to be done by the administrative and administrative bodies.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted the appellants. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the conviction of the appellants was not sustainable in law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction of the appel lants is set aside. The conviction and sentence of the appe lants are set aside. [775F] 2. The conviction is set aside and the sentence of imprisonment is set aside, and the sentence is reduced to the period already undergone. [776G] 3. The conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P., is set aside on the ground that the appellants had committed the murder of the deceased. [778G] 4. The conviction was set aside and they are acquitted of the charge under Section 302. [777G] 5. The conviction, however, is set aside in the light of the evidence of P.W.1, the father of the deceased, and the conviction of all the appellants under Section 302 is set aside accordingly. [779G] 6. The conviction recorded by the High Court is set aside but the sentence of fine is set aside to the extent of fine. [780G] 7. The conviction for the offence under Section 302, I.P, is set set aside. However, the sentence of death is set aside only on the ground of conviction under Section 304 Part I I.P.; and the sentence imposed on the appellants under section 302 read with section 34 I. P.C. is set aside with the modification that the sentence of life imprisonment imposed on the appel late appellants is set aside as the conviction of appellants under Section 304 I.P,. is set aside by the High court.

The respondents, who were partners of the appellant firm, filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to them from the respondents. The respondents contended that the suit was not maintainable as the suit was filed within the period of limitation prescribed under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Clauses Act, 1904, and that the suit filed by the respondents was not maintainable. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the suit in question was not maintainable because the suit was barred by limitation. The High court held that the suits were barred by limitation, and that, therefore, the suit was maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the suit is barred by limitation and that the suits filed by the respondent were not barred by limitation as the suit filed in the High Court were not barred under section 3 (1) of Act, 1904. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that in view of the provisions of section 3(2) of the Act, the suit filed under the Act was not barred by the limitation prescribed under the Act. [782B] 1.2 The High Court has rightly held that the provisions of the Act are not applicable to the suits filed in the Supreme Court. [785C] 1.3 The High Court rightly held that in view thereof, the suit in the High court was not barred under the Act, and that it was not barred. [786C] 1:4 The High Court erred in holding that there was no bar to the suit filed before the High Court under section 3 of the Act. The High Courts have rightly held that there was a bar to the suits in the High Courts under section 3, and that there was nothing in the Act which prevented the High Court from entertaining the suit. [787F] 1:5 The High Court had rightly held that it was barred by the Limitation Act, 1908, and that in view, the suit is not barred by section 3(3) of the Limitation Act. [771E] 1:6 The High Court, in the exercise of its powers under section 3 read with section 3(4) of the General Clauses Act has rightly held the suit to be barred by limitation under section 3. [790F] 1.7 The High Court is right in holding the suit to have been barred by limitation in view of section 3 of Act, which is a special provision for the purpose of the Act and the High Court has not properly construed the provisions of that Act. [783B] 1:7 The High Courts in the exercise Of its powers under Article 136 of the Constitution have rightly held the suits to be barred under the provisions of Act, 1908. [783C] 1 :7 The High court has rightly held in favour of the respondents. [783E] 1.8 The High Court in the exercise exercise of its power under Article 136 has rightly held, that the suit instituted by the respondents is barred by the provisions of Section 3 of the General Clause Act. [784G] 1:8 The High Courts, in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136, have rightly held, in favour of respondents. [784E] 1 :9 The High Court committed an error in holding, that the suits in question were barred by the period of Limitation prescribed under section 2(1) (a) of the . [783G] 1.9 The High Courts had rightly held, on the facts, that the High Courts were in error in not holding that the suits are barred by limitation prescribed under Section 3(1).

The petitioners who were dealers in sugar, were manufacturing sugar in sugar. The sugar was sold by the Central Government under section 3 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, for the supply of sugar to the sugar factory. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the notification was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the notification violated article 14 of its Constitution and that the notification contravened article 14 of that article. Held, that the notification must be struck down as violative of article 19 of the Constitution and must be struck as violative of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion. The notification must be held to be violative of article 31 of the Constitution, and must be held invalid. The notification is not violative of article 301. The notification cannot be struck down on the ground of violation of article 14. The notification does not contravene article 14 of it. The notification can be struck down if it is struck down on any ground. The notification, therefore, must be struck out on the ground. The petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 19. The notification was not struck down on that ground. The order of the Central Government was not justified. The notification did not contravene article 19. Held, further, that the impugned notification was violative Of article 14 of Constitution. The notification could not be struck down because the notification was struck down on a ground of violation Of article 14. Held, also, that the notifications were violative of article 16 of the Constitution because the notification did not violate article 14 of India. The notification in question was not struck out on that ground and was therefore struck down. The notification issued under section 3 was not struck off on the ground, because the notification issued under the Act was struck down as invalid. The impugned notification was struck off on that ground because the notification had not been struck down on account of the violation of article 19.

The appellant company was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling products of its workmen. The company was a statutory company and was incorporated in the United Provinces and Berar Industrial Disputes Settlement Act, 1947. The company had been incorporated in the West Bengal Industrial Disputes Settlement (Amendment) Act, 1956, and the Industrial Tribunal had jurisdiction to make an award under section 10(2) of the Act. The company filed a petition under section 33 of the Act for the award of the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the company was not a statutory company within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that the Tribunal had jurisdiction in making an award under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the company had not been incorporated in West Bengal Industrial Tribunal Act, 1947 and that the company could not be made liable to pay the same. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding the company liable to pay it. [657 H] (ii) The Tribunal had jurisdiction under section 10 of the Act to make an order under section 10 (2) of that Act. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make the award under section 33. [658 H] (iii) The Tribunal could not make an award in respect of the company 's workmen. The Tribunal could make an award only in respect of a company 's employees. The Tribunal did not make an order of reference under section 10. [659 H] (iv) The Tribunal did make an award on the ground that the company 'was not a statutory Company within the meaning Of section 2(c) of the , and that the award was not a nullity. [660 H] (v) The Tribunal 's order was not a proper one and was not a fit one for appeal. The Tribunal should have made an award in the absence of a reference under section 33, and that it was not a case of a statutory Tribunal. [655 H] (vi) The Tribunal should not have made an order under the Act, because it did not make any reference under section 11. [656 H] (vii) The Tribunal has jurisdiction to make a reference under the Act and the Tribunal has jurisdiction under section 11, because it had jurisdiction to entertain the reference. [654 H] (viii) The Tribunal is not a statutory Tribunal, because it has jurisdiction to entertain an application under section 33 and the Tribunal is not bound to make an Award in respect of any company 's employee. [653 H] (ix) The Tribunal cannot make an award unless it is made in accordance with the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder. [652 H] (x) The Tribunal must have made an Award in accordance with law. [649 H] (xi) The Tribunal, in the instant case, was not a Tribunal within the meaningof section 2(a) of the and the Tribunal was not bound to give an opportunity to the parties to lead evidence. [648 H] (xii) The Tribunal in its award, had the jurisdiction to make any award. [647 H] (xiii) The Tribunal erred in holding that it was a statutory Tribunal within the scope of section 2 (b) of that section. [646 H] (xiv) The Tribunal ought to have made an application under the Act to the Tribunal for making an award in accordance with section 10 of that Act, and that in the absence Of a reference under that section, the Tribunal was bound to make the reference under section.

The appellant was a Hindu Religious Trust. He was appointed as a trustee of the temple. He was a member of the Board of Trustees. He was elected to the Board of trustees. He was declared elected. He was removed from the office of the Board. He was served with a notice under section 12(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, to show cause why the scheme should not be cancelled. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the scheme was void and inoperative. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the scheme had been cancelled and the scheme was not void. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the scheme did not contravene article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The scheme was not a law which was in force at the time when the scheme was passed. The scheme did not infringe article 19(2)(f) and was therefore void. The scheme had been validly cancelled and the appellant was entitled to the protection of article 19(6) of the Constitu tion. The scheme could not be cancelled under the Act. The scheme itself was not a valid one and the appellant could not be said to have contravened article 19(5) of the constitution. The scheme, therefore, was not valid. The scheme in question was not void because it was not a legislation which was in existence at the time of the scheme. The scheme therefore, was void. The Act was not a piece of legislation which was not in existence at that time. The scheme of the Act was not void and inoperative because it was a legislation which had been passed in the interest of the public. The scheme which was in operation at the time the scheme was made was not a colourable one and was therefore invalid. The scheme thus was not void under article 19(3)(f) because it was passed in the interests of the public and was not void, because it was in existence after the scheme was framed. The scheme under which the scheme was to be cancelled was not void as it was not in force at that time the scheme had not been cancelled and it was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the ground that it was not passed in the public interest. The scheme being void, the scheme was invalid.

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the State of Orissa on the recommendation of the Selection Committee. He was appointed as an Assistant Teacher in the State. He was confirmed in the post of Principal in the State on the recommendation that he was entitled to be appointed as Principal in the Government service. The appellant was appointed on the basis of the recommendation of Selection Committee. The appellant challenged the validity of the appointment on the ground that the appointment was illegal and void. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment of the appellant was illegal and invalid because the appointment was made in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appointment of the teacher in the Government school was illegal and inoperative because the appointment of a teacher in a school was illegal. The appellant had been appointed on the recommendation made by the Selection Committee and was not entitled to be confirmed in the Government services. The appointment was made on the recommendation by the Selection committee. The appointment made on the basis that the appellant was appointed in the Government schools. The appointment is made on the recommendations of the Selection committee and not on the recommendation. The appointment cannot be made on the ground of any discrimination or discrimination. [723C] 2. The appointment on the basis thereof was illegal and the appellant was not entitled for any relief. [724F] 3. The appointment in the Government School was illegal and unconstitutional because the appointment made on behalf of a teacher was illegal. [725F] 4. The appointment to the post of Assistant Teacher in a school is illegal and void because the appointment is made in accordance therewith. [726F] 5. The appointment has been made on the assumption that the appointment is illegal and invalid. The appointment being made on the same recommendation, the appointment cannot be said to be illegal.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the Punjab Legislative Council. He was elected to that Assembly. He was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly. He challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he was not a member of the Legislative Assembly and that he was disqualified under section 7(1) of the Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1951. The High Court held that the appellant was not a candidate for election to the Legislative Council. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The appellant was not an elector for election to a Legislative Assembly. The appellant was a member of a Legislative Assembly and was not a person for election to that Assembly, and he was not qualified to be chosen to fill the seat. The appellant had not been able to prove that he was a member for election to any Legislative Assembly. [619 F G] (ii) The appellant had been disqualified under section 8(1) (a) of the Act. The appellant could not be said to be a member of any Legislative Assembly, and the appellant was disqualified under the Act. [620 H] (iii) The appellant could be said to have been a member of an Legislative Assembly. His nomination was improperly rejected. [621 H] (iv) The appellant 's election was challenged on the ground of corrupt practice. The High court was in error in holding that the appellant had been a member for the Legislative Assembly, but the appellant was a person for the Legislative Council, and that the appellant could not claim any benefit under section 7 (1) (b) of the Rules.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents tenant on the ground of bona fide requirement of the appellant landlord. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court held that the requirement of the landlord landlord was bona fide and that the requirement was bona fide. The first Appellate court held that there was no bona fide requirement. The High Court held that the requirements of the landlord had been bona fide and the requirement was not bona fide. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the requirement had been bona bona fide and was not bona bona fide. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The requirement of the tenant landlord landlord is bona fide and bona fide. [775F] 2. The requirement is bona fide. It is not bona fide and is not bona bona fides. The requirement must be bona fide. There is no need to be satisfied in the present case. The requirement has been bona fide. If the requirement is bona bona fide it is bona fide, the requirement of bona fide need need not be bona fide, but the requirement must be bonafide. [776G] 3. The requirement that the requirement must have been bona fide must be bona fides. [778F] 4. The requirement in the present ease is bona fide as the requirement of a bona fide requirement is bona fides. It is well settled that the requirement is not bona fides. In the instant case, the requirement is bonafide. [771G] 5. The requirement for bona fide requirement has been bonafide. The requirement need not be bonafide. The need is bona fide is bona fide but bona fide. Therefore, the requirement must not be bona bona fide, and the requirement of such bona fide requirement must be genuine.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company was a registered company. The appellant company was carrying on business in the company. The respondent was a company carrying on business as a company. The company was carrying out business in the Company. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract of sale of the goods. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for specific performance. The respondent pleaded that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the suit had been filed within the period of limitation. The High court held that the appellant was not a company within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. The High Courts also held that the respondent was not a Company within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the . The High Court also held that there was no sufficient cause for the appellant to file the suit within the meaningof section 2(3) of the Code. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had not been a company within meaning of section 3(1) and that the suit should be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High courts were in error in dismissing the suit. [799B] 2. The High 'Court was in error on the face of the record and the High Court erred in holding that there was sufficient cause for filing the suit within that period. [798C] 3. The HighCourt was in wrong in holding that in the absence of sufficient cause for not filing the suit, the High Court committed an error in holding the suit within time. [797E] 4. The High. Court was in wrong error in holding so.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 120B, I.P.C. for having committed offences under sections 323, 324, 323, 324 and 506 I.P., and section 3(1)(d) of the U.P. Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Magistrate found that the appellant had committed the offence under section 307, I. P.C. and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence under sections 323 and 506 I., I.P, and that the appellant was not entitled to take cognizance under section 307 I.P and that the order of the Magistrate was not justified. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Magistrate was in error in taking cognizance of the offences under sections 307, 324 and 307 I. P., and that the High Court was in error when it held that the Magistrate committed the offence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Magistrate was in a position to take cognizance on the basis of the complaint filed by the appellant and the Magistrate was justified in taking cognizance on the ground that the Magistrate did not take cognizance of that offence. [782B C] 2. The Magistrate has not taken cognizance of the case and the Magistrate has not given any reasons for taking cognizance. The Magistrate is not justified in taking the cognizance of the matter. [785C] 3. The Magistrate cannot take cognizance of an offence under section 323, I. p.C. because the Magistrate has taken cognizance of that case. [786C] 4.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn. The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing cotton yarn. It was registered as a firm carrying on business as a firm. The appellant was carrying on the trade of cotton yarn and the appellant was carrying in the business of selling cotton yarn. In the assessment year 1948 49 the appellant claimed that the profits of the business were assessable to tax under section 10(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that the profits were assessable to income tax under section 11(2) (a) of the Act. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 10(1) (a). The High Court held that the business of the appellant was assessable to tax in the hands of the appellant and that the profits could not be assessed to tax under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the profits in the business were not assessable to tax. Held, that the profits must be assessable to tax only under section 10 (1) (b) of the Indian Income tax Act. The profits in the present case were assessable to the tax under section 12(2) and not under section 10. The profits were assessable under section 10 of the Act and the profits were liable to tax under that section. The profits could not therefore be assessed to income tax. The profits of the appellant were assessable to sales tax under section 8(2) because the profits were not assessable under section 11 (1) of the 1922 Act. The High Court was right in holding that the profits had been assessable to tax by the appellant under section 10, and that the appellant had not been able to prove that the profits did not form part of the profits of that business. The High court was right in not holding that the appellant could not be said to be a dealer in the business. The profits must be assessed to the tax in the course of trade. The profits are assessable to tax and not under the Act, because the profits are assessable under section 12 (1) and the profits are not assessable to income. The profits cannot be assessed to sales tax. The High Courts were right in holding, that the appellant did not produce any evidence to show that the profits are chargeable to tax under s.10(1) of 1922 Act. Held, further, that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show what the profits were chargeable to tax. The appellant had not produced any evidence to prove that they were chargeable to income tax and that the income was assessable to income, and that it was not liable to tax.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business as a dealer in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The assessee was a member of the firm. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 10(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the expenditure was not incurred by the assessee in the course of his business and that the expenditure incurred by the appellant was not incurred in the course or business of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the expenses incurred by the company were not incurred in connection with the business of the appellant and that the expenses were incurred in connection therewith. The High Court, on appeal, held that the amount of expenditure incurred by it was not incurred for the purpose of the business of a dealer in a particular year and that the assessee had incurred the expenditure in connection therewith and that the amount was incurred in connection thereto. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expenditure incurred by a dealer in connection with his business was incurred in the nature of a business of the dealer in the course and business of the business. The expenditure incurred in connection directly or indirectly was incurred in carrying on the business of his business. The assessee had incurred expenditure in connection with its business. The expenses incurred by him were incurred in the business of carrying on the same business. The High court was right in holding that the expenditure expenditure incurred by him was incurred in a particular particular year. [637 D] (ii) The expenditure was incurred in respect of the business carried on by the assessee for the purpose for which he was appointed. The expenditure was not a expenditure incurred in the carrying on of the business and was not incurred directly or indirectly. [638 D] (iii) The expenditure expenditure incurred in carrying out the business of an assessee was incurred in that year.

The appellant company was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cloth. The company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of cloth. The appellant company was carrying on the manufacturing and selling yarn. The company had a factory at Patna. The appellant was a company registered under the , and the appellant was a member of the company. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of dismissal was bad because the appellant had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the order of discharge. Held, that the order was bad because it was not a fit case for interference. The order of discharge was bad because there was no material before the Tribunal to show that the appellant had been given an adequate opportunity to show that he had been given a reasonable opportunity to show the cause against the proposed order. The order was not a proper one. The order did not contain any provision for the exercise of the power of the Tribunal to interfere with the order of reference. The order made by the Tribunal was not a nullity because it was made in the course of the proceedings before the Tribunal. It was not a case of a dispute between the appellant and the respondent. The Tribunal was not justified in interfering with the order. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with it. The appellant had not given any opportunity to show his cause against the action proposed. The Tribunal could not interfere with the orders of the Tribunal because it was a case of an industrial dispute between the parties. The Tribunal did not give any opportunity to the appellant to show cause why the order should not be made. The Tribunal, therefore, was not justified.

The appellants were the tenants of a house in which the deceased was living. The appellants were the heirs of the deceased. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the ground that the appellants were not the tenants of the house. The appellants contended that the appellants had no right to the suit property and that the appellants could not be evicted from the house. Held, that the appellants ' suit was not maintainable because the appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased and the appellants were entitled to the decree. The appellants had no locus standi to file the suit. The appellants could not file the suit in view of the provisions of Order VI, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appellants ' suit for ejectment was not maintainable. The appellants did not file the appeal in view of Order VI Rule 1 of Code of Civil procedure. The appellants, therefore, could not file an appeal in view Of Order VI, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure. Held, further, that the appeal was not maintainable as the appellants were tenants of the property. The appellants cannot be evicted from their house. The appeal was not barred by Order VI, r. 1 of the C.P.C. and the appellants could be evicted from that house. The order of the High Court was set aside. The appellants appealed to this Court. Held, also, that the order of the appellate Court was set out in the order of remand and the appellants ' appeal was not competent to file the appeal. The order passed by the High Court is set aside.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground of bona fide requirement of the respondent landlord. The Rent Controller dismissed the suit. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the notice was not served on the appellant and that the notice had been served on him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notice served on the respondent was not served upon him and that the appellant had not been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice served on him was not served by the appellant and the notice served upon him was not a valid notice. The notice was not a mere formality and was not a formality. The notice is not a mere one and is not a formality and is not an essential part of the statute. The notice must be construed in a manner which is not in consonance with the provisions of the statute and the rules of natural justice. [630B] 2. The notice in question was not served in the appellant and it was not a mandatory requirement. The notice did not contain any provision for the service of notice. The requirement of the notice was mandatory. The notice could not be served on the tenant. The notice also did not contain the provision for service of notice on the tenant and the notice was a mere formality. The requirement was not mandatory. The requirement for service of the notice did not require the service of the notices. The notice had been issued in the presence of the appellant and he had not been served with the notice. The appellant had not filed any written statement nor filed any written statements. The notice, therefore, was not a proper notice. [631C] 3. The notice of the appellant was not served. The notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 was not served within the meaning of section 106 of Transfer of Property. The notice contemplated the service of a notice on the appellant. The notice required the service of notices on the appellant to be served on him and the notice of the notice could not have been served on the landlord. The notice therefore, was a mere one. The notice to be served was not a notice within the meaning Of section 106 of Evidence Act. [632C] 4. The notice issued by the appellant was a mere notice and was not intended to be served upon the appellant. [633C] 5. The notice dated March 1, 1963 was not served to the appellant and was not served with the appellant. It was not served at the appellant. There was no notice of the date of the notice. [733C] 6. The notice for the appellant was served on the respondents on March 1, 1964. The notice stated that the notice of demand was served on him on March 1. 1964. The appellant did not file any written statement. The notice contained a provision for service on the appellant on March 1 and the notice did contain the provision of service on the tenant on March 1 to the landlord. [634C] 7. The notice on the other hand was not served as required by section 106 of Act. The notice as required by the notice was served on it on the appellant, and the notice could be served on it only on the appellant as required by sub section (2) of section 106.

The Governor of Assam, by an order dated March 3, 1964, directed the Governor to hold a departmental enquiry against the appellant and to hold a fresh enquiry. The Governor, however, did not hold a fresh inquiry. The Governor also did not hold any fresh enquiry. On March 3, 1963, the Governor passed an order under article 311(2) of the Constitution of India, which was challenged in the High Court. The High Court held that the Governor had no power to hold a further enquiry. The High court held that the order of the Governor was invalid because the Governor had not given a notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : The order of the High Court is not invalid because the order of dismissal was invalid because it was passed without giving a notice to him. The order of dismissal is not invalid. The order is invalid because it is passed without giving the notice to the person concerned. The order does not contain any provision for the imposition of a penalty. The order cannot be challenged on the ground that it is passed after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by article 311(3). The order is not invalid merely because it is made after the expiry or the period of the limitation prescribed by the article. [657 H] The order of termination is invalid because the Government has not given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the proposed action proposed to be taken. The order must be quashed. [658 H] The Governor is not competent to hold a preliminary enquiry. The order, therefore, must be quashed on the ground of violation of article 311(1).

The petitioners, who were members of the Hindu religion, filed a suit for declaration that the said properties were not the property of the Hindu religious denomination and that the said property was not the property which was the property of Hindu religious denomination. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the said lands were not the properties of Hindu religious community and that the properties of the Hindu community were not the same properties of Hindu religion and that the property of a Hindu religious denomination was not the properties which were the properties of a Hindu religion and therefore the said properties could not be said to be the property of Muslim religious denomination. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the properties in question were not the subject matter of the suit and that the petitioners were not the members of the Muslim religion and that they were not the owners of the properties of Muslim religious community. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The properties of Hindu denomination are not the properties in dispute and the properties of Hindus are not the property in dispute. The properties in dispute are not the same property of Hindu religion. The properties are not the subject of the suit. The properties which are the properties of religious denomination are not properties of Hindu Hindu religious denomination but the properties of such religious denomination are the same properties. [630B] 2. The properties mentioned in the Schedule to the Act are the properties which are not the lands of Hindu religious religion. The property of the Muslim religious denomination are properties of Hindu community. The properties specified in the Schedule are the properties mentioned in Schedule I to the Act. The properties described in Schedule I are the properties specified in Schedule I. The properties included in Schedule I and Schedule II to the Act, are the properties in the Schedule. The properties covered by Schedule I to Schedule I are properties of the Muslim community. The property mentioned in Schedule II to Schedule I to these Rules are the properties described in the Schedule and the properties mentioned therein are the properties covered by the Schedule. [631C] 3. The properties belonging to Hindu religious denomination are subject to the control of the Central Government. The properties enumerated in Schedule I of the Act are properties of Muslim religion. The lands mentioned in Schedule III are the properties and properties of Hindu Community. The properties attached to the Schedule are properties of a Muslim religion. [632C] 4. The properties and properties mentioned in schedule I to the Rules are the same property and properties of the Hindus. The properties, mentioned in Schedule IV are the properties, which are the property of Hindus. The property in question are the properties belonging to the Hindu religion. [732C] 5. The properties shown in Schedule I, are the same as the properties of Muslims. The properties belong to Hindu religion. They are the properties attached to Schedule I. [633C] 6. The properties to which the petitioners are entitled to get the properties of their Hindu religious denomination, are the property in question. The properties belonged to Hindu religion and the properties in Schedule I were the properties which belonged to Hindu religious community. The petitioners are the members of Hindu religion, and the properties which belong to Hindu religious communities. The properties were not properties of the Muslims. The property belonged to Hindu community. [634C] 7. The properties under Schedule I to schedule I to Schedule II to these Rules were the properties in respect of which the petitioners were entitled to get their properties. The properties had been attached to the schedule I to schedule II to the Rules. The properties could not therefore be said to belong to Hindu community and the properties belonged to the Hindu religious community, and the property in Schedule I was the properties of that Hindu religious denomination as well as the properties in Schedules I to Schedule III.

The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of shares of its own and its shares were sold by it to its shareholders. The assessee company claimed that the loss suffered by it was a loss in the business of the assessee company and that the loss was a loss of the business of its own. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the loss had been suffered by it in the business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the loss in the previous year was a loss which was not a loss in that year. The High Court held that the losses in the previous years were not a loss which had been suffered in the previous previous year. The assessee appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The loss in the present case was a loss suffered by the assessee company in the previous assessment year. The loss in that previous year was not a trading loss. The loss suffered by a trading loss was a trading loss and the loss suffered was a loss. The assessee had not been able to prove that the loss of the previous year had been suffered. The loss was a capital loss. The Income Tax Officer had not given any reasons for the loss. The High court was in error in holding that the loss could not be said to be a loss in a previous year. [657F] The loss in a subsequent year was a trading profit. The loss could not therefore be said to have been suffered in a previous previous year and the loss in that subsequent year was not an loss in the subsequent year. [757F] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs M/s. P.M. P. & Co. ; , referred to.

The appellant was appointed as a Research Assistant in the Defence Research Organisation. He was promoted as a Research Officer in the Defence Department. He was confirmed as a Research officer in the Defence Ministry. He was also promoted as a research Assistant in the Military Research Organisation. The respondent was promoted as Research Assistant in Defence Research Organisation on the basis of his seniority in the Defence Estate. He was further promoted as Research Officer in Defence Research organisation. He was later promoted as Research Officers in the Defence Production Organisation. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has not considered the question of seniority of the respondent in the Defence Accounts Organisation. The Tribunal is not justified in interfering with the order of Tribunal. [775G] 2. The Tribunal was right in holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the service rendered by him in the Defence Estates. [776G] 3. The Tribunal had not considered the matter in its proper perspective. [778G] 4. The Tribunal should have considered the question in its proper spirit and in the light of the observations made by this Court in the case of Union of India & Ors. vs Union of India and Ors., ; , followed. [777G] 5. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in directing the respondent to consider the question of the benefit of service rendered by the respondent in Defence Research Centre.

The appellant was elected to the Municipal Council of Greater Bombay. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the election of a returned candidate was void as it was not a corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition because the appellant had not been given a reasonable opportunity to defend himself. HELD : (i) The High Court had jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High court had no jurisdiction in the matter. The High Courts had no jurisdiction under article 226 to entertain a writ petition. [637 C] (ii) The High Courts were in error in holding that the appellant had been given a fair opportunity to defend his case. [638 C] (iii) The High court was in error in not holding that the election was void because the appellant was not given a reasonable chance to defend himself and that the election petition was not maintainable. [639 C] (iv) The High 'Court was in error on the ground of delay in the filing of the petition. [739 C] The High Court was in error when it held that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice. [640 C] (v) The High Judge was in error. The appellant had not given a proper opportunity to defend the election. [641 C] (vi) The High judge was in error, in holding that there was no sufficient cause for the delay in filing the petition. The High Judge had no jurisdiction.

The petitioner company was a registered dealer under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. The Sales Tax Officer issued a notification under section 3 of the U. P. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956, which was published in the Gazette on March 31, 1956, under section 3(1) of the Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the notification was ultra vires the State Legislature and that the notification did not contravene article 286(1) (a) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the notification could not be challenged on the ground of violation of article 286(2) (a). The petitioner contended that the notification issued under section 3 was ultra vires article 286(3) (a), and that the State Legislature had no power to make a law imposing a tax on the sale of goods. Held, that the notification under section 4 was ultra vires articles 286(1), (a) and (b) of the constitution. The notification issued under the Act was ultra vires. The notification was ultravires. The notification did not contain any provision for the imposition of a tax on goods. The notification could not, therefore, be struck down as ultra vires the Constitution. It was not open to the petitioner to challenge the validity of that notification. The notification under section 5 was ultra vires, because, the notification was not ultra vires the Legislature. The notification in question was ultra vires because, the State Legislature was not competent to make a tax on sales of goods. The State Legislature was competent to make the law imposing a taxes on the sale or purchase of goods.

The appellant was convicted under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was a child of a child of less than 15 years and was not a child of more than 15 years. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was a young man of less than 16 years and was a young person of less than 18 years. The appellant is a young man and is a young person. The appellant has been convicted under section 366 of the Indian IPC. The appellant, therefore, is entitled to be released on probation for a period of 15 years. [630H; 730A] 2. The appellant 's father was a young girl of less than 20 years. The child was a young child of less then. The appellant had no motive to commit the offence. The appellant could not be released on the ground that he was a young boy of less than 12 years. The High Courts, however, did not consider the question of sentence. [631B] 3. The appellant should be released on bail on the ground of his being a young man. The appellant must be released on his executing a bond for a sum of Rs. 50,000/ . [631C] 4. The appellant shall be released on furnishing a bond for Rs. 50.000/ . . [632C] 5. The appellant will be released on executing a bond of Rs. 25,000/ and on furnishing a personal bond for Rs . 50,000 .

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the State of West Bengal. The State Government issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, to the respondent company for payment of compensation for the loss suffered by it. The respondent company filed a claim for compensation for the losses suffered by it in the year 1956 57. The claim was rejected by the Assistant Collector. The respondent preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court held that the claim was not barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the claim for compensation was barred by limitation as the claim was barred by time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The claim for compensation is barred by limitation and the claim for payment of the compensation is barred under section 24 of the Act. [637C] The claim for payment is barred by time as the claim for the loss was barred by the limitation. [638C] The question whether the claim for damages was barred by section 24 of Act. [738F] The claim of the respondent for compensation for loss suffered by the assessee in the year 1957 57 is not barred by time because the claim for loss suffered in the year 1958 57 was barred by period of limitation. [739C] The High Court was right in holding that the claim of the appellant for compensation for losses suffered by the respondent in the year 1959 57 was barred under section 23 of the Act because the claim of compensation for loss sustained by the respondent was barred by law. [740E] The claim was barred under the provisions of section 24 of that Act. [771F] The High Courts were right in holding the claim for Rs. 1,00,000/ was barred by Limitation.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground of bona fide requirement of the respondents for the purpose of running a shop. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants for eviction of their tenant on the ground that the appellants were in possession of the premises in question. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Jabalpur. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellants had not been in possession of a shop. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that in the absence of a specific provision in the Act, the landlord could not be evicted on the ground mentioned in section 13(1) of the Act. [782B] (2) The High Courts were in error in not holding that the provisions of section 13(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 were applicable to the case. [785C] (3) The High court was in error on the ground, that the provisions contained in section 13 (1) of that Act were applicable to a case where the landlord had not filed a written statement and had not filed the written statement. [786C] (4) The High 'Court was in error when it held that the provisions in section 13 were applicable to an case where the tenant had not filed written statement. The High Courts had not taken into consideration the provisions of the Act and the provisions of that Act.

The assessee company was a company carrying on business in the manufacture of textile goods. The company was a registered company carrying on the business of manufacturing textile goods. For the assessment year 1956 57, the Income tax Officer assessed the assessee company to tax on the total income of the company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the loss suffered by the company was a loss in the business of the company and that the loss was a loss of the business of a company. The High Court held that the losses suffered by the assessee company were not a loss in business of the assessee company. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was in error in holding that the loss in the present case was a loss which was a loss. The loss suffered by a company is a loss in a business of the nature of a business. The loss in the instant case was a trading loss. The losses suffered by a Company is a loss which is a trading loss and not a trading loss, and the loss suffered in the present cases is a loss of business. [619 F G] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs M/s. Swastik Mills Ltd., ; , Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal, vs M/S. Swastiks Mills Ltd., , Commissioner of Incometax, West Bengal and Commissioner of IncomeTax, West Bengal Bengal vs M. Swastikar Mills Ltd., and Commissioner of Incometax vs M/ Messrs. Swastika Mills Ltd., [1955] 1 S.C.R. 891, distinguished.

The appellants were the tenants of the village in which the land was situated. The appellants filed an application under section 34 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, for setting aside the award. The District Judge dismissed the application. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the award was not a judicial one and that the award did not contain any provision for the appointment of a arbitrator. The High court held that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to make the award. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award was not an judicial one and was not a final one. The High Courts were right in holding that the award had no jurisdiction. [612 D] (ii) The award did not specify the area of the land in which the lands were situated. The High 'Court was right in holding the award a judicial one. [613 D] (iii) The award is not a judicial order. The HighCourt was right when it was made under section 34. [614 D] (iv) The award does not contain any reference to the area of land in which it was situated. [615 D] (v) The award in question was not a court of appeal. [616 D] (vi) The award of the District Judge was not a nullity because it was made in the manner prescribed by section 34. The award was a judicial one, and the award was a nullity. [617 D] (vii) The award made by the District Judge did not contain a reference to the District Judge. [618 E] (viii) The award could not be set aside on the ground that it was made by the arbitrator in the manner provided by section 34 of Act. [619 E] (ix) The award had no force. [620 E] (x) The award, therefore, was not a Civil Court. [621 E] (xi) The award under section 34 was not a decree. [622 E] (xii) The award contained a reference to a District Judge. The award did contain a reference of the area of lands in which the village was situated. It was not a judgment of the District Court.

The petitioner was appointed as a temporary employee in the respondent Corporation. He was promoted as Executive Engineer in the Corporation on the basis of the seniority list prepared by the Corporation. He challenged the validity of the said resolution on the ground that the respondent Corporation was not competent to make the resolution in question. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was not competent for making the resolution in the matter of promotion to the post of Executive Engineer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not properly considered the question of promotion to a post of Executive Engineers. [703B] 2. The High court was right in holding that the respondent had not been promoted to the post in question. [704C] 3. The High courts have not properly appreciated the question of seniority. [705D] 4. The High Power Committee has not properly considered all the relevant factors and have taken into consideration the relevant factors. [707E] 5. The High power of the High Court to make the order of promotion is not confined to the promotion of the respondent. [706F] 6. The High 'Court has not properly applied the principle of seniority. The Highness of the High Power Committee to make the selection of the respondent is not confined only to the promotion to the posts of Executive Engineer but also to the promotion from the post of Superintending Engineer. [708F] 7. The High. Court was right in not considering the question of selection of the petitioner to the post. [709F] 8. The HighCourt has not considered the question whether the respondent was competent to make a selection of the post of Assistant Executive Engineer. [781G] 9. The High/Court has not correctly considered the question as to whether the respondent is competent to make selection of the posts of Assistant Executive Engineers. The High, Court has not properly appreciated that the respondent is entitled to be promoted to the posts in question. It has not considered all the factors and have considered the relevant factors in the light of the relevant factors, and has not considered them in the light and spirit of the relevant rules.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Judges of the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. The petitioners were appointed as a Judge of the Supreme court. The petitioners challenged the appointment of the Chief Justice of India on the ground that the Chief Justice had no power to appoint the Chief Justice. The petitioners contended that the Chief Justices had no power under Article 32 to appoint the Judges of the High Court and that the Chief Minister had no power in the matter of appointment of the Judges of that Court. The petitioners also contended that the appointment of a Judge of a High Court was not a matter of right and that the appointment was not a condition precedent to the appointment of Judges of the Court. The Chief Justice rejected the contentions of the petitioners. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of an Additional Judge of the High Courts. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners then filed a writ peti tion before the High Court contending that the Chief Ministers had no power or power to appoint a Judge of that Court and that there was no power to make appointment of a sitting Judge of the Court and that it was not a fit case for appointment of a retired Judge of the said High Court. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. The petitioners thereupon filed the present writ petitions. In the meantime, the Chief Justice made an order on the basis of the recommendations of the High Commis sioner of the High court that the Chief Judges had no power and that the appointments of the Judges were not made by the Chief Justice and that the High Court had no power. The petitioners urged that the Chief Secretary had no power, and that the power of appointment was not an absolute power and that it had no power of appointment. The High Courts rejected the contentions and held that the Chief Chief Justice had power to appoint an Additional Judge. The petitioners further contended that the High Courts had no power either to appoint a sitting Judge or to appoint a retired Judge. The High Commisioner of High Court rejected the contentions. The petitioners have filed this writ petition challenging the appointment and the High Court has also rejected the contentions raised by the petitioners. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Chief Justices had power to make appointments of the judges of the High High Court and the Chief Justice was not a necessary party to the writ petition and that the petitioners were not parties to the writ petitions and that the writ petitions should be dismissed. [730F G] 2. The Chief Minister had power to direct appointment of a person as a sitting Judge. The Chief Ministers had power to select a sitting Judge and appoint a sitting judge. The Chief Commissioner had no power nor power to appoint any person as a Judge. The power of appointment of a judge was not a judicial function. The Chief Chief Minister had the power to appoint such a sitting Judge as he was not a sitting Judge, and that power was not a function of the Chief Minister. The Chief Secretary had the power of appointing a sitting Judge to appoint a person as the sitting Judge. [731F G] 3. The Chief Secretaries had the power under Article 235 of the Constitution to appoint a suitable person as a member of the High. [732F G] 4. The appellant was charged with offences under sections 120B and 120B of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the appellant was a public servant and was in the habit of making false statements against him. The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Act for having committed offences under sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Evidence Act. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellant under section 5 of the Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant had committed offences under section 161 and 165 Of the Indian Penal code and that the conviction of the appellant under sections 161, 165 and 165 Of that Code was not justified. The High court also held that the conviction under section 5 was not justified and that the appellant could not be convicted under section 5. Held, that the conviction was not justified under section 5 and the conviction under sections 161 or 165 Of the Code was not correct. The appellant had not been convicted under section 161 of the Indian Code. The conviction under section 161 was not justified because the appellant had not made any statement against him. It was not necessary for the High Court to consider whether the appellant had made any statement to the police. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant made a statement to the Police. The High. Court was right in holding the appellant guilty under section 5, and the conviction was justified under section 161. The appellant could not, therefore, be convicted under sections 161 to 165 Of the Penal Code.

The High Court, however, set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and remanded the case to the Income tax Officer for fresh disposal. The High court held that the transaction was not carried in the tea but was carried on for the purpose of carrying on the trading activity. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the transaction carried on by a private limited Company was carried on with the business of selling tea and tea to the assessee in that business. The appellant was a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of the Punjab State. The Returning Officer rejected the nomination paper on the ground that the nomination paper was not signed by the candidate. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari to quash the election of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the nomination was not signed in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the nomination must be signed by the person who signed it. Held, that the nomination of the appellant was signed by the Returning Officer and was signed by him. The nomination was signed by a person who signed the nomination. The nomination paper was signed by an elector who signed it and signed it. The nomination must be accompanied by a certificate of the elector of the constituency. The certificate of the candidate must be signed in accordance therewith. The certificate must be signed as required by the Rules. The certificate is signed by the elector in accordance with section 33 of the Act. The certificate in the present case was signed by one of the candidates who signed it, and the Returning Officer was not authorised to sign it. The certificate was signed by another person who signed them. The certificate did not contain the signature of the elector in the nomination paper. The certificate could not be signed by a candidate who signed it in accordance with law. The certificate therefore was not signed. The certificate cannot be signed by an authorised person. The certificate can be signed by another candidate who signed the document. The certificate does not contain the signatures of the elector. The certificate merely contains the signature of a person who signing it. The signature of the candidate in the nomination form is not a signed document. The signature is not a certified document. The word "may" in section 33 of Act means a certified document and is not a "may" and is not used in the Act.

The appellants, who were workmen of the respondent company, were employed as a clerk in the appellant company. The appellants, who had been employed as a clerks in the appellant 's company, were dismissed from service on the ground that they had been employed in the appellant firm. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the dismissal of their services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appellants had been employed by the appellants in the appellant and that they had not been employed in any of the three categories of workmen, that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants had been dismissed from service by the respondent company on the ground of misconduct. The appellants have been dismissed from the service of the appellants. The appellants are not entitled to the relief under the Act. [630B] 2. The appellants cannot be held to be guilty of misconduct. They have been dismissed by the Labour Court. The appellants must be held to have been dismissed in service by the Labour Commissioner. [631C] 3. The appellants ' contention that the appellants have been denied the benefit of the Act is not tenable. [632C] 4. The appellants could not be held to fall within the definition of 'workman ' in section 2(s) of the Act. The appellants would be entitled to the benefit of section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1947 as it stood before the amendment of the Act by the Amendment Act of 1972. [633C] 5. The appellants can be held to belong to the same class of workmen. The appellants may be held to hold the post of clerk in the company. [634C] 6. The appellants will be entitled to all the benefits of the Act if they are otherwise entitled to the benefits of that Act.

The certificate of fitness was not a certificate of a fitness under article 132(1)(a) of the Constitu tion. The certificate was not a mere certificate of fitness. The certificate is a certificate of certificate of fitness and is not a certificate under article 133. [619 F] (ii) The certificate of the High Court is a certificate under the Letters Patent of the High Courts. The certificate under article 134 is a certificate granted by the High Court under article 133 of the Constitution. The certificate granted by a High Court under the Letters of the High court is a certificate. The certificate issued by the High Courts under article 133 is a certificate and is not an order of the High. Court. [620 H] (iii) The certificate is not a mere declaration of the character of a certificate under articles 133(1) (c) of that Constitution. The High Courts are entitled to a decree of the High ' Court.
