Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of compulsory retiring the appellant from service is violative of Article 16 of the Constitu tion. The order is not violative of Article 311 of the Constitution as it is in violation of Article 14. [630B] 2. The order passed by the compulsorily retiring the appel lant is violative of Articles 16 and 16 of Part III of the Constitution, and is violative of article 14. [730C] 3. The order has to be read in the light of the provisions of the Rules and the Rules. The order cannot be read in isolation. The order does not contain any provision for the compulsory retirement of the appellant. The order can be read in conjunction with the Rules. [731C] 4. The order under challenge is violative of articles 14 and 16. [732C] 5. The order impugned is violative of the Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as the order of the compulsorily retiring retiring the appellant is not violative in the Articles. [733F] 6. The order was passed by the President of India under Rule 8 of the Rules. There is no provision for compulsory retirement of a Government servant on attaining the age of superannuation. The order could not be read in a manner which is inconsistent with the Rules and is violative Of Article 14. The order did not contain any provisions for compulsory retirement.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1945 46. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the assessment order, held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that there was no provision in the Act for the computation of the profits of the assessee for the assessment years 1945 46 and 1945 46. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the profits of a registered firm were not liable to be included in the profits of that registered firm. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the profits were liable to be excluded in computing the profits of an unregistered firm. The profits of a business carried on by the assessee were not liable for the assessment for the assessment of the assessee under section 10(1) of the Act. [455C] (2) The profits of an assessee were liable to tax under section 10 of the Act, and the profits of such business carried on were not liable under section 10. [456D] (3) The profits were liable for the tax under section 9 of the Act and the profits were not liable in respect of the profits. [457F] (4) The profits in the present case were not liable as the profits were assessable under section 10, and the losses were not liable. [458F] (5) The profits for the assessment period 1945 46 and 1946 46 were not liable, as the profits of business carried on in the business were not liable on the basis that the profits in the business carried on for the assessment periods 1945 46 and 1944 46 were not assessable under section 9. [466F] (6) The profits which were liable to income tax under section 8 were not liable only under section 10 but also under section 10 and the profits in that business were liable to assessment under section 10 for the assessment assessment year 1945 47. [459F] (7) The profits made by the assessee in the present cases were not liable merely because the profits were assessed under section 10 in respect of that business. [460F] (8) The profits, in the present ease, were liable to the tax under the Act. The profits were not assessable in respect of those profits. [416F] (9) The profits arising from the business were liable for assessment under section 9 for the assessment under section 8 for the assessment to the extent of the profits which were assessed under the Act, but were liable to pay tax under section 11. [446F] (10) The profits and gains of the business were assessable under the Act for assessment under the Act and not under section 10 because the profits in question were liable to a tax under section 7. [447F] (11) The profits under the Act were liable to taxable under section 10 as they were assessable under that Act. [416G] (12) The profits could not be included in computing the income of the assessee in respect of which the profits were chargeable under the Act in respect of a business. [416E] (12 ) The profits of the business carried by the assessee could not be said to be assessable under section 8 because the profits of each business carried on on by the asses see were not liable ' to be included under section 10 unless they were actually assessed under section 9, and the income of each business was assessable under section 11 for the assessment.

The notification has no application to the facts of the case. The notification does not contain any provision for exemption from the levy of sales tax. The notification also does not contain the provision for exemption. [781D] (f) The notification was issued in the years 1983 and 1983. The appellant firm was a Hindu undivided family. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the firm to tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer, however, held that the income of a Hindu undivided firm was not liable to tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and that the income was liable to tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court, on appeal, held that section 10(1) of the Act was not applicable to the case. The High court, however, set aside the order of assessment and remanded the case to the Income Tax Officer for fresh disposal. The Income Appellate Tribunal, however, did not pass any order under section 10 of the Act. The High 'Court, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Income Tax officer was not competent to pass any order of assessment under section 10. The Income ' Appellate Tribunal was not competent in the case of a Hindu Undivided Family. The High, Court was right in holding that the income from the firm was liable to be assessed under section 10, because, the income from a Hindu undivided Family was not liable for tax under the Act. [657 D] (2) The Income tax officer was not justified in passing the order of reassessment under section 10 because, the Income Tax officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order of re assessment under section 11. [658 G] (3) The High Court was right, in holding that section 10 of Act was applicable to the cases of a Hindu joint family. [659 G] (4) The High court was right in not interfering with the order of a Appellate Assistant Commissioner under section 10 and the High Court was in error in holding that it was not open to the Income tax Officer to pass the orders of assessment under the Act, and that it was open to the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner to pass the same order under section 11, because, it was open for the Income tax officer to pass the said order under section10. [660 G] (5) The High Courts were right in holding the order of an Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the High Courts were in error in not holding that the order of Income Tax Officer was not justified. [655 G] (6) The High 'Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that the income in question was liable to income tax under the Income Tax Act.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the adopted son of the respondent. The appellant, a member of the joint family, was a member of a joint family. The respondent, who was the adopted adopted son of a Hindu undivided, filed a suit for partition of the joint properties of the appellant and the appellant was the adopted daughter of the respondent and the appellant claimed that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the suit had been barred by limitation and that the suit should be dismissed. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the suit must be dismissed. Section 4 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1950, which provides that the Court shall have jurisdiction to try the suit. Section 5 of the Madras Act, which provides for the jurisdiction of the Court to try the suits, is a self contained code and does not provide for the jurisdiction to try suits. The provisions of the Act are not intended to be exhaustive of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. The provisions in the Act are intended to be in addition to the provisions of section 5 of the Act. The provisions contained in the Act do not provide for any provision for the jurisdiction which the Court has to try. The provisions are intended to provide for the procedure of the suit. It is not intended to provide a machinery for the procedure to be adopted in the suit. There is no provision in the Act which provides for a procedure to be followed in the suit to be followed by the Court. The provisions do not provide any machinery for the jurisdiction. The provisions relating to the jurisdiction of a Court are intended to give a machinery for determining the jurisdiction of an Court to try suits and to give a proper and fair trial to the parties. The provisions which are intended to confer jurisdiction on the Court to entertain suits are intended to serve the purpose of the Act and the provisions of sections 5 and 6 of the Act do so are intended to have a limited purpose. The provisions, therefore, do not provide a machinery to be adopted by the Court in the suit and the provisions relating to jurisdiction of the court to try the case. The provisions for the jurisdiction are intended to operate in the suit in order to avoid unnecessary delay in the disposal of the suit and to avoid unnecessary litigation. The provisions regarding jurisdiction of the courts are intended to achieve the purpose of section 5(3) of the Act, and the provisions in the Code of Criminal Procedure are intended to save unnecessary litigation.

The appellant, a public limited company, was granted a lease of a plot of land for a period of five years from the date of the application. [798F] 1.(a) The High Court should have exercised its jurisdiction in dealing with the question of breach of the principles. [799F] (b) The High Courts should have exercised their jurisdiction in dealing the question of infringement of the principles, if any, of natural justice or of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court. Court should have acted in a manner not in accordance with the principles of Natural Justice. [772F] (ii) The High Committee should have taken into consideration the relevant factors and should have exercised due care and caution. [703F] (iv) The High High Court should not have interfered with the order passed by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under article 226 of the constitution. The appellant was a factory in Bombay. The factory was situated in Bombay. It was used for the purpose of the factory. The factory had been used for the manufacture of salt. The appellant company was a registered company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The company had a factory at Calcutta. The appellant was appointed as a Sales Tax Officer in the Tamil Nadu State. He was promoted as Sales Tax Officer on the basis of a confidential report. The petitioners were convicted for offences under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The petitioners challenged the order of the High Court in a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition under Article 32 of the Constitution and that the High Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to try the petition under article 32 of the constitution. The High court has no jurisdiction to deal with the petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. [775G] 2. The High courts have no jurisdiction in respect of the petition under Articles 226 and 227. [776G] 3. The High power under Article 32 is not a matter of course. The High jurisdiction is not a mere formality. It is a matter of discretion and is not a substitute for the exercise of the power. It is not a judicial function. It is only a matter of choice. It is the duty of the High Courts to deal with petitions under Article 32. [778G] 4. The High Power under Article 32 has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection and caution. The power is not a part of the power but a part of it. It is an essential part of the process of the court to deal with cases under the provisions of the Code. [777G] 5. The power of the High court to deal in cases under the Code is not a discretionary power. The power to deal with applications under Article 32 must be exercised sparingly, with circumspection and circumspection. [785G] 6. The power under Article 226 is not a power of the court but a discretionary power and it is not a discretion of the court. The power must be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily. [786G] 7. The power conferred on the High Court under Article 32 cannot be exercised arbitrarily. [771G] 8. The power given to the High Court to deal with a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is not a function of the court and is not an absolute power. The High 's power under Article 136 is not a statutory power. [787G] 9. The power can be exercised sparingly with circumspection and that too in the interest of justice.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that the appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute and that the respondent was not a tenant of land in dispute. The notices in question were not within three years from the date of the notice. The notices under section 8 could not be served within the prescribed period. The notices of the petitioners were within time. There was no reason why the petitioners could not be evicted. Held, further, that the notices were within time and were not barred by limitation. The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The assessee company was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. HELD: (i) The profits of the assessee company were taxable under that head. The profits of a business were taxable under this head. The business of the assesses was not taxable under section 10(1)(xiv) of the Income tax Act. [408 D] (ii) The profits in the present case were taxable under any head of business. The profits were taxable in the hands of the assessee and the profits of that business were taxable. [409 D] (iii) The profits were not assessable under the head head of business but were taxable under item No. 2(1) of the First Schedule to the Act. [416 D] (iv) The profits which the assessee company had to pay to the assessee were not taxable in the sense that the profits had been taxable under the said head. [410 D] (v) The profits could not, therefore, be taxed under that head because the profits were received by the assessee. [412 D] (vi) The profits received by the assesses were taxable under items 2(1), 2(1A) and 2(1). [412 E] (vii) The profits arising from the business of the assessees were taxable under Item No. 2 (1) of Schedule to the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1952. [413 E] (viii) The profits made by the assessee were liable to be taxed under item No 2 (1). [416 D E] (ix) The profits earned by the assessee in the course and business of the business of selling sugar were taxable under sub item (1) (xv) of section 2(2) of the said Act. [414 D] (x) The profits, if any, received by the assessees in the course, were taxable under clause (xv) and the profits received by them in the course were taxable under those clauses. [414 E] (xi) The profits and gains of the business, if any received by the asses see were taxable under these clauses. [414 E] (xii) The profits or gains of the assessee 's business were taxable in that sense. [415 E] (xiii) The profits derived by the assessee from the business were taxable as they were received by it in the course. [417 E] (xiv) The profits from the business could not be said to be taxable under the terms of the agreement between the assessee and its partners. [419 E] (xv) The profits are taxable under the aforesaid head. [414 G] (xv). The profits and losses of the assessee are taxable under section 4(1)(xi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922.

The plaintiff, a Hindu, was the owner of a land in the suit lands. The defendants, who were the owners of the lands, claimed that the lands were not the lands of the defendants and that the defendants had not been able to prove that the lands had been granted to the plaintiff. The defendants contended that the lands in question were not the properties of the defendants, and that the lands of defendants were not the property of the defendants. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that the lands granted to the defendants were not 'land ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bengal Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, and that they were not the land of the defendants as defined in the Act. The High court also held that the defendants were entitled to the benefit of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The defendants were entitled only to the benefit under the Act. They were entitled to a decree for possession of the lands. The High Courts were right in holding that the defendants did not prove that the defendants ' lands were 'land '. The High courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the defendants could not prove that they were 'land owners '. The defendants had not proved that they were the lands of a Hindu, and that their lands were 'lands '. The plaintiff had not proved the existence of the lands of which they were 'lands. The defendants were not entitled to the protection under the Act, and the defendants were, therefore, entitled to the relief under the Act in respect of the lands granted by them. [632 C] (ii) The defendants had proved the existence and the existence of a title to the lands. They had not proved their existence. The defendants could not be able to prove the existence of title to the land. The defendants did not adduce any evidence to show that they were in possession of the land. They had proved the fact that the defendants, in their written statement, admitted that they were tenants of the lands in dispute. The defendants ' plea was that they were owners of the land and that they had not proved them. The defendants relied on the evidence of the defendants that they were lessees of the lands and that they did not prove the existence. The HighCourt was right in holding the defendants ' plea. [633 C] (iii) The defendants ' contention that the lands which were granted to the plaintiffs were 'land holders ' was not accepted. The defendants also relied on the presumption that they were lands of a public nature and that they could not prove the fact that they were granted the benefit of section 2 (1) of Act. [634 C] (iv) The defendants did prove the existence and existence of title in the lands. [635 C] (v) The defendants could prove the existence or existence of title. The defendants failed to prove the fact of the existence of any title. The High, Court was right in coming this conclusion. [636 C] (vi) The defendants failed in proving the existence of an title. The plaintiff was entitled to the benefits of section 2 of Act. The defendants must prove the existence, existence and existence. The plaintiff must prove the fact. The defendants have failed to prove that they had been in possession of lands in dispute and that they are not 'land owners.

The appellant was the owner of a agricultural land in Bombay. The land was purchased by the respondent from the appellant. The appellant was the tenant of the land. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the appellant was the landlord of the land and that the suit was barred by section 14 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit had been barred by section 15 of the Act. The High Court held that the suit having been barred by the provisions of section 14 of that Act, the suit was not barred by section 29 of the Act and that the plaintiff was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The High court held that the plaintiff had not been a tenant of the agricultural land and that he was not entitled under section 29 of that Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit being barred by section 30 of the Act, the plaintiff was entitled to the reliefs claimed by him under section 29 and that the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was barred under section 29. The suit having been filed by the plaintiff, the civil court was competent to entertain the civil suit. [637E] 2. The civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit. The civil courts have jurisdiction to entertain such a suit. It is not open to the civil court to entertain a civil suit. The jurisdiction of the civil court is not limited to the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. [638E] 3. The civil Court has jurisdiction to try a suit. In the instant case, the civil Court has no jurisdiction to try the suit. The Civil Court has jurisdiction. The civil jurisdiction is not limited. The civil Courts have jurisdiction to try such a suit, and the civil court has no jurisdiction. [639E] 4. The civil suit is not barred by the principle of res judicata. The civil and revenue court has jurisdiction.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of steel products. The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business as a result of which the assessee company was manufacturing steel products. For the assessment year 1959 60, the assessee company claimed exemption under section 10(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee company had a manufacturing plant and that the business was not a business within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the business carried on by the assessee company in the manufacture and sale of steel products was not a commercial activity within the meaning Of section 2(h) of the Indian Income Tax Act. The High Court, however, held that the activity carried on by it was a business within section 2(k) of the 1922 Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the business of the assessee was a business carried on in the manufacture or sale of steel product and that the activity was a business in the nature of a business carried by it. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The business carried on was a business of the company and the business carried by the assessee was not a trading activity within the definition of business in section 2(s) of the 1961 Act. [775B] 2. The business of the appellant company was a business carrying on the business of manufacturing steel products and the business was carried on in that business. The business was carried out in the manufacture, sale and sale of the steel products. It was not a trade carried on by its employees. The business did not carry on the business. The activity carried on in it was a trading activity. The business could not be carried on by a company. [776B] 3. The business in the business carried out by it was not a manufacturing activity. The activity was carried on by an employee in the manufacture. The business consisted of a business carrying the business of manufacture and sale. The business is carried on by him in the manufacture in the manufacture for sale. The activity is carried on in a business carried out in a business. The assessee is a trading activity and the business is carried out in that business and the business carries on the business in the same business. The profits of the business carried in by the assessee are not profits and gains of the business. [778C] 4. The business carrying on business is carried in the same manner as the business carried forward by the assessee. The business carries on business in different parts of the country. The business carry on the same business and the profits of the assessee are profits and gains. [777C] 5. The business which carried on by them is carried on with the business of selling steel products. In the instant case, the business carried upon by the assessee is carried on on by the business carried carried on by by the assessee in the manufacture by the assessee and the business carrying on of the business is carrying on the same activity. The profits and gains are not profits or gains of the assessee. [785D] 6. The business does not carry on business in any other manner. The business cannot be carried on in any other way. [786F] 7. The business can be carried on only in the same way as the business is being carried on by another person. The business may be carried on with another person. [787F] 8. The business must be carried on on in the same or different manner as the one carried on by each other. [790F] 9. The business should be carried on for the purpose of carrying on the trade.

The appellants were the descendants of the temple. They were granted a lease of the lands in dispute. The appellants were granted a permanent lease of the land in dispute. They were entitled to the grant of permanent lease. The appellants filed a suit for the declaration that the appellants were entitled to a permanent lease. They also claimed that the appellants had no right to the grant. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellants ' suit was barred by section 14(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950. The High court held that the suit was barred under section 14(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants were entitled only to the grant and not to the grant, and not to grant permanent lease. [657 F] (ii) The appellants had no title to the grant in dispute. In the present case, the appellants were not entitled to the permanent lease. There was no evidence to show that the appellants was entitled to the temporary lease. The grant was not a permanent lease and the grant was a permanent lease, and the grant did not amount to a permanent grant. The grant did not relate to the grant but to the grant which was a permanent grant, and the appellants were, therefore, entitled to the benefit of section 14(3). [657 G] (iii) The grant was a temporary lease. [757 G] The grant was for a permanent lease but was a permanent one. The grant could not be said to be a permanent lease because it was a permanent right. The grant of permanent leases was a permanent and temporary lease. It was not a temporary lease but a permanent lease which was a temporary one. The appellants had not been able to prove that the grant was permanent. [658 G] (iv) The grant did relate to the permanent grant. [659 G] (v) The grant could be said to have been permanent. The grant in dispute was a permanent or temporary lease. There could be no doubt that the grant did relate only to permanent grant. But the grant was for permanent or temporary purposes. The grant, therefore, was a permanent.

The appellant Municipal Corporation of Indore, was assessed to tax under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1950, on the basis of the assessment list prepared by the Municipal Corporation. The appellant Municipal Corporation levied a tax on the basis that the assessment list was prepared by the Municipality under the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1951, and that the assessment was prepared by a Municipal Corporation under the Madhya Madhya Bharat Municipalities (Amendment) Act, 1954, and that it was not necessary to assess the tax on the ground that the assessment lists were prepared by the municipality under the Madhya Raj Adhiniyam, 1952, and that they were not prepared by the municipal Corporation under the Act. The appellant Corporation filed a suit for a declaration that the assessment of the tax was illegal and ultra vires the provisions of the Act. It was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the assessment made by the Municipal Commissioner under the Madhya M. P. Municipalities Act, 1952, was illegal and void as it was not passed by the Municipal Committee under the Madhya Gwalior Municipal Act, 1952. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the assessment in question was illegal and invalid as it was passed by the municipal council under the Madhya V. P. Municipal Corporation Act, 1952 and that the tax was not payable by the Municipal Council under the Madhya P. Municipalities (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1952; and that the levy of the tax on buildings was not valid. The High court held that the tax levied by the Municipal Board under the Madhya Act was illegal and the tax was liable to be assessed under the Madhya Municipalities Act, but that the tax could not be assessed under section 3(1) of the Act, and that, therefore, the assessment of tax was illegal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the tax imposed by the Municipal Act, 1951 was illegal and that the imposition of the tax by the Municipal Corpora tion was not valid because the tax was levied by the municipal corporation under the Madhya. Act. [408 C D] The High Court had rightly held that the levy was illegal and not ultra vires the Act. [508 C] The levy of tax by the municipal corporations under the Madhya, Act was valid. [509 D] The levy was not valid as it was made by the municipal board under the Madhya law. The levy was therefore valid.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The assessee company sold its sugar to the assessee company. The assessee sold its sugar in the year of account. The assessee was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. The sale was made in the year in which the sale was made. The assessee paid the price of the sugar to the company. The price of the goods was fixed at Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee claimed that the price of sugar sold by the assessee was not the price of its sugar sold by it. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The High Court held that the price paid by the assessee to the company was not the sale price of the assessee. The High court held that the sale price was the price of a sugar sold by a company and that the sale was not the result of sale. The High, Court held that there was no sale price of sugar. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sale price of a commodity sold by a Company is the price of which the sale price is the price. The sale price is not the price at which the sale is made. The sale is not the sale of the commodity sold by the company. It is the price at the sale price. The price at which it is sold is the price which the sale proceeds are sold. The sale proceeds are the price at that sale. The sale of the goods sold by the Company is the sale price at which sale proceeds are to be sold. The price is the sale proceeds. The sale in the present case was the sale price and the sale proceeds were the sale proceeds of the goods. The sale, therefore, was not the sales price. [808 D E] (ii) The sale of sugar sold in the present year was the sale proceeds and the sale price in the present cases was the sale of sugar. [809 G H] (iii) The sale proceeds were sold by the sale of a commodity and the sale was the sale sale proceeds.
